"IMPROPER EARMING."—In a case tried at the County Court, Faringdon, lately, the owner had occupied the farm (about 80 acres) up to his death, and it -was continued by his trustees, until let to Mr. Akerman, an amateur farmer, in 1880. On his entry of the 20 acres of arable land he finds the previous crops to have been five acres of wheat, ten acres of barley, and five acres roots. His crops per acre he tells me in 1881 were 24 bush, of wheat, 30 of barley; in 1882, 24 bush, of wheat, 30 of barley, and 36 of beans; and in 1883, 36 bush, of wheat, 40 of beans, and 36 of barley. TO THE SNOWDROPS. Ye graceful flowers, whose drooping heads Bend bashful o'er their snowy beds. Ye come as heralds of the Spring. And what a host of dreams ye bring— Dreams of warm, bright and sunny hours, A world of fragrance and of flowers; Of almost endless Summer days, Spent in the pleasant woodland ways, Where no harsh sound of strife pervades The calm that fills the silent glades •, Of songs from feathered songsters throats, And the sad cuckoo's mellow notes ; Of happy hours spent by the brooks, With no companion but my books ; Of say, when hawthorn blossom blows, And Jane, that brings the sweet wild rose, The bonniest flower that ever grew, Or drank the cool refreshing dew ; Of haytime, when each verdant field 41A1 Its rich and fragrant crop will yield, To soon be gathered by the aid Of sunburnt youth and buxom maid, Whose laughter cheers the fleeting hours, As leaves are brightened by cool showers. p Then comes the thought of Autumn time, When nature revels in her prime, •i And all the waving corn-fields show The colour of the sun's bright glow, 'Tempting the owner of the soil To reap the fruits of all his toil, While his glad heLart swells with delight, Each time he gazes en the sight. And harvest o'er, his days be spent Through Winter in well-earned content. - These are the radiant dreams ye bring, Pale heralds of the coming Spring. . +--Leeds 3fercury Weekly.

COTTAGE GARDENING The best-looking cm) in the garden at p%esem The shoal:a Cabbage. In most instances the plants a-A% forward and fairly even in size. Where vacancies 17.43% been made by they be Ailed up slags or any other cause, without needless delay from the reserve bed. If such a provision has not been made, we woul.a tate lap an outer row to make good the others. The groluld thus gained would be suitable for a row of Broad ileana,which should be sown as soon as the state of ice ground will permit. We find that soil which will produce good Cabbage will also grow good Broad Beans. The drill for the Beans may be drawn within a foot of the Cabbage, for they will be ready for cutting, or rather pulling, before the Beans require the space. The depth of drill should be about 41n., and the seeds deposited in a single row, 2in. to 3in. distant, or, in a double row, with 4in. between each seed. For this mode of sowing the drills should be made rather wider at the bottom, which may be done by drawing the soil to each side. For our earliest variety we select Early Mazagan or Early Long Pod. If, in previous years, mice have been accustomed to attack the seeds, we would advise that the red lead preiltntative be adopted, the same as we described for Peas last week. PARSHIPS.—Every gardener admits that these cannot be I sown too early. This is an advantage, because it admits of proceeding with some of the important operations of the garden at an early period of the season. So soon as we can catch the surface of the soil sufficiently dry, we shall give it a forking preparatory to drawing the drills. We anticipate there will be considerable trouble this season , in getting the land into a suitable state to receive the small I seed crops. The soil will be lumpy, and will involve much labour in breaking, but if they can be caught at a certain stage of dryness, they separate much more readily. THE Facuir GARDEN.—Roses trained against the dwelling or fences should now be pruned, and though some of the varieties may be identical with those cultivated as standards or dwarfs, their pruning mast be executed in quite a differ- ent way. We allude more especially to the hybrid per- petuals, the most vigorous of which are selected for the purpose of covering bare walls. Here one of the objects in view is to cover as much space as possible in the shortest time; so we only thin out the weakest shoots by removing' them entirely. The moderate growth is shortened one-half, whilst the very strongest are reduced one-third. The Ayr- shire Roses require very little more than thinning, so that their shoots may be about 41n. to din. distant. If the lower portion of the space intended to be covered is too naked, some of the long shoots may be bent with an easy curve so as to direct them towards that part. Most roses have this natural tendency of getting naked below, so mach so that we have found it imperative to remove some of the main branches, and in some cases cut the plants within a foot or two from the base, and have a fresh start. But with an occasional removal of a main branch, and the shortening of others, there will be no need to have recourse to these drastic measures. That general favourite tea rose—Glorie de Dijon —requires pruning similar to the Ayrshire roses, and the shoots that project outwards may be cut within three or four eyes of the base. This rose, under favourable circum- stances, will make shoots in one season 12ft. long, from which side shoots proceed, carrying one or more flowers. At one time these strong shoots used to be cat away as greedy feeders, but experience has taught us that they are the ones to leave, and that those which looked naked and hungry should be moved to make room for them.—Clematis: Some of these have made sufficient growth to require tying, which may be done to either string or wire. They should not be allowed to becomeentangled, for it is a most difficult matter to undo them without breaking. THE WINDOW.—The fern case may now be planted. The arrangement of the plants should be made a matter of con- sideration. Those that are likely to grow the tallest should be placed where they can have the most room to develops, and where they will not interfere with the welfare of their weaker neighbours. All the plants are best in a small state, as more fresh soil can in that case be introduced round them; and, with ordinary care it will be seen that they will thrive and soon fill their allotted space. Old plants, though small, that have been starved by standing in their pots too long, should be rejected in favour of young thriving plants. A few pieces of Lycopodium planted here and there will soon make a green carpet. The fern case may be converted into a nursery for raising seedling ferns, and it would be difficult to conceive any contrivance more suitable. Its atmosphere, when judiciously regulated, is most conducive to the germination of the spores or seeds of ferns, and when soft stone is used they will actually grow for a time on the stone itself. By introducing a mixture of fine peaty soil and chopped moss in proximity to them their roots speedily find it, and when established in it they can be moved and potted in small pots, which may be left in the fern cases. That is just what we have frequently accomplished when these self-sown seedlings have appeared in spots where they could not long exist, and where an attempt to remove them would be a perilous proceeding to the existence of the baby fern. Any quantity of young ferns may be raised by filling a garden pan three parts with stones broken to the size of a walnut and less, filling all the cavities with peaty soil and sand. Bog earth or turf may do for any hardy sorts after it has been exposed to the weather, but the exotic kinds must have that supplied by nurserymen, adding one-sixth of silver sand. The fronds of any fern or ferns from which it is desired to raise seedlings, should be placed on the sur- face of the soil spores downwards, or the fronds may be shook over it. The pan must be covered with a bell glass or a flat piece of glass. No water must be given overhead, but the pan mast be immersed to the rim till the whole is soaked.

THE MAYOR ON RELIGIOUS 4 The annual congregational tea meeting iribonneetien with the Golborne-street Baptist dhapel, Warrington, was held on Tuesday evening. About 170 persons sat down to an ex- cellent tea in the schoolroom, the tables being presided at by the following ladies :—Mrs Bamford, Mrs Baxter, Mrs Crowder, Mrs Dodd, Miss Dunn, Mrs Few, Mrs Fieldhorase, Mrs Gough, Mrs Hall, Miss Jeffrey, Mrs Lee, andl,drs Long- shaw. The subsequent proceedings were held in the chapel, and his worship the Mayor (Alderman J Harrison) occupied the chair. There were also present the Rev E Moore (resi- dent minister), the Rev W Pilling, of Hill Cliffe, W P Lockhart, Esq, of Liverpool, and Mr Bate, of Tarporley. The meeting was opened with singing and prayer. The MAYOR then addressed the meeting. He said he could assure them that if it was pleasing to them that he should be there that night it was very pleasing to him in- deed to be present—(applause)—for two reasons. First, he thought it was becoming and befitting to the person holding the office of Mayor to identify himself with objects of that kind—(hear, hear)—and in the second place, because he was one of those who took a so.newhat broad view of their religious duties, and he could only wish that people of all different religious persuasions were in the habit of more frequently mixing together and identifying themselves with:each other's objects, showing sympathy and kindness for each other. He was satisfied that if they did so, great good would come from it. (Applause.) On the previous Saturday he met a friend who said to him, "so I see you are going to take the chair at the Baptist tea meet- ing ?" and he (the Mayor) replied,' Yes, I think I am. If all be well Ido intend to do so." His friend added, "I am surprised at it." " For why ?" be (the Mayor) asked. "Well, you know you area Churchman." He (the Mayor) replied, "Yes, I am a Churchman, and I am a member of the Church of England, and rejoice that I am a member, but I am satisfied 1 shall be no less a member of the Church of England because I happen to go and preside at a Baptist tea party. SCIENTIFIC NOTES, A BMW:Man Exritantztrr.—An interesting experiment Is to be made by Dr. Zintgraff, who, in company with Dr. Cheyenne, is about to visit the Congo and the interior of Africa. He takes with him a phonograph wherewith to fix the speech and melodies of hitherto unknown tribes, which, thus received by the instrument, will be forwarded to scien- tific men in Germany. The apparatus (which will be used for such a purpose for the first time) has been made by Mr. Fuhrmann, of Berlin, and exactly corresponds with one he has in that city, so that the plates used in Africa can be sent to Berlin to be unrolled by that machine and caused to re- emit the sounds received. THE ORIGIN OF THE WORD "ARGOSY."—We take the I following from the Athencum :—For part 2 of the "New English Dictionary," Dr. Murray has been assisted by Mr. Arthur J. Evans,the well-known author of "Through Bosnia and the Herzegovina," in an historical investigation of the alleged derivation of the word argosy from Ragusa. The result is to completely establish the point, and to show that an argosy, also in 16th century argusea, and ragusye was simply una Ragusea (nave). Ragusa itself appears in 16th century English as Aragoase, Aragosa, whence the natural substitution of argusea for ragusea, without any reference to the ship Argo. The merchant Cossacks of Ragusa (Its. guess) were famous for their size and rich cargoes, and well known in England. CROSBY HALL.—The Rev. T. Ellison Gibson, author of " Lydiate Hall and its Associations," has received permis- sion from Colonel Blundell, of Crosby Hall, Lancashire, to print such portions of the family documents as may b. found useful or interesting. He has already edited from these sources "A Cavalier's Note-book," and has now pre- pared for the press selections from the diary of Nicholas Blundell, Egg, extending from the year 1702 to 1728. This diary covers a period singnlatly barren of authentic records, and notices of Liverpool are not infrequent. He was pre- sent at the opening of the earliest dock, and gives the name of the first vessel which entered it. This dock, with St. Peter's Church and the Bluecoat Hospital, both then newly erected, were the chief objects of attraction to the squire's visitors—a curious contrast to the miles of shipping, nu- merous churches, and handsome public buildings that now adorn that city.

The RANGE OF VisroN.—As some readers may not readily credit the possibility of seeing to so considerable a distance, I may mention that a few days previous to the ascent of this mountain, when upon the summit of Hare Island (1,800 feet), about sixty miles to the west, at mid- night, I recognised in the north the mountain near riper- nivik called Sanderson's Hope, and to the south-east the mountains at the extreme southern end of the Waigat Strait—the former being 150 miles and the latter above 110 miles distant from me. This, with one exception, is the greatest distance at which I have recognised objects during mountain expeditions, the one exceptioa being the Pacific Ocean seen from a height of 18,000 feet on China- borazo.—" Explorations in Greenland," by E. Whymper, in " Good Words." PrLoarmAoss TO JERUSALEM.—From an early period in the history of the Christian world, it had been usual for the devout to make pilgrimages to Jerusalem and the surround- ing country; but when Palestine was taken by the Saracens, this could be done only by favour of the conquerors. The earlier Mohammedans, however, were men who combined a certain amount of tolerance with their fanaticism, and who did not forget that, in the opinion of their own lawgiver, Jesus was one of the line of Prophets, and indeed, the greatest, with the exception of Mohammed himself. They accordingly allowed the Christians to build a church and a hospital in Jerusalem, and to visit that city in vast num- bers. As the power of the Church increased, ihe habit of seeking the holy soil of Jadtea became more widely diffused, and every European country tarnished its devotees. Those who had committed great crimes believed that a paint al journey to Jerusalem would expiate their guilt; others went there out of a genuine sense of piety; while some, perhaps, simply followed a prevailing fashion. When a man had , determined to perform this journey, his pastor delivered to him a long walking-staff and bound him with a girdle to which a leathern scrip was attached. His pilgrim dress consisted of a long garment of coarse woollen, for all osten- tation was forbidden to both rich and poor. On his return, he brought with him a branch of the sacred palm-tree of Jerusalem, which he suspended over the altar of his church, as a proof that his vow had been accomplished. Religious thanksgivings and popular rejoicings followed; and the palmar, as he was called, was thenceforward revered, fts hadjz is revered in all Mohammedan countries.—" Cassell'. WAVEHLEY ABBEY.—The Abbey had been wrecked and despoiled, when visited by Aubrey 200 years since, though he described some parts as being in fair condition, and made special mention of "roundels of painted glass" that still remained in some of the windows; but so often were the hewn stones carried away to build walls, &c., in the neigh- bourhood, that there remains scarcely a vestige of the noble Abbey church, 320 feet long, with its tower and transepts, its many chapels and altars, that possibly vied in grandeur of architecture with Netley or Furness. Of this or a sub• sequent church, in which no fewer than eight bishops have assisted at an imposing ceremony, naught remains but some buttresses and a portion of the outer walls. A mouldering sun-dial, on whose pedestal are carved a couple of bats with outspread wings, stands on what is supposed to be the site of the high altar; and embedded in the tort one comes sud- denly upon a coffin of Purbeck marble that is said to mark the whilom entrance to the choir. Where beneath that emerald sward was the burial-place of the fathers no one seems to know, and of their courts and cloisters, their in- firmaries and their chapter-house, a few broken walls and decaying windows are all that meet the eye.—Cassell's Family Magazine. WHAT IS WORLDLINESS.—There was nothing wrong in the plenteous harvests and the enlarged barns of the pros- perous farmer, but he became a worldly man because these were his all in all. He had neglected that being of his which was made in the image of God, and which ought to have had its life in the spiritual rather than in the.material and temporary. His wealth held him in possession, and he was mastered by the very things of which he foolishly I thought himself the master. A similar spirit of worldli- ness may exist in the poorest as well as the richest. The labourer whose interests are centred on the question of weekly wagea May in this manner be as worldly as the mil- lionaire who spends his existence over his ledgers. It is the like principle which converts the possibly pure gratifica- tion of our social instincts into worldliness. When society with its petty ambitions, its gossip, its trivialities engrosses the mind, SO that in the World of fashion men and women becoaie mere things carried on by the stream, and accept- ing the tone and mannerisms of the hour, without Obedience to the claims of God or of His love—then are they em- phatically "worldly people." And not otherwise is it with that subtle worldliness which so often mingles with the false pietism which affects to be separate from the world. When there is no sincere outgoing of the being towards what is simply just, loving, and dutiful, but when the in- terests of the little or great sect are allowed '-laquestioning iitiprinacy, and conventionalism onteralse their tyranny, and ambition, vanity, re petty intrigues find shelter under the sacred names of Church or Creed, then have we what in unconscious satire is sometimes termed "the religious r,cOrld.—Good Words." THE DUES OF WELLINGTON AT WArnaLoo.—At every moment and at every place the Duke exposed himself with a freedom which made all around him tremble for that life on which it was obvious that the fate of the battle de- pended. There was scarcely a square but he visited in per- son, encouraging the men by his presence and the offieers by his directions. While thus engaged, several guns were levelled against him, distinguished as he was by his staff and the movements of the officers who were passing to and fro with orders. The balls repeatedly grazed a tree near him, when he coolly observed, That's good practice." Riding up to a regiment in front of the line, an,cl even then expecting a formidable charge of cavalry, he said, "Stand fast, my lads; we must not be beaten. What will they say in England ?" On another occasion, when many of the best and bravest had fallen, and the event of the battle seemed doubtful, he said, with the coolness of a spectator, "Never mind, we'll win this battle yet." To another regiment, then closely engaged, he used a common sporting expression, ".Herd pounding, this, gentlemen; let us see who will pound longest." One general officer found himself under the neces- sity of stating to the Duke that his brigade was reduced to one-third of its numbers, and that those who remained were 80 outhunted through hard fighting that a temporary relief, of however short duration, seemed a measure of necessity. "Tell him," said the Duke, "what he proposes is impossible. He, I, and every Englishman in the field must die on the spot we now occupy. "It is enough," returned the general, "I and every man under my command are determined to share his fate."—Christian CuLtono-rmen COUGH LOZENGES, a medicated linseed ex- tra t. They were rather short, elevation of fallen humanity. God had saved them not in his estimation, of intell'gence. There was another on every hand, and to redeem the many thousands who I distinguished ornament of the Conservative party—his were perishing, living in heathen darkness, even`at their j Grace the Dake of Richmond. He was a noble, a gentle- very doors. d He said a great deal had been said about' the ! manly, and a courteous man; and the speaker could not say poor Of London, and thought as much might be said of the anything offensive towards him. He made no complaint poor of Warrington if the truth was only against him, but be did complain against the system that known. It was for every church to become allowed him and his heirs to receive so largely of the State's as it were a tower of holiness—a refuge money as was the case. A certain duke happened to be a and defence for the outcast perishing •Ireatures round about descendant of that grand, most loving, and reverend Charles ' them. There were a vast number of social evil, that needed H. There was a distinguished French lady who WU In the '

service of Louis of France—all the trouble was between Louis and William of England—and she had been sent as a of spy to the court of Charles. She made love to him, and he (the lecturer) sapposed Charles made love back, for .me was very generous in his liberality in that respect— (laughter)—and the consequence was that this lady bore some children, and one was styled the Duke of Richmond— of course. They got large tracts of land given them—he supposed the nation had no need of it then—and if they would copy the Parliamentary papers they would see that the amount of money that had been drawn by the various Dukes of Richmond would exceed, at compound interest, Italf the national debt. The duke of to-day was in receipt pf a pension of £l9OOO a year, and that pension had been manipulated in such a manner that Parliament to-day had really no control over it. The last duke was so rich that he left five daughters for the nation to provide for, and they had to have £2OO a piece from the State coffers, which, be said, was not fair. There was another point. There was reason to believe that the mistresses of this merry monarch (Charles II.) were as liberal as Charles himself, and therefore there was every reason to be- lieve that the nation was not only paying for the progeny which his Gracious Majesty had brought into life, but for the progeny which he had not brought into life. (Laughter and applause.) There was the Duke of Grafton. It wail said on good authority that the Duke of Richmond and the Duke of Grafton together had drawn more money from the IState than would pay off the whole national debt of the country if put out at compound interest. They did not want these men to be deprived of all their money, but they wished to prevent the pensions running on for ever. They did not object to men who rendered the State some service being fairly remunerated, but they did object to its being continued something like it was described in Macbeth,. "to the crack of doom." (Applause.) The "Iron Duke performed great services for this country, but he received a large amount of money for them, and many poor fellows who ran the same risks did not get above 6d. or 7d. a day, and some nothing at all. If it was meet to provide for those who led an army, surely it was meet to provide for the rank and file? Nelson was paid something like £90,000 for his ser7ices, but he paid the last penalty in Trafalgar Bay. His sisters received £20,000 apiece, and why should that be when they had husbands to look after them. (AP' planes.) But there was something funnier than this. It would take all their genealogical knowledge to make out that the present holder of the title of Earl Nelson was a lineal descendant in the male line. He was not a descendant A all; he was not related to the Admiral in a direct male line, although he was in the female line. That gentleman got a pension of £5,000 a year, and £5.475 was the average rent-roll of the property. Not only that, but he got nearly all the £1,500 which was left to tbe late admiral's widovrr which was a very strange thing. If they wanted a man to live long give him a pension, for pensioned people nevef seemed to die. Take William Brougham. He had been having £3,500 a year for a long while, and he did not seem inclined to die yet. ffehad drawn about £lOO,OOO, and be was likely to go on drawing, but if he lived no longer than his brother he would die at ninety. He (th 3 lecturer) could point to a score of cases where members of the law whose places were done away with, and there did not seem to be others for them to fill; they al ways seemed to have a way of pensioning these men. Al an instance of this system, Mr. Bannister men- tioned that a case had come under his notice where man who received £7OO a year as salary, when pensioned exceeded £714 a year. They wanted to give pensions on some system. During the Crimean war a rich relative of an aristocratic General who had no administrative power, the Duke of Beaufort, received from the nation £2,000 a year, whilst one soldier in the Crimea, who held out Kars for so long a time, one of the bravest incidents in the war, Frederiala Williams, only got £l,OOO. Most of them would remember the Indian mutiny. If ever there was a grand man and a true soldier, not only of hie country, but of Christ, it was Air Henry Havelock% (Applause.) lie succurabed to the hardships that he bad endured, and the country, wisely, la his mind, left his widow with £l,OOO and the son got it no When Lord Napier went out to Magdala with those Abyssinian mules—(laughter)—the Government gave him £2,000 and sent him to a snug berth of £5,000 a year at the rock of Gibralt<r. Sir Henry Hardinge w55-* lucky man. He did some little service, but they would have to rake out some musty fa;es to tell what it was.. and be got £3,000 a year. Re (the lecturer) wanted then; to consider this question in all its bearings. (Hear, hear.) They wanted England to be ruled not only wisely and well, but as cheap as they could They did not want to be pan+ monious, but there waa plenty of -scope for economy, and he was sorry that they had not more men of the stamp 01 the hon. member for Burnley, who would look after this. Night after night in the House of Commons they passed estimates for the war, admiralty, and other things. without scarcely giving any consideration to them. The estinstateg should be thoroughly looked into. They had neglected this matter too long, and were beginning now to do something to reduce the national expenditure. That was their object in holding those meetings, for the Tories would never move in the matter, and if they ever intended have a reduction they would have to appeal to the Liberal party to do it. The Liberal party- weril going to extend, or rather assimilate, the franchise in 11i8 county to that of boroughs. He had rather have universal residential suffrage, but it was a question of what HAY , could get. It behoved them then to return men to Parlia- ment who would carry out their views, and also to Strengthen the hands of the Government at the present time. They had in their present member for Warrington, Mr. McMinnies—(applanss)—an efficient representative, a man who would look after their interests as well as any men they would be able to bring to the front, and he trusted ;that when the next general election arrived they would be able to give a good account of themsolyes, and that they would send Sir Gilbert, Gireenall back again. If they did that there Was no doubt that they would largely contribute to bring about that epoch In our country's history which they all wanted to try to make it, brighter, better, and more virtuous in the future. If they did that England would bah a "chancel° be what she bad long professed to be; 0, Tire home of the happy, the great and the free,"—tho glorimasly free. (Continued applause.) WHITHAM said that they had certainly listened to a most interesting lecture, given in a most interesting fashion, Though their friend had made them laugh sometimes, they must remember that the thing itself was not a laughable question. They ,in Warrimaton had read pretty well on the subject, and were prepared to support anyone who was pre• pared to go to the front and do away with the pension list • Redid not exactly Wish to cease as a people to give pen- Mons,but thought it was only desireable that pensions should be given to those who devoted their lives to the State, 11° that they should have something to provide for their old age. If they were to look at the Reform Alma flack they would find plenty of cases such al that mentioned by the lecturer where a Von' sioner whose salary had been £7OO a year, received £714. They would find that there were a large number of civil servants who, like Othello, had "found their occupation gone," and these men had been pensioned in the prime of their life. As working men they might work until the very last day of their lives, but there would be no pension for them. Speaking on the subject of the in- significance of the pensions of private soldiers, he said that he thought it was the greatest pity that there should be soldiers at all, aid that the money some of them received was simply a bribo to carry countries into war. Some of these men were in the army, not because they were patriots but because it was a profession for •them; a way of getting a living and being Wooed on the pension list. He looked upon it as a piece of gross swindling and robbery that the big soldiers should receive such large pensions and the others such small ones. They cared nothing about the country, and were like leeches sucking for all they could get. They should make their opinions on this point strongly felt. whether they were Liberals or Tories, for anything that concerned a working man's life was a question for him to Consider. He concluded by moving a vote of thanks to Use lecturer.

The Rear. J. YoNGE seconded. The subject of the le' ture, be said, applied ptrticularly to workingmen, of which the audience WAS largely composed. and he did not thiuk one-tenth of them knew as much before as they had heard that night. They bad had a vague opinion that a large amount of money bad been expended in this way, but the/ had not the facts that Mr. Bannister had given them, and for which their thanks were due to him. Ile thought that the fair spirit in which the lecturer had dealt with his sub- ject should commend itself to everyone, tie concluded by speaking of the franchise. The motion was carried, and the LEcrottan, after acknoW" !edging it, proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman. Mr. F. RonanTs seconded, and Mr. U. ROBERTS sur ported, which was carried.

Mr., H. ROBERTS remarked that the last lecture of the series would take the form ef an answer to the speech de- livered some time ago by Mr. Ecroyd on " Fair trade,' question which was exciting considerable interest is the town. He then referred to a correspondence that had been carried on between himself and Mr. Lftwremion. The meeting dispersed at about 9-30.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 15. 1884.

MISCBLLANWIJS. The sculling match bet seen Bubear, of Putney, and Ross, of New Brunswick, which was rowed on the Thames en Monday, resulted in the victory of Ross by twenty lengths. Two miners were on Monday sentenced to death at Edin- burgh for the murder of two gamekeepers on Lord Rose- bery's estate. The prisoners were poaching, and when detected fired shots which inflicted fatal wounds upon the

keet;erTs—.. At a meeting held in Paris on Monday, attended by 300 shareholders of the lleZ Canal, it was decided unanimously to urge the board of management to postpone the further •COnsideration of the convention of M. de Lesseps with the 'English shipowners, and to appoint a committee to propose

niw scheme. Alfred Herbert Allen, collector of poor rates for the town- ship of Salford, has absconded, and it is believed that he has 'embezzled about £lOOO of the ratepayers' money. In a letter he has sent to the Assistant Overseer for the parish Allen Mates that he has gone to Spain. A warrant has been issued for his apprehmsion. According to the North German Gazette, Prince Henry, of Prussia, and Count Muenster, the German ambassador, were in a room at Paddington station exactly over the spot of the intended explosion of dynamite at the very moment when the portmanteau containing an infernal machine was dis- covered in the parcel office. A Wigan letter carrier named Fawcett was dangerously shot on Saturday through the accidental discharge of a revolver which a comrade named Lucas bad "presented" at him in fun. The weapon had been temporarily entrusted by another man to the care of Lucas, who does not appear to have been aware that it was loaded. A coroner's inquest was concluded at J3atterknowle,-on Saturday, on the body of Sergeant Smith, of the Durham county police, who was attacked on the night of February 23 by Joseph Lowson, William Tiddle, and Joseph Hodgan, Miners, who are in custody. OPERATIONS IN THE SOUDAN. THE MAHDI DEFIANT. The reply of the hostile Sheikhs to General Gordon's proclamation requesting their submission is a long, rambling, and defiant document, and amoanta to a refasal to surrender. Osman Digma announces his intention to "drink the blood of the Turks" and those who aid them, and says that with the sword of the Mandi he will strengthen the religion of Islam. In.a letter to the Sheikh El Morghani, Osman charges him with being more Christian than Mahometan, and advises him to endeavour to convert his English friends to the Mahometan faith. There is con- siderable doubt as to what Osman's action will be. He is said to have visited Sinkat to obtain recruits, and also to have informed his followers that in any coming battle he will watch them afar off, and invoke Allah and the Prophet to give them victory. Firing was heard on Tuesday at Baker's Zereba, the point to which an advance had beers made by a portion of General Graham's force on Monday, and all the troops forming the expedition that is to operate against Osman Digma were suddenly marched to the front, Generals Graham and. Stewart and the staff accompanying them. Whether this movement was hastened by the sound of firing is uncertain. It had been stated that the whole body would advance on Tuesday evening, and the forward march may thus have been intended all along; but it is possible that Osman may have decided upon delivering an attack instead of waiting General Graham's arrival before his stronghold. Recently, Osman's force has been spoken of as numbering about 2,000; now it is said that the chiefs who have signed his defiant proclamation command 10,000 fighting men, and that 8,000 are ready to give the English battle. General Graham, with his whole force, further advanced on Wednesday afternoon to a point about four miles beyond Baker's,zeteba, and immediately in front of Osman Digna's damp. fle encountered no opposition, though the enemy, to the number of five or six thousand, could be seen in front, and small bands were scattered round about. In this advanced position the troops bivouacked for the night, and the battle, if Osman Digna still held his ground, was ex- pected at an early hour on Thursday. The British force is composed of the same troops as were engaged at Teb, with the addition of a number of Marines, and for the defence of Sitakim Admiral Hewett has landed a force of seamen from the fleet. - While General Graham is dealing with Osman Digna, General Gordon does not appeal' to tend the situation much improving at Khartoum, and is now reported to have ex- pressed a desire for the despatch of a force of British cavalry from Suakim to Berber, so that it might impress the tribes between that place and Khartoum. His opinion is that, though the Mandi is powerless as an active enemy In the field, he is able through his emissaries to stir up the tribes along the Nile as soon as they realise the fact that the country is being abandoned. He cannot blame them for rising, he says, when no definite sign is shown of establish- ing a permanent government at Khartoum, and the with- drawal of refugees towards Berber will convince them that a permanent government is not being established. A British cavalry force patrolling along the Nile would, he thinks, act as a valuable corrective. He is "dead against" the sending of any British expedition to reconquer the Soudan, but he thinks what he suggests would lead to no sacrifice of life, and would prevent General Graham's victories from being wasted. The Porte is by no means satisfied with the course of events in the Soudan, but it has not yet succeeded in con- vincing Lord Granville that the present situation can be discussed with advantage. Lord Dufferin bas presented a Note explaining that England is desirous of respecting the sovereign rights of Turkey, but at present British troops are engaged in protecting threatened Egyptian subjects, and the discussion of the matter had better be postponed until after a normal condition of order and public safety has been restored. As Turkey has no mean!, of interfering, no doubt J.ord Dufferin's suggestion will be acted upon; but in the meantime the Porte is endeavouring to assert its position in other quarters, and especially claims a right to be con- sulted on all matters involving an enlargement of the Suez Canal. GREAT BATTLE. DESCRIPTION OF THE FIGHTING. COMPLETE ROUT OF THE ENEMY. A telegram from Souakim at 10-30 a.m., Thursday, says: Fighting commenced soon after day break. The enemy were completely routed from their rifle pits and entrench- ments by the British infantry, assisted by the fire of the artillery. A later telegram states :—The engagement with Osman Digma lasted half an hour. The British victory was of the most complete character. As far as at present known there were only two killed on the British side. A second edition of the Standard published on Thursday morning contains the following Fraham's Camp, Thurs- day daybreak.—At one o'cleck this morning the enemy , opened fire upon us. Our men were he an instant on the I alert, and ready to repel acharge. Ten minutes went by but no attack came, and the men were then ordered to lie down again in their ranks. All night the fire continued, but without drawing an answering shot from us. All were glad, indeed, when daylight dawned. Our casualties during the night have been one officer and twe men wounded, and one killed. We advance at eight o'clock. The men are in ex- cellent spirits. The Daily Telegraph, in a second edition, time 10-30 a:m., published the following telegram dated Souakirn, Thursday morning :—After a weary night, during which a desultory fire was maintained, the advance commenced full of hope and vigour. There is no doubt as to the result. DESCRIPTION OF THE BATTLE. WITH GRAHAM'S FORCE [VIA SUAKIN], THURSDAY, MID-DAY.—For some hours after our arrival on the camping ground yesterday evening all went quietly. Fires were lighted, and the men ate their dinners. Just before the sun set seine parties of the enemy were seen at a distance of about seven hundred yards, and four rounds of shell were fired at them. The aim was excellent, and the natives dis- persed at once. One man, more plucky than his fellows, crept forward to within five hundred yards, and fired twice at us. The bullets pared closely overhead. As darkness CMS on the fires at the enemy's camp, a mile and a half away, were plainly visible from our position. At eight o'clock the bugle sounded, and an allowance of grog was served out to the soldiers Shortly afterwards, Commander Rolls, RN , went out by himeaff to reconnoitre. It was a meet daring action, as no one could say where the enemy might be lurking among the bushes. He first made his way to the spot where our shell had burst, and found three natives lying dead, giving proof of the accuracy of our gunners' aim. He then went on until close to the enemy's watch fires, and found the Arab pickets asleep around them. He returned at nine o'clock. to camp, and as it was evident from his report that the enemy were not meditating an attack, the men were ordered to lie down and get what sleep they could. At one o'clock a sudden fire opened upon us from a short distance. The troops at once stood to arms, and prepared to repel an attack. The fire continued, but the aim was very bad, the bullets all going overhead. The men behind the slight brushwood fence they had on their arrival thrown up were perfectly steady, and not a single shot was fired in return. All night long the enemy kept up their fire. It was a most unpleasant time, for the bullets swept overhead thickly, and there was nothing to do save to bear it quietly. In the centre of the square were budded together cernels, horses, and mules, and several of these were hit by the bullets. As the men were lying down, the number of casualties were light, being only one man killed and an officer and two men wounded. There was a general feeling of relief when day began to dawn, and the long, anxious hours of watch- ing and expectation came to an end. Sunrise, however, brought no relief from the enemy's fire, which was kept up with increasing strength, the immunity from any return so adding to the boldness of the enemy that parties of them advanced to within three or four hundred yards of us. This was more than we could quietly endure, and a nine-pounder and a Gatliog were brought into play, and after a few rounds the enemy retired. The men then took breakfast, and while so engaged the cavalry arrived from the zereba, at which they had passed the night. Orders were given for the advance to be made at eight o'clock, but before we started the cavalry were sent on ahead with strict injunctions to act as niounted infantry only, and on no account to allow themselves to be enticed into a charge. They seerched the bushes in front of us thoroughly, but only small bodies of the enemy showed themselves, and the opinion that the tribesmen did not mean to fight after all began to prevail. At eight o'clock the infantry formed up outside the zereba. General Davis's brigade was in front. It consisted of the Black Watch, who formed the half of the front and the left of the square; the 65th, who formed the other half of the front and the right side, and the Marines who were on the rear face. The Naval Brigade were in the centre of the squire. General Buller's brigade, also in square , form, were echeloned on the right rear of Davis's brigade. General Graham took up his position in the centre of the leading square. and here I posted myself. As we advanced i we saw the cavalry falling back, and the enemy, evidently n great force, following them. The cavalry cleared off to our left, and we could now see crowds of the enemy over the bush in our front. We halted and formed square, and opened a heavy fire with the Gardner guns and rifles upon the advancing mass of enemy. This checked them for a `short time; but, encouraged by their wild Sheikhs, the Arabs steadied themselves, and again came rapidly on. They heralded their advance with a musketry fire, and the bullets pattered thickly on the sand in the middle of Our square. We on our part also advanced to meet the enemy, and now the eNteak;- points of a square against hinetanfdhe fßolae formation at once bimetal" 'visible. The companies ,4)f of r w tahr Wtahtechremianini'nfgront abut companiesswept lof those regiments, which formed, the, side of the square, and which were also expe3ting attack, did not keep up with the rapid forward movement of the front face and the con- -1 Beqaence was that many gaps appeared in what should have I been a solid wall of men. As the front lite approached the [ foe the men began to cheer, and with fixed bayonets ad- vanced at the double, thereby still further increasing the I gap between them and their companions formthg , the sides, and at this moment immense" hordes of Arabs were seen charging down on the tight face of the square. The front line was halted, and the officers of the companies of the 135. th which frdnterillie fresh foe, now pouring down, made every effort tb cloieettp' the gaps, and steady the men to receive the charge. Tito tune, however, was too short to accomplish this, and the'roll'ing fire which was opened upon the enemy both in front and flank drowned the voices of the officers. With a fierce rush the Ar %)s burst down on our right face. The 651 h wavered and be,;. in to fall back on the Marines and 42nd, opening

great gape in the square. Through the smoke the dark figures could be nee rushing on, us- checked, even for an instatnt, by the hail et butler. and in another minute they were 'upon us, and the tight iketme hand to band. The breaking up of we square by the 'twit of the 65th threw the Marines and the Black Watch also into confusion, and the square no longer existed. The enemy pressed upon the front as well as on the right flank, dashing in upon what was now a confused mass of troops, spearing many and dying themselves on our bayonets or by our bullets. In spite of the efforts of the officers the whole body now began to retreat. The Naval Brigade, surrounded by our awn men, had no time to use their guns, and, as the mass fell back, had to leave these behind them. All this time Butler's Brigade, five hundred yards on our right • rear, were moving forward in perfect order, and advancing to our assistance with the steadiness of troops on a parade ground. In front of them were the guns of the Marine Artillery, and these opened fire upon the e emy, but without checking them. Upon getting back in line with Butler's steady Brigade, and covered by their fire, Davis's Brigade rallied at once, and the men very speedily resumed their formation, and, as if determined to retrieve the disorder into which they had been thrown, they now ad- vanced manfully side by side with Buller's square. So ter- rible was the fire which the united Brigades poured into the enemy that their advance was at length checked, but there was no retreat, for few of the impetuous Arabs who had surged down upon us turned face to the rear, nearly the whole beieg swept away by our fire. On reaching the point where the Arabs had charged down upon the leading Bri- gade, the guns which had been abandoned when Davis's square was broken were recovered. Almost at the same moment, a fresh body of the enemy were seen issuing from a broad, deep, rocky ravine, in which they had been lying concealed, this time in even denser numbers than before. Our troops met the onslaught with the utmost steadiness. It was a repetition of the battle of El Teb, but the charges we sustained were made by larger bodies of men, and were even fiercer and more determined than upon that occasion. Of the brava natives who swarmed down upon us none went back; it was, indeed, death or victory with them. It was pitiful to see how the masses melted away under our fire, leaving a trail of bodies behind them, till the last survivors fell close to our ranks. At length the terrible fire of the breech- loaders prevailed over valour as brilliant and heroic as was ever witnessed, and no fresh assailants appeared from the ravine. We marched forward to its edge. There were numbers still within it, now retreating rapidly, some up the opposite side, others along the bottom. A hot shell and rifle fire scattered them still further, but even now there was no sign of panic in the retreat of these gallant savages, for they halted and fired from time to time with perfect cool- ness. The battle was now virtually over, but even when the fighting had concluded it was dangerous to move about the battle-field, owing to the wounded natives lying thickly among the bushes. These positively refused to accept quarter, and those who were able continued loading and tiring at any who came near them, or thrust with their spears at those who passed by. In the bush, too, were many un- wounded men, who, when they saw an opportunity, leapt to their feet and attacked any soldier or soldiers whe came near. I saw one man charge six Hussars, and, fight so des- perately that he was not despatched without great difficulty. The infantry halted after the ravine was cleared, and the cavalry were ordered to clear the bushes. During the fight they had been echelloned on the left flank, and were about to charge upon the enemy who were assault- ing Davis's retreating Brigade, when the rally of the latter on reiching Buller's square rendered Cavalry action unne- cessary. The naval guns were re-taken within a quarter of an hour from the time they were lost. At half-past ten , General Graham re-formed his troops, preparatory to advanc- ing on the Wells, which are about three miles distant from the battlefield. Parties of the enemy were visible on all points of the horizon, loth, as at El Teb, to depart from the spot where they had maintained such a gallant struggle. 2-0 P.m After a short rest the advance was resumed. The enemy gathered again, and it seemed as if they intended to renew the battle. The troops were halted, and the guns opened upon the distant foe. These attempted to reply with a musketry fire, but the distance was too great. Our gunners made good practice, and we soon had the satisfaction of seeing the hostile groups break up and disperse over the country, the greater part taking to the bills; and ere long a, few scattered bodies of men in rapid retreat were the sole remains of the army with which Osman Digna so confi- dently awaited our attack. The force moved forward to Osman's camp. It eas Lewd to be entirely deserted, and Davis's brigade was marched back to the Zareeba, at which I am now writing, while Boiler's brigade remained to set fire to the camp, and then followed Davis. Scattered groups of the enemy again made their appearance, and fired at long distances at our column, but they carefully abstained from any nearer approach. Our loss in the battle is now ascertained to have been about seventy killed and a hundred wounded. By far the greater part of these casualties occurred in Davis's Brigade. The sailors, who stuck to their guns to the last and tried to drag them off, suffered exceptionally, three of their officers— Montresor, Almack, and Houston-Stewart—being among the killed. I can form no estimate of the losses of the enemy. The ground was thickly strewn with their dead as the united Brigade advanced, and I should say that it must have been considerably larger than it was at El Teb. The:Arabs have proved themselves to be as formidable adversaries as any irregular troops in the world. Their tactics are good. They prepare the way for their charge with a heavy musketry fire; in their advance they take advantage of every bush and cover; but they charge with a reckless valour which may well shake the steadiness of the best troops in the world. The breaking up of Davis's Brigade was partly the result of the advance being made too rapidly and to a momentary forgetfulness of the really dangerous nature of the Arab onslaught. Had the square halted, or moved forward with . the perfect steadiness and regularity which characterised General Butler's Bri- gade, the issue would not have been in doubt even for a second. It is due to the troops to say that they recovered very rapidly from their confusion, and that they afterwards fought with the greatest coolness and courage. The battle certainly showed that even the most perfectly armed troops, when engaged with savages animated alike by native courage and religions fanaticism, must act with the greatest prudence and caution, and that unskilfulness in handling and unsteadiness in movement may possibly bring on a disaster. It may be further said, in excuse for the troops who at the critical moment failed to prove themselves equal to the occasion, that the long sleepless night passed under a heavy fire was extremely trying to the nerves, and would certainly detract seriously from their fighting powers. There is very little difference of opinion as to the fact that it would have been far better had we advanced to the fight from the first Zereeba. The seven mile march in the early morning would not have been excessive, the men would have been spared the sleepless night, and the great and un- deniable risk which we ran from camping se close to the enemy would have been avoided.

SITAILIII, 7-15 P.M. I have just returned from the front. When I left there he entire force were marching into the Zareeba we occupied last night. They will remain there until to-morrow morn- ing, and will then march to the next Zareeba, and the fol- lowing day will arrive here. In Osman's camp Bailer's Brigade found many tents. Is one of them was a wounded woman. She had belonged to the Sinkat garrison, and says that the other women who were taken prisoners with her were all sent to the hills' At Osman's camp no water was found, so the brigade returns to the nullah. Upon my way back I passed over the battle field. From what I saw there I should increase my estimate of the killed to at least three thousand. The Arabs lie in heaps, as the Egyptians did in the square on General Baker's battlefield. Alongside of them are the skeletons of the Black regiment annihilated here three months since, andnow terribly avenged. Great credit is due to the men of No. I Battery for the manner in which they stuck to their guns when the enemy were'rushing down upon them. The pre- parations of the Cavalry to charge also did much to check the natives crowding round Davis's dis- organised square. Osman himself is said to have fled to the hills. A few 'days will develops events, but the Idandi's career in the Eastern Soudan has received its final blow. It is most desirable that we should retain a portion of the force here for a short time. In that case there can be no doubt that most of the Sheikhs will come in and surrender, and now that they can see the futility of his pretensions will bring Osman in with them as a prisoner. They are, of course, unaware of our inability to follow them into the mountains, and will hasten to make their peace. An imme- diate withdrawal of the whole of the troops would greatly minimise the good effects of the ,vigtory. Another correspondent eaye.r--4 Our force, having formed up, advanced in two broad squares, marching in echelon. The leading tictiare. was under the command of Davis. The men were in high spirits and anxious to get at the enemy. They had not long to wait. Shortly after leaving the zereba Davis's square was furiouslr charged by a large body of rebels. It was a terrific onslaught. Many of our men were speared by the Arabs. The naval brigade, which was inside the square, at Once formed up, and the enemy were rapidly repulsed, with great slaughter. The advance was then• resumed, but we had not, proceeded far before we were again assailed by immense hordes, who came rushing down upon both sides of us with the wildest impetuosity. The struggle was terrible, the Arabs fighting with the greatest pluck. Nearly every one of them was killed. They. would neither retire nor give up, but fought to the death. After this struggle was over our force halted on a very steep donga, which had pre- viously afforded cencealment to the enemy. Our losses, owing to the fierceness of the attack upon us, were very heavy. The Naval Brigade, the Black Watch, and the 65th Regiment suffered severely. Three naval lieutenants out of five were killed, namely, Stewart, Montresor, and Alrnack. Our total loss is probably about a hundred killed. The rebels fought with their usual tenacity.

IN P ERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.--.4IONDAY. RUSSIA AIID ENGLAND IN CENTRAL subject of discussion was the acquisition of Mery by mats.:ia• —The Earl of LYTTON, io moving for currespondence tween England aod Russia with regard to Mery and Afghon- istan, said that the Czar's acceptance of allegiance from the people of Mery placed within his power the opportunity of menacing India at any time when European complica- tions arse. The plain duty of the English Gnvernment was to take up such a position, military and diplomatic, as would enable them to view with equanimity the doings of Russia in that part of the world.—After remarks by the Duke of ARGYLL and Lord CRANBROOK, the Earl of KIMBERLEY, replying for the Government, said negotiations were now in progress with Russia on this subject. He felt at liberty to say that a near approach of the two great Powers in Central Asia would necessitate a clear understand- ing between them as to what territories should come under their respective influences. Her Majesty's Government were taking action in their own way, and they desired it to be clearly understood that whilst entertaining no alarm they were prepared to take all necessary measures for making the Indian frontier as strong and unassailable as possible.— Lord NORTHBROOK defended the action of the Government as being clear and consistent throughout.—Lord SALISBURY, warned the Government against Russian aggression, which he contended would not stop at Merv.—Earl GrusviLtz promised to produce such parts of the correspondence as it was judicious to make public.—The motion was then with- drawn, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Mposnax. THE SUEZ CANAL AGREEMINT.—The CHANCELLOR OI the EXCHEQUER informed Mr. W. H. Smith that the Com- mittee of British shipowners who had been in negotiation with M. de Lesseps had no legal powers to enter into any arrangement with the Suel Canal Company which would bind the general body of British shipowners and the British I, Government. THE SINKAT GARRISON.—SeVeTaI questions having been put respecting the position of the wives and families of the , commandant and garrison of Sinkat, Lord E. FITZMAURICB said Admiral Hewett had received instructions to do every- thing in his power for their release.—Lord litarriatorrow did not think it would be possible to lay those instructions on the tale at present. TIIE Loss or LIFE AT SEL.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, ques- tioned by Lord C. HAMILTON, stated the grounds of his pre- diction that unless there was legislation OR the subject there would be an increase in the lass of life at sea. EGYPT AND THE SOUDA.N.—In Committee Of Supply on the supplementary vote for the expenses of the military operations in the Soudan, the debate on Mr. Labouchere's I amendment reducing the vote by a sum of £208,150, was resumed.—Following Lord G. Hamilton, Mr. FORSTER rose for the purpose chiefly of speaking a out the future. It was, be said, impossible to ignore the rumour that General 11 Gordon was to be replaced by Zebehr Pasha. If the Govern- , ment should determine to take that course, he hoped they would not commit the House and the country to it without telling them why they had come to the decision, and giving them an opportunity of expressing their opinion on the sub- ject. It was impossible to imagine a course which at the first blush would be more contrary to all our former policy with regard to the African races. He hoped the Government would do all they could to stop the terrible evil of slavery.— Sir GEORGE ELLforr advocated a temporary protectorate of Egypt, a view also taken by Mr. LAING.—The debate was continued by Sir Eardley Wilmot, Sir Harry Verney, who incidentally mentioned that he had voted in favour of slave trade abolition, in 1834; Mr. Whitley; Sir H. Fletcher, who.took credit for the last Government for the success of the recent military operations in Egypt, seeing, as he said, that they had inaugurated the system of moving troops from India through the Suez Canal; Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett ; Mr. John Morley, who, having last year prophesied that if Egypt was not evacuated forthwith the Soudan would keep us there, now ventured to pr diet that if we held Souakim we should remain in the Soudan; Mr. Sclater- Booth, who traced to Mr. John Morley much of the responsibility of the Government; Mr. McCoan, and Sir Richard Cross.—Lord liaanato-rota, rising shortly be- fore midnight, reviewed the course of the debate. With reference to the particular terms of Mr.Labouchere's amend- ment he announced that he was very far from denying that the question of liquidating the Egyptian Debt was a proper one for consideration. But it would have to be done with great deliberation, in concert with the Powers of Europe, upon a full review of the circumstances of Egypt, and could not be undertaken on a small expenditure like that the House was asked to vote. With respect to the future, he intimated the probability of the Egyptian GoYernment having to make new arrangements for defending the Southern Frontier, and for the settlement in the interior of Egypt of a garrison different from the one originally con- templated. Ile also hinted at a change of opinion as to the fighting capacity of the material of the Egyptian army, a matter on which he said the Government were in communi- cation with Sir Evelyn Wood. Amid cheers from the Con- servatives, he declared that it was of great importance that no European Power should be established on the littoral of the Red Sea. With respect to the proposed appointment of Zebehr Pasha, Lord Hartington said that it had received no countenance from the Government, who had telegraphed for further information to General Gordon. Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE described the policy of the Govern- ment as compelling them to swallow camels because they strained at gnats, with the consequence that they were humiliated as never a Ministry was humiliated.—On the question of the reduction of the vote as moved by Mr. Laboachere, the Conservative party, led in this case by Sir S. Northcote, left the House amid sarcastic cheers.—The amendment was negatived by 178 against 13. The minority was composed of a few Irish members, Mr. Percy Wyndham, and one or two Radicals, including Mr. Richard. About a dozen Conservatives voted with the Government.—The vote was then agreed to. HOUSE OF LORDS—TUESDAY. The most interesting event was the enrolment of Lord Tennyson, who took the oath and his seat with the usual ceremony.—Earl DELAWARE then called attention to the alleged death of a child at a Cheltenham Board School from over pressure in the work of education, but after a short debate. Lord CARLINGFORD explained that a post- mortem examination bad proved that school tasks had no- thing whatever to do with the child's death, and that instead of the Education Act acting prejudicially, the health of children had improved during the last ten years.—Earl GRANVILLE then said he could not promise to introduce an Act dealing with Irish land, in the House of Lords.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.--••TIIESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.--••TIIESDAY.

The Metropolitan Water Bill and the Metropolitan Rail- way (Parks) Bill occupied the House for a considerable time; and both measures having bees read a second time by large majorities, Sir W. Harcourt was asked whether his attention had been called to the evidence given at the inquest at Kirkdale Gaol on Monday as to the condition of the hangman when he reached the prison 2—The HOME SECRITARY replied that he had not received any authentic information on the subject, and that the executioner was under the control of the Sheriff; but if occasion arose, it would be his duty to ask Parliament for power to interfere. As yet, however, he bad no information to show that such occasion had arisen. —The House was counted out at seven minutes past eight o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNZSDAY. The second reading of the Copyhold Enfranchisement Bill was moved by Mr. WAnon, who explained that its ob- ject was to do away with copyholds, which since the time of Charles 11. had been a blot on the land laws of the country.—The rejection of the bill was moved by Mr. ELTON.—The HOME SEcarraßT suggested that the second reading should be taken and an effort made to amend details in committee.--lir. ARNOLD said his principal ob- jection to the bill was that it fixed no precise period in the future at which there should be an absolute extinguishment of copyhold tenure, and he hoped that a definite term would be decided on in committee.—Sir R. CROSS opposed the bill, as he thought it was a cumbrous measure, would lead to disastrous results, and would only benefit the solicitors who would be employed in consequence of the great amount of litigation which it would cause.—Several of the supporters of the bill having suggested that it should be sent to a select committee, the House divided and the bill was read a second time by a large majority, and on the motion of Mr. WAUGH it was referred to a committee.—Two Yorkshire Land Regis- tries Bills were read a second time, and were referred to a select committee.—The second reading of the Commons and Enclosures Acts Amendment Bill was moved by Mr. W. James, and was talked out by Lord FOLKESTONE. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tromsnay. The Laßn CHANCELLOR, answering a question put by the Marquis of Huntly respecting the Orr-Ewing case, said the final court of appeal for both the English and the Scotch courts was the House of Lords. He was not aware of any tendency towards encroachment on the jurisdiction of the Scotch courts, and as regarded the case referred to he thought a little good sense on both sides would make it easy to decide under which jurisdiction the trusts could be most beneficially executed. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TnuRSDAY. The POSTMASTER-GENKRAL informed Mr. Slagg that the question of a revision of letter deliveries to Manchester and balford was under consideration, and the saggestion that there should be a later evening delivery was included in the inquiry.—Sir S. DIonTRCOTE inquired if the Government had received any further information as to the fighting which had just taken place in the Soudan.—The Marqais of HARTINGTON stated that he had received a telegram from General Graham, dated from Osman Dignaa's camp, stating briefly that he had taken the camp after hard fighting, that the killed were over 70, and the wounded about 100. Be had telegraphed to General Graham congratulating him on the success of his engagement and on the conduct of the gallant troops under him; and asking him to report fully On the situation as soon as possible.—Sir W. HAR- COURT, upon being questioned on the subject of crema- tion eaid he should not give any encourage- , men't to the system—first, because he I,elieved it WAS repug- nant to the general sentiment ; and secondly, because he believed the practice would piece obstacles in the way of the detection of crime.—The Marquis of HARTINGTON in- formed the House that it would be extremely undesirable, and in fact impossible, to make a full statement of the in- GfoormveartniomnenretcwenetrleysrteilcleiivnedtelfergormapGhiecnecrnaml mGoonrdicaont.iott with the General.—The House again went into CorrunittaOf Supply on the supplementary estimates for the Civil Set- vice.—ln the course of the discussion the ATTORNEY- GENERAL stated that a scheme was being considered, by

which it was hoped the block in the Chancery Division would be relieved It will be proposed that the Chancery Judges ha no longer seat on Mr. cult, and only one judge will be sent to the smaller circuits. In the course of the eveaing Mr. HEALY made a violent lattack upon the administration of justice in Ireland. rum- olaiuing of the practice pursued by the Attorn,y-Gemnal ni changing the venue in the trial of prisoners for alleged agra:ian crimes, and in challenging Catholics summoned on juries with the view of procuring prejudiced verdicts, and accusing the Chief Secretary of having endeavoured to hang au innocent man and an innocent woman. The member for Monaghan was promptly called to order by the Chairman of Committees', and withdrew his offensive statements, though he afterwards repeated them in a milder form. Several votes were agreed to in Committee of Supply.

div.head: tome:LONI NTELLIGENCE.
div.p: tome:LONI NTELLIGENCE.

The Calcutta Exhibition was closed on Monday by the Marquis of Ripon. The treaty of peace between Chili and Peru has been confirmed by the Peruvian National Assembly. The completion of the Mexican Central Railwa.v, from the Rio Grande River to the city of Mexico, is announced. The works of the New Emma Mine have been demolished by a snowslip at Alta, Utah, and twelve persons have lost their lives.

An explosion of fire damp occurred on Ttursday in a colliery in Virginia, and a correspondent reports that 125 men were killed. It is telegraphed from Ottawa that, the Marquis of I ans. downe having been threatened by Fenians, the guard at Rideau Hall had been doubled. The Smyrna authorities have received instructions from the Porte not to interfere with vessels flying the British flag landing passengers or goods in the Bay of Smyrna. The editors of several Liberal Swedish newspapers are to be tried for high treason. The prosecutions are the result of their outspoken opinion on the King's policy in Nor- wegian affairs. A Berne despatch reports the arrest at Fribourg of two Anarchists, named Otter and Falk. Important disclosures are said to be on the tapis regarding the organisers of the recent Anarchist attempts in 'Vienna and Stuttgard. The accounts of the doings of Fenian and other anarchist conspirators in Paris are declared to have been greatly ex- aggerated. Inspector Moser, of Scotland Yard, has concluded a long and close investigation, which has, it is said, con- ' vinced him that the dynamite outrages in England have not been planned in Paris. A report was published at Durban on Tuesday that fight- ing was still going on in Zululand, and that Usibepu bad been defeated. The Times correspondent at Durban tele- graphed on Wednesday that the Cape elections show one- third Ministerialists, one-third Opposition, and one-third belonging to the Africander party. Fifteen thousand labourers are now said to be employed upon the Panama Canal works, and the progress that is being made is described as satisfactory; but,unfortunately, yellow fever has shown itself at Panama, and some Euro- peans who have recently arrived are leaving. Dr Locker, an English missionary, has fallen a victim to the disease. Prince Napoleon has made another speech on the Revi- sion question. The Prince boasted of his poverty as con- trasted with the wealth of the House of Orleans. He ap- pears to have intimated that his chief possession is "an absolute respect for the sovereignty of the people." Some- thing of the kind was said before the coup d'itat by another Napoleon. It is predicted at Calcutta that in the Budget of the Indian Finance Minister, which is to appear in the Official Ga:ette on Friday, the estimates will show a surplus of about £300,000, which, if the year prove favourable, may be considered equivalent to not less than £BOO,OOO on the accounts. On the whole there is good ground for believing that the Budget will show the position to be a satisfactory one. DISASTERS IN AMERICA : Loss OF FIFTEEN LIVES.—A despatch from St. Louis announces the destruction by fire of the grain elevators situated near that city, and the goods station of the Chicago and Alton Railway, together with 140 trucks, many of which were loaded. The loss is esti- mated at 3500,000. The railway station at Woodstock, Colorado, has been destroyed by an avalanche. Fifteen persons were killed. What appears to have been a clumsy attempt to do per- sonal injury to the Comte de Paris has been discovered by the French police. A bag addressed to the Comte having been left at the Lyons Railway Station by a man who gave a false address, the officials became suspicions, the police were called in, and on the bag being opened it was found that an infernal machine was inside, which was intended to explode on the bag being opened. It is stated in the Indo-Persian newspaper the Schems that the Ameer of Afghanistan has determined, with a view to securing his dominions against invasion from east or north, to fortify in accordance with the exigencies of modern strategy Cabal, Kandahar, and the town of Balkh, on the Amon Dania. The St. Petersburg correspondent of the Standard states, " on unquestionable authority," that it has been decided by the Russian Government to complete their recent acquisitions in Central Asia by formally an- nexing all the territory up to the Amon Dana, which will thus become the frontier line of the Russian Empire.

div.head: CAPTURE OF BAC NINH.
div.p: CAPTURE OF BAC NINH.

The French have captured Bac Ninh, with slight loss. The Chinese found themselves attacked on all sides, aud they fled precipitately. Descriptions of tho attack on Sontay by the French have been published. An English correspondent states that the best troops of the French, the Turcos and the Foreign Legion, were beaten back time after time, and that if the Black Flags—whom he carefully distinguishes from the Chinese militia—had had modern cannon the French could not have taken the place except by a regular siege. The Turcos and the Foreign Legion do not appear to have encumbered themselves with prisoners.
IRELAND.

A NEW THEATRE FOR DUBLIN.—The Lord-Lieutenant of 'lreland on Tuesday granted a patent to Mr. Dillon, who will forthwith erect a handsome new theatre and opera. house in Dublin. Mr. Dillon's application was opposed by Mr. Hann the well-known theatrical manager of Dublin and London. Mr. Justice Lawson, in his charge to the Kerry Grand Jury on Wednesday, said that the result of the administra- tion of justices under the Crimes Act had been a striking diminution of crime, the police reports showing only 150 offences since the last Assizes, as against 240 in the cor- respanding periodof last year. Still facts convinced him that the existing salutary restraints ought not yet to be removed. THE DERRY RIOT. At the Sligo Assizes, Thomas Doherty, the apprentice boy, was brought up before Mr. Justice Murphy for sentence he having been on the pre- vious night found guilty of sentence, a shot out of the London- derry Corporation Hall on the occasion of the visit of Mr. Dawson, M.P., Lord Mayor of Dublin. and wounding one of the Catholic processionists. His lordship sentenced the pri- soner to 18 months' imprisonment. In the trial of Michael Muldowney, at Sligo, on Saturday, . .

for taking part in the murder of Pete;Doherty, in November:. 1881, an extraordinary story was told by an informer named Moran. Muldewney was a member of the Royal Irish Con- stabulary, and had been on special detective duty for nine years, and the informer was a man who had" been dismissed from the Army, so that the disagreement of the jury in this case is less to be wondered at than in some others. But if Moran's tale be a fairly reasonable one, the most remarkable thing about it is the light it throws upon the svetem upon which murders were committed. Not fewer than half a dozen men are described as having actively participated in the commission of the crime, and the arrangements included the provision of a car at a given point to carry away the rides, so that after the man had given up their weapons the most diligent search in the district would be likely to be foiled so long as all the murderers were silent.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. In the absence of Mr. F. H. Gossage, Dr. O'Keeffe pre- sided at the monthly meeting which was held at the Board- room. Alforde Chambers, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present :—Messrs. F. ii. Pankhurst, T. Handley, D. Forster, D. Wright, J. Midwood, B. Dutton, J. Houghton, E. Martley, S. Sadler, J. T. Allen (clerk), Higginson (sur- veyor), and Copeland (resident engineer). The CLERK read a letter from the Council of the AssOZit- tion of Local Boards asking if the Board intended to be represented at the annual meeting of the Association which is to be held in Liverpool, on the 19th instant, to consider the vartcms bills affecting Local Boards, which had been in- troduced into Parliament this Session.—lt was stated that the Chairman of the Board and Mt: Wadley had usually represented the Board, but as M. CEcissage Was away on the Continent a fresh arrangement would be necessary.—Mr, Wawa= moved, and Mr. Msnriaim seconded, that Mr. Handley and Mr. Midwood form the deputation from the Board.—Mr. Durum: What is the subscription to this Association, Mr. Chairman ?—The CLERK: Three guineas. --Mr. Lomax : What have we gained by 47—The CLERK : Information is the object.—Mr. Drirras :We pay a lot for 1 information, it seems to me.—The CLERK observed that the Association had not been doing much lately owing to the illness of their secretary. It was coming to the front again owing to the pressure of Parliamentary business.—The motion was carried. GAS A*llT. The minutes of this committee stated that during the past month Dr. Campbell Brown had analysed samples of the water at Stock's well and Netherley and reported that both samples were excellent for domestic use. The illu- minating power of the gas during the month had averaged ' 1611 candles. The month's accounts amounted to £440 $d for the gas works and £l6l 15s 10d for the water works. The Sewerage Committee had instructed Mr. Copeland to get Mr. Vawser ta inspect and report upon the defective' work put in the No. 1 sewerage contract by Mr. Jeffreys. corotraunication had been received from Mr. Jeffrey's solici- tors mating that the surveyor (Mr. Higgioson) and Mr. Copeland would be included in his action for damages.—On the motion of Mr. Mrwoon, seconded by Mr. MARTLEY, the min-ates were approved. REArall COMMITTEE.. The In:Tates of this committee contained the mdical officer's report for February.. The numbrr of hirtba were 83,and the deaths 44, equal to a birth rate of 37 56 and a death rate of 19 92 oar 1,000. The nuisance inspector reported that s there had been several complaints of the nightsoil con- tractor's neglect. 1 tie Contractor (It. mithson) attended before the committee, and was informed that some of the work was being done on his account and at hie expense. He denied having damaged any of the propeity complained of, and the Inspector WaB instructed to inform, the cont. plainants. It was-recommended that the hospital tents- be, taken down, and thc matron given a month's notioe.l--Mr. Meitruty moved, and Mr. HOUGHTON seconded, the adop- tion of the minutes.—The Clifallallatt said the vaccination returns for the six months ending the 31st July last were an follows :—Number of births registered 525, stacceasfullr vaccinated 431, dead unvaccinated 59, postponed by medical' certificate 15, cannot be found 20; no defaulters. The Chairman remarked that this return showed a very satisfac- tory state of affairs. They might take it for granted,everr child in Widnes was vaccinated. Vaccination was un- doubtedly a great protection against BmallpoE and he toped there would be little danger of the disease spreading if it again broke out.—The minutes were adopted.
