A STRANGE &TRADE AT WIDNES: William Henry Wastencroft, a cooper, employed. at Messrs. Gasket!, Deacon, and Co.'s works, committed suicide there, on Tuesday morning, by hanging himself in, the coopers' shed. Ill'had conducted himself strangely for some weeks past, and 'at half-past five on the morning named he left the house hurriedly, although he bad not to com- mence work until helf-past !even. About half-past sitrhe was found hangingin the place named. He had appaready tightly tied a " ctolhes line" round his neck, whilst stand- ing on a plank placed across a tub, and then allowed hia, legs to slip off. The drop would be about four feet. Mr. W. T. HuSband, the deputy coroner, held an inqyeat on the body of the deceased on Wednesday afternoon, at the. Wellington Hotel. Mr. Matthews was the foreman of lie jury.—Mary Wolstencroft said the deceased was her son, and lived with her at 33, Willingtoa-street, Widnes. She last saw him alive at half-past five on Tuesday morning, when he went to his work. He s.ierned to be very much agitated, and when she askad him why he was going so early. he ran downstairs and out of the house. He did not usually go to work until half-past seven. Al that hour be was brought home dead. The deceased had been ver7 much tronbled in his mind for five or six weeks, and his manner had been very peculiar. A week last Monday he ought to have been married to a young woman named Margaret Reynolds. He was not married. She did not know why he was not married. She did not think the proposed mar- riage had had any effect upon his mind. She thought he was mehtally deranged. It was true that the young woman, whom he had been caurting for a lung time, hat had a child Amy him. By Mr. Stringer: The deceased was in a position to marry. His wages were £2 per week. She thought he was of unsound mind. She could not tell why the marriage did not take place. He left borne mys- teriously on the night previous to the day fixed for the ceremony. By Mr. Stone: He had never denied that the child vaas his. In answer to another juryman, witness said the de- ceased had not been threatened with a prosecution; and she told the Coroner that the deceased and Reynolds were always on friendly terms. William Wolstencroft,the brother of the deceased, said he worked at the Widnes. alkali works, and gave evidence of the peculiarities of manner which the deceased had displayed for some weeks past. The deceased hanged himself with a piece of "clothes line." They had similar rope at the house. Margaret Reynolds stated that she lived with the mother, of the deceased in Wellington-street. She was engaged to be married ta the deceased, and the ceremony was fixed to take place on the morning of the 3rd instant, but at half- past seven on the night previous he left the house and did ' not return until half-past ten on the Monday night. He had never explained why he went away. For some weeks past he had been very queer in his ways, and had been in the habit of looking at his reflection in the mirror for long ; periods. By Mr. Stringer: Sue was 19 rare of age. Her parents lived in Warrington, and had sanctioned the marriage In answer to questions by P.S. Clarkson, the witness said ; on Monday morning the deceased went to her bed side and I said "Ara you happy, Margaret ? " She replied yea; and he then asked "Is the child hippy too ?" She said yes; and he added "I am not hippy, but I soon will be." Timmas Ankara, 21, John-street, employed as a " die- charger " at Messrs. Gasket}, Deakin, and Co.'s chemical works, deposed to finding the deceased hanging by the neck in the coopers' shed. In answer to Mr. Stringer, the witness said the body was first discovered by a man named Robert May, who, however, ran away, and did not inform anyone of what he had seen. Mr. Stringer: How long after the body was discovered was it cat down ?—Witness: Ten minutes.
Mr. Stringer : Shocking. His life might have been saved had he been cut down at once. I think May ought to be here. .

The Deputy Coroner said there were some people who were awfully frightened at a dead body. May was present, but the sergeant informed him that he was not in a fit state to be called. Mr. Stringer said if May had been sober, he thought the jury would have expressed their feeling of indignation to him. The Deputy Coroner ohservsd that the question Waft whether May acted from fear, from meanness, or idea.. tionally. There was no excuse for him coming there th..t day in a drunken state, but he certainly should not be sworn I whilst in that condition. People who had an antipathy oc fear when near a dead body were continually met with, but even if May was susceptible to like influences there was no excuse for him for running away and informing no one of what he had seen. The Deputy Coroner then summed up, remarking that it seemed to him that there was nothing in the deceased relations with the girl to make him commit suicide. He seemed to have acted under the influence of some mental disease which could only be discovered by a surgical examination. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased committed suicide whilst of unsound mind. Mr. Matthews, the foreman, then said the jury were glad to find that their neighbour, Mr. Husband, had been ap- pointed deputy-coroner, and he thought that being the first time he had acted in his new capacity he had conducted the business very well. (Hear, hear.) He hoped he would long continue to hold the position be now occupied. Mr. Husband, in replying, said he was pleased to hear such eulogistic remarks. It gave him great pleasure indeed to act as deputy-coroner, particularly in Widnes, where he was known amongst so many of them. Mr. Brighouse had given such great satisfaction that it must be a little disap- pointing when he was not present. At the same time he (Mr. Hasband) could only say that if he could act on Mr. Brighouse's behalf with the same amount of satisfaction he shenld do all he thought he ought to do.

Margaret Wilkinson, who stands remanded at Knutsforcl, Cheshire, charged with attempting to murder her daughter and son-in-law, William and Mary Burgess, by administer- ing a large dose of oxalic acid in the tea-pot. Was further remanded on Thursday morning. the p.is,mer still being too ill to appear. How JUVENILE CRIME IS FOSTERED—At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Saturday last, before Mr. John Fairclough and Alderman Chandley, Margaret ELlen Healey, Of 60, Foundry-street, a native of 'J ipperary, was brought UP in custody on a charge of saving received stolen pro. petty from Andrew Kearney, well knowing it to have bean ' stolen. From the statement of the Chief Constable. (Mr. Hunt), it appeared that the prisoner knew the lad Andrew Kearney and induced him to take things out of i f his mother's shop, who is a second-band clothes dealer living n Queen. street, promising him a penny for each pair of boots Of other article that he brought her. . This system had been carried on by the prisoner and her victim for some time and was not discovered until the lad, when having an interview with his mother before going to prison for stealing money, made a confession to her which resulted in the prisoner being secured on His present charge. Two pairs of boots were traced to two pawnshops In the town and identified by the prosecutor, and it was proved that the prisoner had pledged them personally.—lhe prtaouer protested her inno- cence, declaring that she had wanted the boy not to steal, but the Bench committed her to hard labour for three months, Mr. Fairclough remarking that it was the worst case that had came before the magistrates for some time.

LORD SALISBURY has at last propounded a programme. Speaking at Chelsea, on Wednes- day evening, to an audience not altogether in sympathy with the aspirations of the noble Marquis, the leader of Her MAJESTY'S Op- position in the House of Lords was asked to state the Conservative programme, and for once, at any rate, his lordship was equal to the emergency, for he straightway announced that the policy of the Conservative party could be summed up in few words—viz "An appeal to the people." After this candid disclosure Lord SALISBURY proceeded to shape his course accordingly, and made what will, we think, be admitted on all hands to be an excellent electioneering speech. It was, we need scarcely say, full of statements aud professions on his part inconsistent with themselves ; it grossly misrepresented facts ; it was of course strongly condemnatory of the Government; but it was nevertheless just one of those characteristic utterances which show that whilst Lord SALISBURY may pos- sess the dash and go requisite to lead a poli- tical party not ;et quite effete, he is a very dangerous man to entrust with the destinies of this country. Egyptian affairs came in for a fair share of attention. The noble Marquis has, however, so frequently delivered himself on this now threadbare topic that we fail to discover anything new in what he fold his hearers on Wednesday. He is as anxious as ever to increase our responsibility in Egypt and the Soudan. Though he professes to agree with MT. GLADSTONE in his policy of "rescue and retire," he shows by hi 3 words and acts that he would not hesitate to waste the blood and trea,are of England in recon- , Tiering the Soudan for Egypt annexing both, I and ruling them with the sword. This, at any rate, is not what an appeal to the people , will endorse. We do not, however, believe that Lord SALISBURY cares a jot for the opinion of the people. He has too often placed himself in antagonism to theirinterests, and he has so repeatedly shown by his con- duct that he would if he could deny them their rights, that any appeal to the people suggested by him must be regarded by them as another effort to delay the progress of those useful measures of legislation for the passing of which they are now so anxiously waiting. The mere fact that he refuses to endow about z,000,000 people with the rights of citizenship, of which they have been so long and unjustly deprived, shows that he has no confidence in the people as a whole. He may have confidence in a select few like him- self. But at the present time and under exist- ing conditions there is no probability of ac- curately ascertaining the opinion of the constituencies, a eratc of things which ought not to be permitted. he aggregate number of voters in the United Kingdom is now something like 3,000 000 and it is ad- mitted that there are neariv z 000,000 more persons in the country capable ol exercising the franchise, who are excluded, but who ought to be placed upon the register of voters. The Ref,2-m !lin proposes to do this, and, therefore, we c that if there is to be any appeal to 'id p,-oole at all'on an early date it shouhl be af er the passing of the Reform Bill, and not hef ..e If there is an appeal to the country be ihe Bill is passed two thirds of the people wil: b, excluded from declaring their opint,,n, and. tnerefore, the

Poll could only represent the decision of a tninority ; but if it is taken after the Bill has become law, then there will be fair grounds or accepting the result of the poll as the de- liberate voice of the country. We have no idea that in either case the decision would be in favour of placing Lord SALISBURY in power, though we admit that the chances would be More in his favour before than after the pass- ing of the measure. No one is more alive to this than Lord SALISBURY himself, hence, 1 While his primary object is delay, there is no doubt he has a selfish motive as well in recom- mending an appeal to the constituencies now. lie must, however, learn to first trust the people , before he dares to appeal to them for their ' sYmpathy and support. Lord SALISBURY waxes wroth over the Merchant Shipping Bill, as indeed he would over any other Measure having Mr. CHAMBERLAIN for its author, and condemns it as not only a fan- tastic but horrible attack upon the shipping interests Every reasonable person knows, and so does Lord SALisAuRY, that this dis- cription of the Bill is altogether extravagant. The Bill embodies the piinciple of the ' Employers' Liability Act, and if employers Onshore are to be heldresponsible for injuries Caused by their negligence to their workmen, surely it is not too much to ask that em- Voyers of labour on the high seas should be Aeld similarly responsible for results which flovir from their negligence. Under any CirClinnstances it should not be possible for the owners of a vessel to stand to lose more by the vessel being lost than by his venture being brought to a satisfactory termination The Bill is not aimed at shipowners who take a pride in. sending their vessels to sea fully equipped and manned, and who have no desire to evade the law or evade re- responsibility; but it is designed to get at a set of owners who are regardless alike of life and property provided they are amply reimbursed for the money they embark in any shipping enterprise. It is stated on the highest authority that vessels ,Se often sent to sea in an unseaworthy con- cl. ition—either overladen, undermanned, or insufficiently found; also that sometimes the owners, at other times the masters, are to blame for this; and if the vessel is lost from either of these causes it is certainly desirable that punishment should follow whoever is responsible. Wil! Lord SALISBUiCi bolcrly SaY that the loss of life at sea must continue, a..nd that it must stillbe permitted to be pos.. Able or owners to make capital out of these N.'rAsitalties • for it appears f.. 3 us he must do so if he will oppOse tile- Merchant Shipping- Bill. I ;Zn the whole Lord SALISBURYcS spPecia may ::)I an admirable one for an election platform, the programme it enunciates may, in the absence of a better, suit the exigencies of the moment, but both are altogether unworthy of any Person claiming to be a Statesman,

THE Soudanese have suffered another de- feat, though it must be admitted that they fought bravely to avert it. We gather, in- deed, from ttle accounts of tilt: bat.le which has been fought that at one time there seemed a hope of success resting with their arms. The steadiness, oluck, endurance, and valour of the British soldier, however, proved too Many for the undisciplined Soudanese hordes, Who were consequently dispersed' in all direc- tions. The encounter, it seems, took place at a point called Tamanieh, where, since his defeat at El Teb, OSMAN DIGMA and his re- bellious followers had encamped themselvas, fortified their position as best they could in their own rude fashion and quietly awaited The advance of the British force. Overtures had of course been made to OSMAN to surrender, but he superciliously rejected all advances of the British commanding officer, and expressed his determination to resist any forward movement of the British troops. Ac- cordingly General GRAHAM'S force, which was massed at Souakim on return from the relief of Tokar. commenced to advance on Tuesday, and on Wednesday evening reached a hill calledßiountEassim,only a short distance from 43,sAIA.tes camp, in which were a number of rifle pits and entrenchments. On this hill General GRAHAM'S army bivouacd the night, during which the enemy kept firing from time to time, but withoilt drawing an answering shot. At daybreak the British force marched forth to the attack, the infantry advancing in a formation Which would admit of their being rapidly &ruled into two squares. It would appear that Th Soudanese were on the alert and in readi- "flees, for they swooped down upon the British force in such numbers and with such an on- laxight and rush as fairly for the moment to (Werwhelm our men, who were borne back several hundred yards. An opportunity was thus aflOrded the Soudanese to obtain posses- •si°". of our ,Gatlings and Gardners. This 'Posseszion was, however, only temporary, for 9ur men very soon rallied, and after two hours !lard fighting the guns were recaptured The battle was of the most sanguinary cha- ,racter, whilst it lasted there were many hand .0. hand conflicts the rebels fighting despera- IPJ3l.lkishbut in the result victory .rested with the , who completely routed the enemy from their rifle pits and entrenchments. The enemy's loss is said to be something over 4.000, and the loss to the British 100 killed and about 150 wounded, which is rather severe. This is now the second defeat which has been inflicted upon OSMAN DIGMA. This last is certainly much more •decisive than the first was, but what may be its political significance it is as yet difficult to say. It is certain that the followers of OSMAN, whose escape is to be regretted, will mow begin to dis- credit him; whilst he was successful they were willing to be led by him but now that success has forsaken him his' leadership will doubtless be repudiated. We hope that one result of the battle will be the complete submission of OSMAN and other re- bellious Shiekhs. If it is not, then we shall eagerly watch what the next step of the eltpeditionary force will be. It was sent to protect the Red Sea ports, and that has been accomplished. it was also instructed to dis- perse OSMAN and his followers, and that also has been achieved. Surely General GRAHAM not.be ordered now to follow OSMAN, and SO cause further bloodshed; yet it seems to us that now the Government have set to work to subdue this rebellion they will ex- perience the same difficulty that they did in that in retiring. It is important, therefore, ;flat our position and responsibility should be boldly faced, and that every effort should be Put forth to end this unfortunate war as early as possible. General GORDON seems to be sPecially endowed with the gift of settling complications of this character with Arab tribes, and the Government ?light to keep him in the Soudan until peace 13 established. It is rumoured that the k,.sieneralidesires to replace himself by Eriiisa. rAcRA, who has been notorious as a slave hunter, but we hope that ta such a proposal Governavnt wjl; give no countenance

div.head: ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE AT -WESTON.
div.p: ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE AT -WESTON.
SUOCKING TRAGEDY.

A shocking domestic tragedy took place at Weston, on Monday morning, when a young married woman, named Eccleston, attempted to take the life of her infant 'child, and also to put an end to her own existence.—lt appears filet the woman is the wife of William Eccleston, a weigher at the Weston Chemical Works. For some time the couple, with their family, have lived in a house in Collier's-row, tenanted by Mrs. Jones, to whom all the furniture belonged. Eccleston had no belongings at all, and if rumour is to be believed he provided very little of the necessaries of life for his family, who were in. destitute circumstance', About 14 days ago Mrs. Eccleaton was confined, and during hit prostration she received great kindness from a neigh-. I hour named Mrs. Dawson, the wife el a grocer, who keeps an adjacent shop. On Monday morning Ecclestoa lighted the fire, prepared his own breakfast, and went to his work about five minutes past eight. His wife and child were then in bed. Shortly afterwards Mrs. Dawson sent her servant, Alice 'Butler, to the house with some tea. Mrs. Ectleston was sitting on a chair near the fire Dlr. daily dressed, and appeared to the girl But- ler to be in a very ne-,vous and excited state. -Contrary to her want she was anxious to be alone, and told the girl that if she did not go back soon Mrs. Dawson, would be angry. The girl censequently returned to her mistress. A 'few minutes had only elapsed when Eccleston't eldest girl told Mrs. Dawson that her "mamma was had." Mrs. Day- ton a,Aain sent her servant to the house to ioqUlre the cause. 'She quickly returned ins, state of great excitement, saying Mrs. Eccleston was dead, and Mrs. Dawson, 'hurrying to the hones, found Mre. Eccteston lying on the Hoer in a pool of blood, which was escaping from an sofa' cash in her throat. A razor 'covered with blood was lying on the floor near by, as though it had dropped from the woman's hand. Horrified, Mrs. Dawson rushed hero the house, and alarmed the neighbours, who arrived en 'the scene in con- siderable numbers, and rendered every 'resistance to the injured woman. 'A search was then math for the infant, about seven days old, and after some time a man named, Job Wright, who lodged next door, found it lying concealed. in the bed clothes, with its throat eut feces ear to ear. In, the meantime Mr. Percival, landlord of the Prospect KUO,t drove to Runcorn to inform the police and obtain surgicsd, assistance, and he quickly returned accompanied try Dr. MacDougall. The doctor found that the wounds were ; of a serious 'nature, rendered considerably worse by great loss of blood. The gash on the child's neck whilst cutting the wind-pipe was not so deep as the one the woman bad inflicted upon herself; but they were both of a very dan- gerous character, and the doctor only held out s light hopet of recovery. During the day a clue to the ca use of the woman's rash act was found. Written in•Llack lead en the mantleshelf was the one word " trouble;" and after her wound had been stitched and handl wed by the doctor She continually murmured "It's ala trouble, trouble." The neighbours agree that the demestic4 troubles of the unfortunate woman have been many.and he [ivy, and while speaking of her as a quiet, well-behaved striving woman, they express great indignation against the husband, who they state has cruelly neglected bar. l'hat the strictures of the neighbours are deserved, the following faotei will tend to chow. On Monday afternoon the house did .not- contain a mouthful of food, and Dr. MacHot...gall, who had been assiduous in his attention to the case, told the husband that if the life of his wife and child were to be saved be must make arrangements to provide them with nourishing food and stimulants. About three o'clock, however, Eccleston left the house and did not return, leaving his wire. and child dependent upon the charity of the neighbours., Happily the neighbours have emulated the goo?. Samaritan, and provided every requisite for the sustecauce of the family. Mrs. Gomerville, a neighbour, is tenderly nursing the infant.

div.head: MATH OF MRS. ECCLESTON.
div.p: MATH OF MRS. ECCLESTON.

In spite of the best efforts of the doctor, and the assiduous attentions of the neighbours, Mrs. Eccleston died yesterday morning at half-past eleven, and the Coroner has been duly warned: The child is progressing favourably, and, we understand, will in all likelihood recover,

div.head: __WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: __WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.

RUNCORN COITNTY COURT—The cause list at this court, on Tuesday, comprised 90 original plaints and 15 judg- ment summonses. The cases of interest will be found else- where BRUNSWICK BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN.—The last meeting of the season took place on Monday, when Mr. T. Simister presided. There was a large attendance. An excellent pro- gramme was gone through. FARNWORTIL GRAMMAR ScKooL.—Wit understand that Mr. J. T. Brunner—formerly a partner at the large works owned by Messrs. Hutchinson, at Widnes—and Mr. Mond, have each given £l.OO to the Farnworth Grammar School. building fund. CRUELTY TO A HORSE IT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Edward Gould, the son of a grocer at Widnes, was summoned for cruelty to a horse.—P.C. Lamb said about half-past ten o'clock on Friday, the 29th ult.' he was on duty in Waterloo-road, Widnes, when he Saw the defendant driving a horse and cart. The • animal ap- peared to be in great pain, and consequently he stopped and examined it. Under the saddle he found a raw wound about two inches in diameter.—The father of the defendant said he was not aware that the animal was suffering from any sore —A fine of 10s and costs, 12s was imposed. ALLEGED THEFr AT RuNcoßN.—Before Mr. Brundrit, at Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, Mary Skehling, a mar- ried woman, was charged with stealing a shirt, the property of Mr. W. Blythe, clothier, High-street. —About two o'clock on Thursday afternoon, the 6th instant, the prisoner entered Mr. Blythe's shop and purchased a patch of corduroy. She was left alone a short time while Mrs. Blythe went into the kitchen to fetch some change. Subsequently the shirt was missed, and on the following afternoon she offered it in pledge at Messrs. Marsh and Smith's shop. She was given into the custody of P.S. McMichael, to whom she stated she had purchased the shirt from a Scotchman.—She was committed to Xnutslord Sessions for trial. THEFT BY A GIRL AT WIDNES.—A girl 'aged 17, named Norah Hind, was charged at Widnes Police Court, on Tues- day, with stealing a pair of boots, value 5s Ild, the property of Messrs. Freeman, Hardy, and Willis, Victoria-road.— It appeared that on Monday night a boy named Platt, who is employed by the prosecutors, heard a noise at the door of the shop, and on going there he missed a pair of boots, and saw the girl running away. lie caught the girl, and she dropped the boots and then ran off. She was followed to a entry in Thomas-street by Mr. Shadbolt, the manager of the shop, and as she ran away she dropped the shawl produced. Mr. Shadbolt gave the shawl to the police, and P.S. Clarkson found that it belonged to Mrs. Smith, of Water-street, who had lent it an tour before to the prisoner. Sly this inforrnAtion the prisoner was discovered.—She was sent to prison for 14 days. A WARRINGTON MAN DRUNK IN WIDNES COURT.— Tames Toole, marine store dealer. Warrington, was charged before the Widnes magistrates on Wednesday with being drunk at Widnes on the Bth inst., and also with being drunk in court on Monday.—lnspector Wood said he found the de- fendant in a helpless state of drunkenness in Waterloo-road on Saturday evening. He was locked up for safety, but later in the evening his man came with a horse and cart from Warrington, and witness allowed him to be taken home on promising to attend in court on Monday morning at tee o'clock. He did not appear at ten o'clock, bat at a quarter to eleven o'clock lee came into court in a drunken condition, and the magistrates did not think he was in a at state to be tried.—The Chairman said it was disgraceful for a respect- able man, as the defendant appeared to be, to appear drunk in a police•court. For the first offence he would be Suer; and costs, and for the pecond 10s and costs; total, 38s. CLAIN FOR WAGES AT AtniconN. Henry Owen, a "J'Outh, sued gorge Ciorer, grocer, Ranoorn, for 5s 13c1 for :rages. Mr. Lake appeared for defendant.—The plaintiir, who was assistant baker to the defendant, said that he was engaged by the week, and towards the latter part of Feb-, ruary he gave a week's notice to leave, to exire on a Satur- day. On the day before the es 1 baker ordered him to ';.Tgation of the notice the norne as he was not pleasing him •-w., • was performing his duties, and as he was passing through the shop the defendant's son, Robert Goret, who is manager of the shop, told him to go back to his Work and serve out his week's notice, otherwise he would not be paid his wages. In spite Of this, he persisted in going, and on Mr. Gorst refusing to pay his wages lie put the case in court.—Without calling upon Mr. Lake, his Honour said it was quite clear from the plaintiff's own I statement that he could not recover. He appeared to have I left his employment without having served his notice, and in direct opposition to the commands of his master. He , should give judgment for the defendant. CONTEMPT OF C UHT AT RUNCORN: A WARNING.—At Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, before W. Wynne Ffoulkes, Req., judge, Wm. Burrows, of Overton attended pursuant to an order made by the Judge on the last court day to show cause why he should not be fined £lO for con- tempt of court in not attending at the last court in accord- ance with a subpoena which had been served upon him. His . explanation now was that his employer bad to go to Liver- pool, and that consequently he could not leave the shop. He had a letter from his employer, but the Judge declined to see it, saying if his employer was in court he would hear , anything he had to say, but the letter he could not look at. His Honour said there was no doubt it was a very serious offence to entirely disregard a summons served upon a per. son, and showed great contempt of the court. He had the power te punish a person guilty of this conduct severely, and although he did not intend to inflict the full penalty in the present case, still he could not let him escape, and as t the plaintiff in the eases in which Burrows had to give [ evidence had been put to a loss of over £2, he thougkt he should not be justified in inflicting a less penalty than £4. He hoped it would be a warning to anyone in future.

Gstoss CRVELTY TO A HORSE AT RoNconx.,-At Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday. George Clare, a boatman, was charged 'with having, on the 25th February, cruelly ill- treated a horse.—P.C. Smith stated that about a quarter to four on the afternoon of the day named he was on duty in Elalton-road, when he taw the defendant in charge of a horse which was attached to a boat on the Bridgewater Canal. A WAREINGTON MAN's Faut.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Captain C. W. She threatened to poison or kill him and his chil- dren with some deadly weapon. Mr. Stubs granted him a warrant, and she was brought before the magistrates and locked up for a month. When she came out of prison she went to Wilderspool and knocked at his door. He opened it. She said. "I am not coming in. I can get my living without you." OUR LONDON LETTER.

THE PREMIER'S COLD-ITS SECRET HISTORI - RESIGN OR RESUME-THE CHIEF CONSERVA- TIVE FJRCE IN ENGLISH POLITICS-THE PREMIER ON FRENCH BEAULT-COOKED .OR CURRIED?-AN EPIDEMIC OF COLDS-WORK IN PARLIAMENT-"GETTING NO FORRADER"-THE NEW CONSERVATIVE PROGRAMME-BUDGET PROSPECTS-A SONG RECITAL-PLACE AUX DAMES IN THE INSTITUTE OF WATER-COLOURS -THE ARTIST AT WORK.
LONDON, Thursday.

There has been a great gap in the House of Commons this week. The seat towards which all eyes instinctively turn as either member or stranger enters the I.louse has been empty, and we have had a chance of realising what the place ,would he like if Mr. Gladstone were gone. As it is he has been suffering from nothing worse than a cold, though profoundly wise people will net accept such an explanation. They know very well that there has been a terrible row in the Cabinet. The old forces have been ranged in battle array, the Premier, Lord Granville, and Mr. Childers on one side, against that terrible couple, Sir Charles Dilke and Mr. Chamberlain, with Lord Hartington looking on, wishing to Heaven he was out of the whole business. In this case Mr. Gladstone has been worsted, and has pettishly made up his mind to resign, though what is to become of Lord Granville and Mr. Childers is not stated. One eminent Conservative, who sits on the Liberal side, told me with Mud Circumstance that the real fact is Mr. Gladstone had this little ilifins for the purpose of obtaining time to think over the matter. Tile ;:lifliculty arose on Saturday. On Sunday morning he was resolved to retire, and on Sunday afternoon the happy thonolat of the et!. :.....2errad to him. I So he shut himself up in his room. "But," said my friend, speaking yesterday, "As three days have gone by without his making any sign, he will come back all right. When he takes time to think he always makes up his mind to ac- cept the situation, and make the best of it ;" which is a very comfortable turn of prophecy. Mr. Gladstone is sure either to resign ...or resume, and the prophet will be justified. It is an odd thing, and in some measure goes to justify the characterisation of the Conservatives as the stupid party, that they should so earnestly desire to see an end of Mr. Gladstone's public life. He is, paradoxical as it may appear, the strongest Corieerlative power hi the country. It is he who acts as a break upon the forward impulse of Mr. Chamberlain, Sir Charles Mike, and Sir William Har- court, as will become apparent when he no longer sits in the Cabinet Council. It is a matter of history that the broader pkases of the last Irish Land Act were won bit by bit against his unwilling consent. The very title of the Bill was long a matter of dispute. He desired to call it " a Bill to amend the Land Act, 1870," which was held by SODAS Of his collea- gues to be a fatal initial step. According to them, the Land Act of 1871 WAS erroneous in principle, and to undertake to amend it would be like patching up a coat that never fitted.' In the end they got their way, and Mr. Gladstone, once con- vinced, threw himself With ardour into the advocacy of the Bill. It was exactly the same in respect of the amendment of Parliamentary procedure. It was months before he could be induced to deal with the matter. He approached it at first by the adoption of half-measures, which proved, as was foretold, Is be of no avail. It is the same in respect of all proposals to deal with established institutions. When once set in motion, he proceeds at full speed and with ir- resistable force. But he is hard to move. It must be conceded to the wise men in the Conservative side that Mr. Glachatone's indisposition was very sudden, lie was dining on Saturday evening at Sir Arthur Hayter's, and both at the dinner table and the reception which fol- lowed seemed is the best of health and in the highest spirits. He is at the dinner table as great a talker as in the House of Commons, and discusses every subject with the same fulness of information, At the dinner table on Satur- day Mary Anderson's name came up, and "the question was" whether she or Mrs. Langtry were the prettier. Mr. Gladstone threw himself into the controversy with all the ardour and, it must be addei, all the discrimination, of a masher discussing the comparative merits of Comic Gil- christ end Nellie Farren.. He was very much ticirled at the recollection of a verse which privately circulated at the time of his trip to Norwaa 'in Sir Donald Currie's steamer This ic it—

The Grand Old an his place has hooked. • And off to sea has hurried. The vulgar herd are only looke4 The Grand,Old Man is Curried. ,e matter of fact. he surmised, to ba "personally con- ducted" by Currie was an improvement on the ordicary arreugement,

If Mr. Gladstone has not had a cold he has been an ex- ception to the ordinary run of humanity in London during the past week. Ido not remember any time when so many people one knows were suffering from cold. It was said on Monday that every minister but one had a cold in the head and no one could nd out who was the one that was free. Mr. Mundella hac had te lay up, and I can run off on my ,fingers the names of seven members who are just now ab- sent from the House kr the same reason. But to the un- iversality of the epidemic the curious thing is the sudden" ness of its descent. A learned man accounts for it by reference to "germs." It seems that the atmosphere is capable of distributing germs which develop into influenza ,ld and strike the population of a great city as the plague once struck Loudon. Politics remain in much the same chaotic condition as they have been. On the Conservative side they continue to take the form of obstruction, which, is perhaps scarcely worth the name of politics. The whole aim of the great Conservative party at the present time is, not to argue about sprinciples, but to obstruct measures; and it must be ad-

mitred that they succeed only too well. We are now enter- ing on the seventh week of the session and Ministerial Bills, like the farmer drinking dinnerelaret,"get no forrader." They will, nevertheless, have to be passed, and what pre-

cent obstruction comes to is future working of double tides. The School of Westminster will certainly be "kept in" till it has finished its allotted tasks. In the meantime Lord Salisbury has hit upon a new cry which with some pains he has formulated into four words, "Appeal to the people."

Oddly enough this is now, as it was thirty-five years ago, the watchword of the Bonapartists in France, a resemblance which perhaps Lord Salisbury would not like to call to mind. Regarded as a programme the formula is obviously incomplete as applied to the present situation of affairs. If the people are to be appealed to they will ask on what grounds, and if it be simply the choice between Lord Salis- bury and Mr. Gladstone there can scarcely be any doubt of the response.

The national accounts are now being made up, and show, as is the happy custom when the Liberal Government is in power. a considerable surplus. This is a result so much taken for granted that the Government receive scarcely ad- equate credit for it, though, perhaps, when Lord Salisbury has his will, and the people are appealed to, they will call to mind that whilst a Liberal Government invariably his a surplus, a Conservative Government infallibly make a de- ficit. What adds sharpness to the contrast is tlic. fact that ths year's account includes considerable items for war ex- Penditure. But this year, as in previous years when this une,esirable feature appears in be ledger, the bill is paid

out of the revenue. Sir Stafford Northcote, it will not be forgotten, paid the war bill of a Conservative Government by the convenient process of handing it over to Mr. Glad- stone, whose ministry during the first two years was bur- dened with the debt of an unneceaary war, against which the Liberals had protested with all their might. It is too early yet to make toren Ists with confidence; but the proba- bility is that another penny will come off the income-tax in the new financial year. Mr. Frederick Cowen seems to be outstripping all corn- petitors for popular favor in the production of taking songs. Yesterday a brilliant audience assembled at Steinway Hall, where he gave what he called ". a song recital." His songs were Bung by Madam Antoinette Sterling, Mr. Santley, Miss Mary Davies, Miss Carlotta Elliot, Miss Edith Santley, and Mr. Frederick King. Amongst the most charming songs were the selection from "Sunlight and Shadow," and a ballad called "Lullaby," one of a set of quite new songs, heard for the first time by this favoured audience. For a concert of songs of one man's composition it was a remarkable collection, and formed a most successful enter- tainment.

A controversy started a few days ago about the free schools of the Royal Institute of Painters in water colours is becoming amusing. One correspondent accuses the mem- bers of injustice in establishing free schoole which exclude female students. Mr. Linton, the preeident, replied with a gentle, harmless statement, that not having at present room for students of both sexes, they accept males only, until, he might have added, the funds admit of things being done on a more extensive scale. Immediately several aggrieved "self-protecting ladies" rise up in arms and accuse him of want of chivalry. Now there is no more generous and chivalrous a man than Mr. Tinton ; and his fellow-workers at the Institute share his anxiety to bestow every attention to the merits of lady artists. Pardonably enough they thought that young men had the first claim on an institute which owes its existence and progress entirely to men. There are many branches of art in the way of decoration) design, and art needlework in which ladies have all the field to themselves. In matters of art training and the ex- hibition of their works, one has only to go round the gal- leries, or read the lists of contributions in the catalogues, to see whether their talents are recognised or not. Their complaint of illusage is, I am assured by a lady artist, quite groundless. Yesterday I met Felix Moscheles just home from America and it was interesting to compare his experiences with those of Oscar Wilde. He does not wear knickerbockers, nor is he a worshipper of dee tying lillies, and he found the better class of the New York people, appreciative, artis tic, and indeed eclectic, They crowded to one of his lectures the Americans seers to love a lecture at which it was announc3d he would "talk on art. The painting was pretty well known, for three of his portraits in New York had bad great suc- cess, and the audience found him on the plat- form with a pretty little Yankee girl beside him, and brushes, paints, canvass, and all the furniture of the studio. The painter took his public into his confidence as to what he was to do with the girl. There was the blank canvass, and her face tilllSt ti pi on it in the next half- hour. But how? Would she do for Lucrezia, Borgia, er Cleopatra, or any great murderess? Would she do for the Queen of the Amazons, or Boadicea, or Tennyson's Prin- cess, or Bloody Queen Mary? She was a sweet little inno- cent girl of 15, with a wistful face and dark pathetic eyes, with a kind of confiding, and yet half fareuche look. Mos- cheles decided, and his audience agreed, that she looked neither heroic nor blood-thirsty. Somebody suggested Goethe's Mignon. It was the only thing, and so the painter, "talking art" all the time, showed how the thing was done. In fifty minutes the fsc3 was on the canvass, end the audience would see hott. mucilwas mere portraiture, and how much thtl taking of hints which nature gave and the adding of the poetry which comes from the artist him- self. The Yankees are a singular people. Here was one of the most practical lectures on art that could well be given. The talk did not end in talk. Much was learned, and some- thing was done. The conclusion was the most Yankee thing of all. The audience insisted that the sketch should be sold to the highest bidder, and that bidder g^.ve a big price for it.

RA.TEPAYERS' MEETING. A general meeting of the members of the Widnes Rate- payers' Association was held at the SiMM'd Cross Hotel, on Tuesday, to consider matters connected with the forth- coming election. Mr. D. Wright presided, and there were present Messrs. J. Midwood, S. Sadler, T. Sadler, W. Sadler, R. Webster, J. Briggs, J. Heath, J. Smith, Ilewson, Beach, J. Deakin, Ankers, G. Chrimes, and S. 0. Owens, (secre- tary.) Mr. OwEss said it had been hinted tohim by the Owners and Occupiers' Association, that if they were prepared to stand by their original proposal to only nominate Mr. S. Sadler, it would very likely be agreed to with a view to avoid a contest. The owners and occupiers would be al- lowed to nominate four candidates. Mr. T. Samna observed that if they had not a contest this *time they would have to fight a severe battle next year, when, as they would remember, five of the association's nominees would have to seek re-election. The Owners and Occupiers Asso- ciation 'would :not let them have any of their own way at that time; and he should like to press upon that meeting the necessity for running four candidates at this election. He made a motion that the association nominate and sup- port four candidates. Mr. HRWSON seconded the motion. Mr. BRIGGS proposed that a compromise should be ac- cepted. At first he was as full of fight as anybody, but having carefully considered the matter he had come to the conclusion that their association would he best off if they did not contest the election. If they fought this time it would be go expensive that next year when the term of five of their nominees expired they would not be.in a position to conduct a vigorous contest. Mr. Briggs pointed out that the association had eight nominees out of the 15 on the Board now. They did not claim a monopoly, and, even if they lost one next year, they would be on a level wittl the other association. Mr. SMITH seconded the motion. Mr. BEACH remarked upon the expense which a contest would inflict upon the town, and the association by making a compromise would reserve their funds and gain the con- fidence of the ratepayers. Mr. MIDWOOD was in favour of a compromise, and re- marked that the association's first proposition was not re- jected by the substantial men of the other association. Mr. Carlisle was the worst against the proposal, and aleo Mr. Wareing and Mr. Heyes. The best men of the owners and occupiers were quite agreeable that Mr. Sadler should be returned. (Hear, hear.) Seeing that the Ratepayers' As- sociation would not lose anything by a compromise, he thought it was far better for their purpose that they should keep social and agreeable in the other association in the most respectful way they could. (Hear, hear.) He did net I think it was wise to get at loggerheads with them. At pre- sent the Ratepayers' Association had a fair representation on the Board, and it would be unreasonable to attempt to get any more. The best course in his opinion would be to re-elect the retiring members. (Hear, hear.) l• Mr. T. SADLER asked if the associations agreed to a com- promise would a contest be saved? Mr. MIDWOOD believed there would be a contest. Certain outsiders would be brought forward by the leading spirits of the other associations in the hope to split the votes of the associations. The CHAIRMAN: Den't say leading spirits. Call them minor lights. Mr. T. SADLER: How are you going to save the rate- payers' pockets by compromising when a contest was to take place? Mr. Banns believed they would strengthen their hands by compromising. Mr. SADLER said that being a member Of the Board he felt diffident about speaking on this question, but he thought it was only right to say that he placed himself entirely in the hands of the association. Whatever the decision the meeting came to would satisfy him. Mr. OWENS said there was an advantage in retaining ,members of the Board who had acquired experience. The gentlemen who were now retiring from the Board had spent a considerable time upon committees, they were conversant with the requirements of the town and the various duties attached to the office. Let it be understood unmistakably that the leaders and moderate men of the other party were satisfied with Mr. S. Sadler as a representative—(hear, hear) —and wore glad to have him ass colleague. (Hear, hear.) They bad even written letters privately expressing their satisfaction with Mr. Sadler's abilities. Depend upon it thet when the other association found them reasonable they would be prepared to consider their wishes, not only with regard to representation, but wit regard to other matters, and he strongly giwported a cerapromisc. Toe NAilimAN said as they knew three years ago Mr. S. Sadler seas the only representative of the Ratepayers' Asso- elation on the Bsard, and he had an up-hill battle to tight until he got reinforcements. For the past two years they had held a goodmosition on the Board, and they were pre- pared to give an account of their stewardship before the public—(hear, hear)—but next year they would have a much better Cudget. The Board never stood in such an excellent position with regard to its finances as it did now. (Mr. MIDWOOD : Never.) A few years ago they had to pay the beak large interest for borrowed money; now they had a credit balance at the bank—(hear, hear)—and they were looking forward to realising a profit on the water this year —the first time in the history of Widnes. When the public became aware of these facts they would accord the Ratepayers' Association their support. Though the nominees of the association ought not he quite so polished as some of the men who had sat at the Board, they worked and endeavoured to do their duty and promote the welfare of the town at large. (Hear, hear.) The results would speak for themselves—(hear, hear)—and he really felt con- fident that if they came before the public next year with fads that they should get their support. After referring to the abilities of Mr. Sadler, and their universal recognition by marnbers of the Board, the speaker seidMr. Gossage had strongly expressed himself in favour of a compromise, and stated that Mr. Sadler ought to be strongly supported by the Owners and Occupiers' Association. (Hear, hear.) He knew that at the meeting of that association some time ago five names were mentioned, and Mr. Sadler's was amongst them, but some of the "small fry" said they could not accept a man who belonged to a counter association, as the rules would not allow it. Mr. Frank Geskell afterwards searched the ruler., and could not find anything that sup- ported much a view. During some further conrersation it was stated that Mr. W. H. Kershaw had decided not to offer himself for election andsome feeling was evinced against Mr. Carlisle being put 1 into the Vacant place 'should a compromise be agreed upon. Several members said they should prefer a contest rather than assist at the election of that gentleman. The GRAIRVAN observed that Mr. Holbrook-Gaskell, jun., would without dogeg be the fourth nominee of the Owners and Oocupiers' Association. A tompromisevas then agreed upon by eight rotes to loar,and Mr. Midwood and the secretwy were appointed a deputation to confer with the rival association. "yesterday afternoon the members of the Owners and and'Occupiers Association held a meeting in the officers' 100n1 of the Drill Hall, to consider various matters in con- nection with the forthcoming Local Board election. Mr. 'Frank Heyes presided, and there were present Messrs. S. K. Muspratt, Jones, Eleary Wells, Holbrook-Gaskell, jun., Wareing, Garlile, Panaburst, Matthews, J. W. Taylor, D. Vointer,'F. Liddell, Edwards, F. Gaskell (sec.), tn. Mr. W. Kereheav having decided not to offer himself for eleetion, it was resolved that the Association only nominate four candidates—viz., Messrs. F. H. • Gonage, E. Carey, T. Handley,and H. Gaskell, .kan. It was also agreed not to , offer any opposition to the return of Mr. S. Slater. The members of the Ratepayers' Association also held a meeting last evening, under the presidency of Mr. Beach. Various matters were discussed, but no departure was made from the resolution arrived at on Tuesday. recorded above. Some feeling was expressed at the action cf the Owners and 'Occupiers' Association, who, while promising not to oppose the return of Mr. Sadler, would neither support him nor amalgamate with the Rate- payers' Lesociation. It was decided to call another meet- ing on Monday, and further discuss the situation and form some decisive action. Mr. Wright said he was prepared to stump Widnes through against any candidate of the Owners and Occupiers' Association, and show the work that had been done during the past two years. When the Ratepayers Association went upon the Board, at least £l,OOO a year was being paid for interest upon overdrafts at the hank, while now they were simply paying the treasurer £5O a year, and not a penny more. Many old debts had been paid off, agreements of long standing met, the lowa kept in good Condition; and yet the rates had been reduced, and the work of the town was proceeding satis- lector-Iy. .it was strongly felt that if the Owners and ACccupi-rs' Asseciation would not support Mr. Sadler, there would be a-contest between the two associations for euprem- atm and no ,7ear was expressed as to the result.

'SUPPOSED INFANTICIDE AT T. lIELENS.—An inquest Ins held in the White Hart hotel, St. Helens, on Saturday act, regarding-the body of a male infant which bad been found in the St Helens canal on the previous Thursday. The body had been found tied up in a market bass by a boy named James Deley, in the canal near the Globe Alkali works, and with a brick laid upon its breast, evidently for the purpose of sinking it. It was examined by Dr. Jamison, who found no marks of violence upon it. The doctor was of opinion that the child had had a separate existence, but be could not be pocilive owing to its &tate of decomposition. —The fury returned the verdict "That deceased, being newly-Corn, was foucd dead in the canal, having apparently been in the water forcome time, but bow it came by its (I.lth „Ticl hJIV it c:tme into the water there was no evidence to show. - - -

B LAR Y AT ST. iti.LENS.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Tuesday, a robust young fellow named Thomas Kennedy was charged with two separate offences of having broken into the house of Mr. E. Barlow, St. Ann's, and stealing therefrom a sealskin jicket, counterpanes, hearth. rug, and several other articles. It seemed that both on the night of the sth instant and that of the 7th, the prisoner had obtained an entry to the house by breaking panes of the dining rum and scullery windows and turning latches, and also by way of the cellar. On the second night P.C. Mil- lington had neticed the broken windows and janocked Mr. Barlow up, am' a search of the house was made. The pri- soner was not at first found, but was afterwards discovered by Sergeant Montgomery hiding behind a sofa in the draw- -1 ind-foom. It aprearecr that he had pawned some of his I first night's i !under at Mr. Royle's pawnbroker's shop, Parr. ‘Frisoner was committed to the Aseizes on both charges.
A TRIVIAL QUARREL AND eTS
RESULT-S AT WIDNES.

I At the Widnes Poles Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. ' Holbrook Gaskell, jun., Walter Clarke, 20 years of age, was charged with unlawfully wounding a young Man named. Michael Joseph Curley.—Prosecutor whose head and race were enveloped in surgical bandages, said that both Vie prisoner and himself were carters in the employ of Mr. Edward Percy, contractor, Sutton's-line, Wialrees. ALout half-past seven o'clock on Monday morning prisoner put the prosecutor's bridle on his horse's head, and prosecutor told him to take it off, but he refused to do so, as be said "the master" had told him to take it. Prosecutor was in the act of taking the bridle away when prisoner caught him - by the collar. Prosecutor put his foot behind prisoner and knocked him down. On getting up prisoner seized a brick, and, throwing it at prosecutor, struck him on the left eye with it.- Prosecutor sabsequently went to take the prisoner's horse out of the shafts, telling the prier at the same time not to Come near him again. Prisoner, however, took no heed of the caution, but picked up two more bricks and struck prosecutor on the top of the head with one. Prosecutor then threw him down, but on hie promising not to repeat the assaults, he was allowed to get en Instead of keeping his word, prisoner stuck prosecutor with the other brick on the head over the left eye. He afterwards tried to hit prosecutor with another brim—Henry liarrop, another carter in the same employ, said both the prosecutor and pri- saner bled like two pigs that had just been stuck, but Curley was bleeding most. Evidence corroborating the prosecutor'e statement was also given by William Leman and John Smith, fellow-carters in Mr. Percy's eavloy.—Dr. Cooper said prosecutor received a severe blow On the left eye, three cuts on the head, one on the upper portion of the forehead about an inch and a half long, which penetrated through the scalp, and another in the centre of the top of the head tmerquarters sA an inch long, which also penetrated through the scalp. There were other contused wounds on the hack of the had, which injured the superficial part of the scalp. The wounds were dan- gerous, and might bring on erysipelas —Police-constable Strickland said he apprehended prisoner on a warrant at a quarter to 7 o'clock on Monday evening, and in reply to the charge prisoner said, That is not so; Carley assaulted me first."—Prisoner, in reply to the magistrates, said, "If you will let me off, I will pay the doctor's bill."--He was com- mitted to take his trial at the Quarter Sessions.—As soon as he heard the drcision of the Benc`i rieoner l.iitrst into tears.

div.p: TIIE HEALTH OF WIDNES.

At the monthly meeting of the Widnes Local Board OD Tuesday, Dr. Cooper, the medical officer f uealth, presented his report for the year ending the 31-t I).,ccaiber, :883. It read as follows: During the year 1883, 498 deaths were registered in the township of Widnes, and calculating on a population of 2,600 persons, this gives a death-rate of 1915. per thousand of population for that year. From the principal zymotic diseases 61 deaths were recorded, which gives a death-tale of 2-35 per thousand from that class of disease. Therwere as follows :
Smallpox 5 Scarlatina 22 Mea.les..., 8 Diphtheria Whooping cough 8 Typhus fever Typhoid fever Diarrhoea

el Notwithstanding the outbreak of smallpox which took place in Widnes during the summer and autumn, it is gratifying to find that both the to at death-rate and that from zymotics compare favourably with those for last year, which were respectively 20 56 and 312 per thousand. The deaths of children under one year, including premature births, numbered 170, or 5•8 per thousand of the population, just one less than last year; and thosr of children bAween one and five years, 102, or 391 per thousand-32 lees than last year. The following table epitomises the ages at which the deaths occurred throughout the township:— Deaths of persons under 1 year over 1 and under 5 years lO2 ~ 5 15 n •• • 30 15 25 1, ••• 24 „25 „ 60 „ 117 n 60

498 The birtha registered during 1883 nuaibered 1,045, giving a birth-rate of 401 per thous Ind of population. I will now refer briefly to the outbreaks of zytnetic diseases during the year, and the steps taken to arrest the spreid of each diseases. Saute Pox.— On the 14th of May a boy living in the upper part of the township was attacked by small pox. His parents kept a small shop which was closed by order of the Sanitary Commlitte, the boy isolated, and every one, except the father and mother, sent out of the house. No fresh case occurred until the 23th of Jsly, when a man, living at some little distance from the scene of the first outbreak, took the disease. This case was quickly followed by three others among the members of the same family, who bad been removed to enother house as soon as the disease appeared. The streets in which small pox patients resided were con- stantly disinfected ; both these suffering from the disease and their attendants, were so far as was possible under very adverse circumstances, isolated from their neighboura. Vaccination aud re-vaccination were strongly recommended and needed out whenever it could be discovered that they had not been already submitted to. I may mention that the sanitary inspector was untiring in his efforts to prevent the spread of this awful disease, and to him .very great . credit is due ; in fact, had he been lt ts vigi- lant, I have little doubt the epidenic 7culd have spread far wider and been more fatal than it was. Notwithstanding every precaution, Case after cite occurred, and it became necessary to take some further steps ; conse- quently in October my Board purchased two hospital tents, and Major Cross, a gentleman who formerly resided in this neighbourhood, having kindly offered a piece of land for the purpose, the tests were set up and fitted most completely with every convenience; a wooden kitchen and a nurse's room were also erected. Finally an excellent nurse was engaged to take charge of the patients who were to be treated in the hospital tents. Out of the 36 cases of small- pox which occurred during the outbreak only six proved \ ' fatal, and of these six four died unvaccinated. I would draw special attention to this as a noteworthy face One roan_ died from smallpox at the Workhouse Etrpitit,i at PreseCt- to which place, being a pauper,he was obliged to be removed'. His death took place before the tent hospital was estab- lished. I sin happy to say there has been no fresh case for some time, and we have dismissed the last patient from the hospital tents. SCARLITINA.—Daring the autumn there was an epidemic of scarlatina, but with a few exceptions the cases were cf a mild type; they occurred chiefly in the outskirts of the town, and were not traceable to any particular cause. MEASLEB.—There were several cases of measles cluing the year, but the disease was not confined to any special locality, nor prevalent at any special season. Similar means to those mentioned in last year's report were taken to prevent the spread of both this and the last-named malady. 1 TYPHOID FEVER.—I am happy to say there were only four fatal cases of typhoid fever during the year, just half the number which occurred from this dissase in 1882. TYPHCIS FEVEE.—One fatal case of typhus fever war re- corded. . . -

Dm/amis.—There were four fatal cases oi dipthkmia occurring at different 80390/18 of the year, and vari;, localities. DIABRIIINA..-001V 24 deaths were.cansed by this d:seaso, as against 38 last year. All the fatal cases were of young children, chiefly infants in arms. Carelessness in preparing food and bad noising are the causes of the great majority of deatha from diarrheas °centring in young children. WHOOPING -,otrOn —Three cases proved fatal. PUBLIC WORKS.—The main sewerage of a large potion of the township is progressing, but is not yet completed, although it is being carriod out as rapidly as possibte. WATER Statrtmr.—The water supply is pure aud show- dant.

SCAVENGING.—The scavenging has been carriai aut in a far more satisfactory manner than during 1881 an 1582. OFFENSIVE TitenEs.-The only trade which provtal uffeuaive to the inhabitants during the past year was the manufacture of glycerine. The proprietors of the works causing the offen- sive smell, have been requested by the Sanitary Committee to abate this nuisance, and they are now taking 11-1,-;', to do so. DISPUTED FOOTBALL MaTCH. r,—Whfist reading the reports of football matches in your last issue I came across statements which were er- roneous concerning the Vulcan U. Warrington Wanderers second teams. The errors being first with regard to the team that journeyed to Warrington, and second as to the score. I did not take any of the Newton football members with me, as reported. The score was one goal, one try, to nil, whereas you have merely got one try. We never need trouble any club for players, as we have plAnty reserve after a third has been selected. The Wanderers do not say any- thing of the help from the Warrington town club, and I hope the next meeting with these teams will have a more eatisfoctory result.—l remain, yoers, TtIOMAS LIAISON, Captain V. F. C. u I can Foundry, Mara, 1594. DISESTABITiaIifENT. ,

Sir,—.ln your last issue Mr. John Peers asks me 'to show the analogy between the voluntary raised trust funds of Dissent and the compulsory levies of the State Cburch." Now, sir, I suppose he is "still harping on my daughter," viz., tithes alone, and if I am right in my supposition that this is so, then I'll endeavour to point out the " analogy." The greater pertion of the voluntary trust funds I suppose Were left to the religious body Mr. Peers belongs to, and were invested in stocks, dm New, sir, what is the other side of the picture? It is this. The "compulsory levies of the State Church " were left in tithes for the support of the clergy. The only difference I can see is that Dissent endowments were left in hard cash, whereas the Church of England's were a tenth portion of the produce of the land. In my last I pointed out to Mr. Peers how this unjust tax upon the land could be removed, but he conveniently closed his eyes to the fact. While I have the pen in my hand I should like to call the attention of Mr. Peers, and ask him a simple question, hoping to get an equally brief answer. Is Mr. Peers aware that the following bishoprics have been established within the last few years :—Liverpool, Truro, Newcastle, St. Albans, and Southwell ? Before any ef these bishops could be appointed at least £lOO.OOO in each ease had to be raised. This makes alone £500,000. Now, Mr. Peers, who does this half a million belong to, seeing it was raised by the Churchmen and Churchwoman of this country? If Mr. Peers is to have a share of this £500,000, then am I not morally entitled to a share of the trust funds of his chapel? If this question of disestablishment was more coolly considered, I think we should all fall into less mis- takes on the subject. I should like Mr. Peers also to tell us if disestablishment and disendowment is such a grand thing whet he would do with say our Warrington churches, are the Roman Ltatholics to have the Parish Church and St. Paul's as their portion, the Salvation Army St. Barna- has, Trinity Church to be given to the Unitarians, and St. Ann's to the Baptists, for helping on disendowment ?—Yours truly, A CHURCHMAN. P.B.—The "Free Thinkers" would also be entitled to a building. FARN WORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL AND THE LATE

know. Indeed at that time I was toe much occupied, and I may say too ill, to take much isterest in anything. Mrs. Raven had been lying between life and death, and was, I believe, only saved through God, by the almost brotherly devotion of her medical attendant, and during that time I think I may say I had not two hours of consecu- tive sleep, so that I was in no state to meet the Commis- sioner, and in fact only saw him for a few minutes. But, sir, it is little use going on with this; the trustees neither re-appointed me nor said that they wouldn't; they only refused to pay although the foundations had been going on at their express wish. Both my wife and myself were get- ting beyond work. In August, 1878, we removed once more to Oxford, and had only been there five weeks before my system completely broke down, and I have been an helpless invalid from that day to this. Such, sir, is the plain statement of my case. I should not have troubled you and your readers with these letters, only the building of new schools, which has con- fiscated all the money I had spent, is such a sweeping censure that I could not let it pass without pro- test, while I should be sorry to say anything unjustly of the trustees, I feel firmly convineed that had they permitted me to retire, when I first asked, I should have been a strong man to-day—it was the tension of the last two years at Farnworth that completely shattered me, and I regret now that the trustees did not do what I think was, after 15 years service, certainly due to me, viz., intimate to me that they did not intend -to abide by the terms on which, and on which alone, they had procured my resignation. Breaking up my house at Oxford was not unattended with great ex- pense and considerable loss; but instead of doing this the conduct of the chairman was equivalent to a strong iavitation for me to return and that return cost me from first to last, directly and indirectly, a money loss of upwards of £2,000. The school had received a great shock, and did not pay expenses but it would have quickly recovered had it not been for the uncertain state in which the conduct of the trustees kept it; and during the 18 months the direct money loss was £650; and besides this I was forced to sell a security in March, 1878, for £450 which, from 1879 to the present time has paid an annual interest of £Bl, and has been, and is now, worth £1,400 in the open market. This I had intended as a small provision for one of my daughters and, had I re- mained at Oxford, cettld have kept it intact; for I was able to earn my living by tuition. Sir, thi3 loss and the confis- cation of the buildings, which I erected, have deprived me of an income of fully £350 a year, for every penny of which, in my judgment, and, I think, in the judgment of all right-feeling men, the trustees of Farnworth School are responsible. I say nothing of the loss of compensation from the Charity Commission, which could hardly have been less than £l,OOO. I am now in my help- lessness, indebted to a few kind friends for the bread I eat land for the roof that shelters me; the future of my children is blasted, and what will eventually become of us God slone knows. We are all of us, I suppose, in the hands of a great invisible power, who, according to the clergy, is all bene- ficence, and upon whom the ancient poet, Pagan by acci- dent of birth, Christian by nobility of soul, teaches us to rely in the f ollowing splendid verse :-- " Hine omne principium, huc refer exitnm." With many thanks for your kindness, I am, sir, your faith- ful servant, JAMES RAVEN.

div.head: HEAD MASTER.
div.p: HEAD MASTER.

Sir,—l regret to ha—v;*l;;;-;;;-bre-lo write sooner. On Mr. Hrchinson's assumption of the duties of head master I took my wife and children to Oxford. Teaching-power, j sir, is a unction of many variables, and it requires a life- time of varied experience to become even mederately pro- ficient in the art of conveying knowledge. I had not been able, as a youth, to enter either of car great Universities, and determined to spend the holiday, I hoped to take, in our most important educational centre. lam one of those to whom it is a matter of small importance where, or under what circumstances, a man acquires his knowledge provided he has acquired it; but to me, as a teacher, the great charm of living in the midst of an active educational centre was the perfect freedom with which diverse opinions may be advocated, and the extended field it opens for observing the various methods of approaching individual minds. I had only been in Oxford six weeks when I was summoned to return to Farnworth. The circumstances which caused that return are 8f so pain- ful a nature, and are besides so well known in the neigh- bourhood, that it is not neceseary to recapitulate them here. I will only state two facts, and those only as a duty in justice to myself, for I think there was some misapprehen- sion with regard to them. When the suspicion firstdawned upon me that Mr Hutchinson might not be in a position to carry on so large an undertaking; I had on the morning before I left Farnworth offered to return to him the money he Lad paid and revoke the contract, and when I came down from Oxford I again offered, if an examination of his posi- tion at all warrantPd it, to assist him as much as I could ' over the diilloullV ; I could do no more I would now wish to draw particular attention to the fol- lowing circumstances. I had, as stated in my last letter, given in my resignation on the distinct pledge that, in the event of Mr. Hutchinson not meeting his obligations, I should be reappointed to the school. I therefore called upon the Vicar and explained the circumstances to him, and after some little talk the following are the exact words in which he t xpressed ihimself, "The trustees will be very glad to have you back." After arranging matters, I was .obliged to go back to Oxford for a fortnight on account of term not being ended, and Mrs. Raven returned to Farnworth to superintend affairs as well as she was able during my al.sence. Mr. Holloway, the vicar, kindly saw her, and almost his first expression was "Mrs. Raven, the trustees Will only be too pleased to get Mr. Ravenlback." Further, as only junior masters were with my wife, Mr. Holloway offered to come down daily until my return, and very kindly -did so ; at least, if not daily, very frequently. There is yet another circumstance. The boys were in the habit of giv- ing an annual concert at Christmas, but Mr. Holloway sug- gested their not having it, as his idea was that the more quietly I returned the less the school was likely to be dis- turbed, and the greater probability of its returning to its normal condition. In deference to his opinion the concert was given up. Now. Sir, all this was done by the chairman of the board, and I will ask you, or any other man, was this conduct consistent with the idea that the trustees would refuse to carry out their solemn pledge and re-appoint me? tic such thought entered my head, and I returned to my duties without the shadow of a suspicion. Of course I could not remove all my family to Oxford, take a house, furnish it, dispose of the house of furniture and bring back my family to Farnworth without very great loss. I bad bad a short holiday of eight weeks; but, altogether, it had cost me dearly. The exact term used on my giving in my resignation was that under certain circumstances I should be " re-appointed." 4 I had been away so short a time that I thought a simple withdrawal of the resignation would save mach trouble, some expense, and be simpler in every way. mentioned this to the v , 'vicar. He said Well, write me a line asking permission of the trustees to withdraw your re- signation, and I will call theist together." I fell into tha trap—for trap it afterwards proved to be—and wrote a few lines as the vicar suggested. Time passed on; I was very hard at work with the school, which had received a very Severe shock, particularly with regard to the outside con- nection, and I was much concerned about my wife's health, who had had another of her old attacks. I asked the vicar once or twice if the trustees had had a meeting. He re- plied in the negative, adding that "they did not like to be summoned ter nothing." I had little• idea of went was going on behind the scenes all this time. This went on until the 25th of March, when, according to the terms of ray resignation, my- connection with the school expired, and on the evening of that day, 1877, I received an official tette- from the trustees'to the effect that they had placed the matter in the hands of the Charity Commission, and that, therefore, they could not give permission for the- withdrawal of my resignation. but added that they wished not to disturb'the education of the foundationers, and that they could continue; sir, they did continue, and the trasteee have always refused to pay for them, and I have never received a penny from that day to this. When I received this 111111,1iVe I went at once to the Vicar. He •exclsimed, " Oh, I thought this would bring volt, but you know it is only official you will be all right." did not see it, and objected to the Charity Commissioners Coming between me and the trustees; stating that my resig- nation had been given under certain conditions, and that thoee conditions most be kept. He persisted in saying that [should be all right, and at last said, "Well, well, I will call another meeting." The foundation boys continued, and things went on as ueual for another two months, and not hearing from the truetees I wrote and formally demanded reappointment. Another meeting was then called, and *her it the Vicar came down to my house and gave met this v,rbal message, "Of course it was understood that you were to be reappointed, and you will be; you need not fear, it will be all right." div.head: NUISANCES IN EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NUISANCES IN EARLESTOWN.

81r,—One would think that the township of Newton, with its Commissioners, surveyor, nuisance inspector., and foreman scavenger, should not have a single nuisance within its coasts for a very prolonged period, but such I fear is the case. Having for the past year or two had occasion several times a day to pass along Haydock-street, Earles- town, it has been my lot to have to put up with a nuisance which has existed over the length of time named, and I believe a good deal longer, viz., a portion of the footpath between Bridge-street and Oxford street. This, I believe, was taken up to make a roadway to the back of some pro- perty in Oxford-street, and has not as yet been relayed or replaced with setts, and it often happens that in wet weather persons find themselves in a small lake of water. I also find that in walking along this street on the same side one is likel to be run over by a baker's horse and van, which is allowed to be drawn over the flags not four yards from the breach spoken of. I happen to know that some time ago another keeper of horse flesh was promised tronble if he did this kind of thing, and to get out of the difficulty he got the Commissioners to lay down setts for him, for which be had to pay. Now, Sir, I should like to know who took up the flags in Haydock-street, and how it is that the present state of things is allowed to exist while we have so many paid officials; also why /a cannot have temporary footpaths provided during the time any alterations are being made to property in principal streets, such as Market-street, which has been a disgrace to any official during the recant altera- tions of property there —I remain, yours, Earlestown, March 13, 1884. A SUFFERER,

div.head: ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION FOR
div.p: ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION FOR
EARLESTOWN.

Sir,—For some time I have been looking forward, in vain it appears, in the expectation of seeing an announcement that a branch of the St. John's Ambulance Association was to be started in this neighbourhood. Surely when such places as Crolborne and Haydock takes the van in a matter of so much importance it must make the inhabitants of Earlestown, who I believe think themselves much more ad- vanced than their neighbours, feel a little ashamed; and Nal assured that if a few workingmen would take the matter up, and seek for help in the proper quarters, we should not be long in having a large branch of the association. How often it happens that when an accident occurs in any of the workshops in the vicinity that our medical men for some time are not to be found; and the poor sufferer, whoever he may be, has to lie in agony, and perhaps through loss of blood adding weeks to his sickness while thus waiting, not that there is no one willing to help, bat because so few are competent to do so. All thanks is due to the committee of the Viaduct Institute for bringing within reach of all the opportunity of studying the sciences, and surely they might take the initiative in this matter also. All information on the subject can be obtained by applyinz to Captain Perrott, St, John's-gate, Clerkenwell, London, where I believe a complete set of diagrams and necessary apparatus can be borrowed for very little expense. Trusting I have net needlessly trespassed upon the space of your valuable paper, I remain,
A WOULI3.I3E-STUDENT. Earlesiown, March 13, 1884.
THE CHAIRMAN OF THE RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY AND DR. GORNALL.

_ Sir,—ln reply to the usual ignorance displayed by the chairman of the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority, I beg to say :—let. That the majority of the cases removed by my recommendation for the purpose of isolation were in no way associated with pauperism, as any ratepayer can verify by referring to my record kept at the Fever Hospital, which includes patients from Sankey Vicarage, Sankey Station House, and from the residences of two members of the Authority—Rev. G. F. Roberts and Mr. Gibson. 2nd. ibat to associate the isolation and treatment of the infective - 'sick with pauperism is contrary to the well being of the community, and will never, I hope, meet with the approval of the ratepayers or the Local Government Board. 3rd. That if Mr. Derbyshire has no regard for the dead he might display a little more feeling for the living relatives, whose loss has been in no way occasioned by personal inattention to cleanliness (as anyone who has had any acquaintance with them must testify), but is essentially due to the pro- motion of unsanitary surroundings by the neglect of the Rural Authority.—l am, your obedient servant, JOHN H. GORNALL. Penketh Lodge, Warrington, March 13, 1384.
