WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. ADJOURNED MEETING'. The adjourned monthly meeting of the Town Council was held on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and there were as present Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Webster, Kean, Pickmere, Chandley ; Councillors Monks, Barker, Dixon, Mackie, Sutton, Wright, Francomb, Hutchinson, Burgess, Whittle, Bolton; Messrs W H Brook (town clerk), J L Whittle (deputy town clerk), C Chorley (borough treasurer), J H Gornall (medical officer of health), T Longdin (borough surveyor), and J Paterson (gas manager).

div.head: -THE PROPOSED ALTERATIONS AT THE LIBRARY.
div.p: -THE PROPOSED ALTERATIONS AT THE LIBRARY.

Alderman WEBSTER moved the adoption sf the minutes of the Museum, Library, and Arts Committee, and in doing so drew attention to the report on the proposed alterations to the Library, to which, he said, the committee had given their best consideration, and they thought the alterations as pro- posed the best means of giving increased accommodation. Alderman PICKBIEBE : What was the estimate?
Alderman WEBSTER said the estimate had not as yet been prepared, but the alterations would cost about £4OO. Mr Owen was preparaing a detailed estimate.

Alderman CRANDL"Er seconded the motion. Alderman BURGESS remarked upon the, decrease In the number of visitors to the Museum, and also in the number of volumes issued to subscribers. He would be very glad if same satisfactory reason was given for this constantly declining condition of things so far as this department was concerned.

Alderman WEBSTED replied that the decrease meant nothing. Last month there was an increase of 44 per cent.. but Alderman Burgess did not see that—he had not got his spectacles on that night. (Laughter.) The decrease simply meant that 16 per cent. of the people bad less time hanging on their hands than before, and consevently they had not felt it incumbent upon them to visit the Museum. As to the decrease in the number off volumes issued to subscribers he thought fine weather affected that. The most pleasing increase in the institution was in the number of readers. In providing accommodation for readers they knew the institu- tion had actually been of service and was doing the good they intended, and in future the institution itself would reap the beneit of this.

Alderman PICRMERN said the decrease in the number of volumes issued to subscribers was probably accounted far by subscribers going to the reading room to read the books. The minutes were adopted. THR "FOLLY FAIR" AND SWING BOATS.

In proposing the contlrmation of the minutes of the Markets Committee, Alderman CHANDLEY said there was one minute that perhaps called for remark, and that was one in respect to the suggested abolition of fairs. There was a communication from Mr. Beamont on this subject sent to the Mayer which was duly placed before the Markets Com- mittee, but they did not see their way to adopt Mr. Beamont's suggestion. There was no special reason assigned why the fairs should be discontinued, and the committee felt the fair was an old institution, and that the accidents which MT. Beamont alluded to might have hap- pened under any other circumstances independent of the Warrington Fair. Indeed, swing boats—through which the accidents occurred—were already erected in various parts of the town, and the fact of discontinuing the fairs would not have discontinued the causes of the accidents to which Mr. Beamont alluded. Therefore the committee were unani- mously of opinion that it was undesirable to abolish the fairs. Cr. Dixast seconded.
Councillor M4CIEIE asked if the amount given in the minutes—£234 for four weeks—represented a decrease or increase in the revenue from the market.

Alderman CHANDLRY replied that the amount was below the average, but the decrease arose from the fact that cattle fairs were now prohibited, and that caused a discontinuance of many of the sources of income. For instance, the butchers' stalls were not producing so much money now as they did when the fairs were held. Councillor MACKIE said the explanation was very satis- factory. He wanted to make sure that the amount men- tioned was not suggestive of any falling away of the market income, because the income of one of the largest and best 'markets in Lancashire—that of Bolton—according to returns presented to the committee last week, was falling at such a rate that it was about £2,000 a year less now than it was seven years ago, and if there had been anything unsatis- factory or suggestive, he would have recommended the Council to do what the Bolton Town Council was doing, and inquire into it. Alderman PICKMERE thought it would be well if the com- mittee prohibited the erection of swing boats. He was told by the house surgeon of the Infirmary that be had to stay in during fair time because he was always expecting some one who had been hurt by these machines being brought to the institution. The swing boats were exceedingly dangerous, and he thought the committee might have pro- ' hlbited them. The MAYOR observed that that was the mainspring upon which Mr. Beamont addressed to him the letter. Mr. Bea- mont did not wish to sweep the fair away, but to limit it to. three days on the ground of the extreme danger attending those children who were in the habit of indulging in swing boats and those horses propelled by steam. Alderman CIUNDLEY pointed out that it would not in any way reduce the danger by limiting the time of the fair. Swing boats had already been erected on waste land in various parte of the borenz,h. Alderman BURGESS asked whether there was any con- , trolling authority, and whether any man in Warrington could set up his swing boat wherever be thought proper. The Tows CLERIC: No, he cannot. Alderman BURGESS: There is a controlling authority ? The Tows CLERK : Yes. Alderman BURGESS asked where the controlling authority was, because it appeared from what had fallen from the chairman of the Markets Committee that there was a condi- tion of things that they could not reach. The Tows CLERK said the Corporation was the controlling authority, but he did not know that they could stop these boats at all unless they abolished the fairs. He did not know any law to prevent them. The boats did not come within any of the provisions of the local authority or bye.
laws. The controlling power was, the Corporation could charge a rate for the existence of the swings. A MEMBER : That will not make it worth while rating them.
Alderman BURGESS: Charge what fee you like? The TOWN CLERK: No, you can't. You are limited by the Act.

The minutes were then passed. THE LONGFORD DEPOT. Alderman BURGESS proposed the confirmation of the minutes of the Sanitary Committee, and alluded to a minute which said the Borough Surveyor had b,ad referred to him the amended estimate of the works at L4agford. He, how- ever, had not yet reported to the committee, but as soon as he did the Council would be made acquainted with the re- port. Councillor SUTTON seconded the proposition. CouncillorrMONKS regretted that it was his duty to pro- test against the minute respecting the estimate of Messrs. Manlove, Alliott, and Co. He believed he was correct in saying the committee had never authorised any amended estimate to be made, but it was done entirely by the autho- rity of the chairman of the committee. As long as he was on the comtnittee (but he was happy to say he did not think lit would be very long before he was free) he thought it only right that these matters should be done properly and in order by authority of the committee. He did not care to go the length of making an amendment, but simply con- tented himself with entering his protest against the way in which this actiot had been taken.
Councillor RotoN supported the minutes, and said he hoped the committee would persevere and let them have the plans to manipulate the whole of the refuse and so get rid of tho nuisance.

Councillor BARKER had hoped the minutes would be passed without comment, as there was nothing at all in them that called for discussion. Alderman HOLMES concurred with the remarks of Coun- cillor Barker, and observed that he could not see any impro- priety in the action of the chairman or the committee. He did not Commit the committee or Council to any expendi- ture of any sort.

Councillor SUTTON, as a member of the committee, was somewhat surprised at Councillor Monks' observation that the resolution did not emanate from the committee. He thought the chairman would easily be able to explain that and show that the minute was properly passed. It was well known that some extension must take place—(hear, hear)—and therefore he was quite satisfied with the resolution that they should obtain an estimate in order to see what the cost would be. If the cost was according to his judgment a reasonable one and the system was also the best that had been brought before them then he should most decidedly go in for it. Until then he did not see that they could discuss the subject at all. Councillor Fnewcomn said every member of the Council could see that there was an unfortunate split amongst the members of the Sanitary Committee. Manlove, Alliott and Co. sent in a tender, and another gentleman did likewise, but the tender happened to be in favour of a person other than Manlovet Alliott and Co. Since then this Nottingham firm had sent an an amended tender, and some members of I the committee believed that they had had a preference given to them, which was net exactly right. He was not going to say that was correct, still there was a very un- happy difference in the Sanitary Committee, and he be- lieved if the committee could be divided and one.half of them resign—(laughter)—they would have the work at Longford very much better done. (Hear, hear.) He thought it was too bad to come here Council meeting after Council meeting for no other purpose than to cross each other. He was AS satisfied as it was possible for a man to be satisfied that the proper mode of dealing with the refuse of the town was to manufacture it. (Hear, hear.) He also felt satisfied they were not justified in spending a single penny of the ratepayers' money until they could destroy the abominable Oink, that existed at Lengferd, (Hear, hear.) If that could be permaneintlY done thed said the Council would be to blame if they wasted a single minute in putting down machinery to deal with the whole of the refuse of the town. He woltld like to see a sub-committee—,l sort of commission—appoin- ted to deal with the matter. There was not a town on earth where the machinery WAS in such perfect operation as it was at Longford at the present time, and he believed their great fault had been that they had been sadly too precipl- tate in their action. They ought to haVe Waited and gained experience from people who were better able to spend money than themselves. Still they were in the race, and he believed if they could only destroy the smell that was doing so much damage at Orford they would be doing something which would very much tend to lower the rates of Warrington. Councillor HuTaitrwsow asked for a return of the cost of the works, giving the wages of each individual employed; and the amount of material produced during the past twelve months. Alderman HOLMES said all the kiformation except the wages was in the financial statement. Councillor BOLTON asked if the proposed machinery was to re-place the worn out machinery on the old principle. Alderman BURGESS said the estimate of Messrs. Manlove, Alliott and Co. was referred to the Borough Surveyor that he might report to the Council, because if the machinery was adopted by the Council and brought down to Longford there would be an amount of work to be done in fixing the machinery. That report the Borough Surveyor would be prepared to submit to the-cominlttee in about a week. As to Councillor Monks's remarks about this being his individual work, he thought it would be in the memory of every member that at the last meeting there was on the agenda paper a minute accepting the tender of Messrs. Man- love, Alliott, and Co. They had such satisfactory evidend of the improvement in the working of the machinery at Longford that some of the committee had accepted, and it was only because they could see their way to doing some- thing on a less scale that this amended estimate had been asked for. Having acquired information from the working of the machinery in the hands of their present manager, he came to the conclusion—and he thought it was a perfectly justifiable course for him to take having come to that con- clusion—to go over to Nottingham. He saw Mr. Alliott bimself and had a long discussion with him, and he asked Mr. Alliott, after giving him figures as to the quantity of material they would have to deal with, did it meet his view that there could be a limitation of the machinery, leaving future extensions to be made as the time for them came. After going very carefully into the matter, Mr. Alliott said he believed with the information then laid before him they could reduce the quantity of machinery put down and reduce the cost to the same ex- tent and at the same time bring the works into such a con- dition that at every point it could be taken up and extended from that point at any future period. He submitted that to the committee, and said Mr Alliott had engaged to let them have an amended 'plan hi a week. Acting under the advice of the Town Clerk, the minute at the last meeting of the Council was confirmed, with the exception of the one on the avenda paper. That amended estimate came, was laid Wore the committee, and the committee acted upon it to the extent they saw there. The result WAS that Messrs Manlove and Company had reduced their original estimate for the extension by £1,200 for £1,300. The minutes were approved.

div.head: SALARY OF THE CLERIC TO THE JUSTICES.
div.p: THE SALARY OF THE CLERIC TO THE JUSTICES.

Alderman WEBSTER moved the following : "That for the future the ealary of the Clerk to the Justices of the borough shall be readjusted every fifth year, and fixed at the average net amount of fees received during the five years immediately preceding such adjustment, and that, the first readjustment be made up to the 25th March inst." Ile said he brought forward the motion for the purpose of preventing constant misunderstanding when the Clerk to the &totices asked for an advance of his salary. The salary was based upon the fees received at the court. From time to time the fees increased, and the Clerk to the Justices asked for an increase, and this often led to disagreeable discussions, although it was a matter which really was be- yond their power in a sense, because the clerk was not a servant of the Corporation. It was true that 20 or 30 years ago the salary was only £3OO a year, and that represented the amount of fees received; but since then the fees had in- creased and the work proportionately increased. In addition to this there was a large amount of work in connection with drunkenness for which no fees whatever were received; and in many boroughs, in adjusting the salary of the clerk, the fees which should have been paid for that work were in, eluded. But here they were not included, and there was a large amount of work done without any fees whatever, and it became all the more necessary that an adjustment should be made.

Alderman Cllernmaty seconded, and asked whether they were compelled to pay a certain sum to their borough justices' clerk or not? He would further like to ask whether lit was not the law that they should not make a profit out 'of the fees of the borough police court. He had been, and still was, under the impression that they were bound by law to pay the clerk to the borough justices such an amount as was equivalent to the amount of fees. If that were so, they might as well make a virtue of necessity by paying the borough justices' clerk according to the suggestion of Alder- man Webster. Alderman Britons said a little more than 20 years ago be ha 1 occasion to go with the then clerk to the magistrates to the Home Office on' this very question. Mr. Robert Davies was clerk to the magistrates at that time, and there had been a deal of difficulty in refereace to the office in consequence of Mr. Nicholson. The fees wore then in excess of the amount of salary. They saw Mr. Waddington, who was then the permanent sscretary under Sir George Corn- wall Lewis, and this matter was brought before his superior. There was not the slightest difficulty regarding the excess of fees over salary, and the clerk to the magistrates and the magistrates themselves were satisfied it was a proper and satisfactory amount of remuneration. That was a proper solution of the question, and for a length of time he be- lieved the salary remained at £3OO a year, as arranged in that. way. .

Alder-man WEssrult asked whether the amount of Salary had not to be based on the amount of foss received. The TOWN CLERK thought his answer to Alderman Chandley would be an answer to Alderman linrgess also. The salary to he paid to the justices' clerk had to be a tell}, sonable salary, and it had to be recommended by the locd! authority—which was the Corporation in this caso—aiti had to be submitted to the Secretary of State for his approval and also to the magis- trates. They were guided in arriving at that recommendation by the amount of fees received; but it as not to be in accordance with the fees—that was to say, be- cause the fees amounted to so much they were not bound to make the salary so much. If the salary was reasonable and the tees amounted to more than the fees then the fees had
ISVVI -min
to be readjusted. The town could not make any profit from the fees.

Alderman PICKMERE: 13y readjustment of fees, do yes mean that the fees can be reduced ? The TOWN CLERK: Yes. The MAYOR: By permission of the Secretary of Sta'er Councillor FRANCOMB maintained that the discussion was out of order, and after a little conversation Alderman Wansima moved that the standing orders be suspended so that the question could be discussed. Councillor MACKIE SOCOBdtd. Councillor FRANCOMB then said he thought this was a shabby way of bringing under discussion the salary of one official.
A!derman WEIBSTER : That is not the subject of dismis- sion.

Councillor Frealtcomn: Yes, it is. Alderman WEBSTER contended that it was not. Councillor FrtaNcotan then gave way, remarking, hovr- ever, that he did not like the older members of the Council to sit upon them. _

The standing orders were then suspended. Alderman WEB&PER again moved his resolution. Alderman PICKMERE thought something of the kind was required, but he also thought the average of five years was too much, and suggested that it should be fixed at two or three years. Councillor BURGESS thought it would be better to have a fixed salary rather than readjust the salary every fVe Tears.

Councillor MONKS was not pre pared to vote on the mo- tion mainly on the groand that he did not think it right after the question had been settled at a full meeting of the Council that it should become the subject of discussion afterwards during the financial year. Alderman BURGESS could not agree to the re-opening ei the question. After the Council had adopted the resolution they had regarding salaries he thought it was hardly if they took up one special case out of the rejected—(hear hear)—and disposed of it in favour of that one official. Councillor SUTTON spoke in favour of, and Councillor BARKER against the resolution, and after a few words from the MAYOR the motion was lost by 10 votes to 6. right

WANTED, A DELIVERER. Councillor MACKIE moved the following motion which stood in his name:—" That no further expenditure be in- curred in connection with the extensions at Longford depot until a competent person has examined and reported to the Council upon the present machinery and any necessary eE tensions." After remarking upon the very gat absence of that mechanical and that chemical knowledge which be thought alone could render a committee like the Sanitary Committee able to carry out their duties properly, he said he thought they would be only acting wisely and well if they called in some gentleman acquainted with these flew systems of manipulating sewage, and, perhaps, for. £lO er £2O, get him to tell them if they were moving in the right direction or not, and whether the machinery, which was said to be in preparation, he believed, to accomplish wonders, could with any reasonable hope be expected to do so. Councillor HUTCHINSON seconded the motion. Councillor FRANCOMB said when he first saw the motion he thought if ever there was a motion which was not r 5. quired this was the one, for certainly there was nothing be- fore the Council from the Sanitary Committee relating to the expenditure of money. For the last three or four years he had been serving an appi enticeship in sanitary matters, and other members of the Sanitary Committee had done everything in their power to gather information that would be useful to the town, They had a most ditfiCult 'probl era Ito SOIVO-ftSuCh a problem as had never yet been solved, and Councillor Mackie's motion referred. to some one who diat not at present exist. As to cly,!mical knowledge, the cbemis, knew nothing about the matter. It was a different material to what he ever had in his life. As to mechanical know' ledge, it was all theoretic d. They had in Meesre, Alliott? and Co.'s machinery. machinery that WAS at present (.I.olng a lot of geed, and of which they had bad the value. The rumoure amongst the ratepayers wets utterly wrong and misleading, for he believed they were really making profit out of the material manufactured. The only thing that deterred them from proceeding further was that thei wanted to be certain of the success of the experiments the/ were now trying at Longford to reduce the smell. ,Whea, that was done he for one would say, expend the ratepayers money, and, more than that, he would like to invest 'none:" in the concern if It wee Made a private speculation. Councillor MONKS did not agree With VA Motion, because he believed the committee had had the information COO' cillor Mackie sought. Whatever machinery they put bent he believed it would be capable of improvement. The sue' cess arrived at was the result of having a praetical many Longford, and he only regretted now that he did not insist upon an idea he had when the machinery was put &Wag that they should get a man of common sense and trust hill; entirely with the management. They would have hat; those results far sooner if they had done so, and he believe it would have also prevented that difference on the cool' mittee that had unfortunately existed. In separating frail the committee, he said he would be glad to see them achieve the success which he believed could be attained without creating the slightest nuisance to the neigh' bourhood.

_______ Councillor SurroN agreed with the principle laid doile in the motion, but at the same time he did not believe fe having the hands of the committee tied. He believed the resolution was altogether premature, and that the committee was quite competent to effect such changes as were nee! is' nary at Longford without being tied in the manner suggeete' by the motion. Councillor BARKER said he would support the motion if the doctor would find a man to do the work—( hear, hear)":, but neither Councillor Mackie nor Alderman Burgess Wl' find the man. Alderman PICKIIERE believed Councillor Mackie bed brought the motion forward with the best intentions, but hes asked where was the man to be found? (Hear, hear./ If such a man could have been found there was no doubt the committee would have had him long since. (Hear, hear. He thought the committee were doing very well, and the" the Council ought in justice to the committee to allow then to spend a little more money to see if they could not CO I quer the difficult es they had in band. Alderman BURGESS pointed out that they in Warringtoe had spent less money than many other towns in England proportion to the population in carrying out this work' They had spent about £9,000; Rochdale, with a pertir tion not very much larger, had spent its £20,000 ; mingham had spent a huge sum of money, and Manchester a still greater amount. The only town that had spent lese than Warrington (and it came very near them) was the small town of Stafford. .

Councillor DIXON corrected Alderman Burgess saying that the latter town had spent £1,400. The Borough Sur' veyor of Stafford told him so on the previous day. Alderman BunnEss was proceeding with his remarkg when attention was drawn to the fact that there tees zig quorum.
The meeting was therefore abruptly conclueled. During the discussion of Councillor Mackie's motion, the chair was occupied by Alderman Holmes, the Mayor havia Left to fulfil another engagement.

The rumour spread with unusual rapidity, and gave rise to numerous contradictory statements—the foundation for which it was difficult to ascertain. Assertions were even made to the effect that the woman's body had been dragged from the canal, but this has been proved to bl untrue, as the one who was supposed to be dead is etil, alive. TUE MANOIIETER SHIP CANAL BILLS On Tuesday the Manchester Ship Canal Bill was before a 4,,eteet Committee of the House of Lords, the Duke of ssichmond and Gordon presiding. The Bill authorizes the Construction of a canal suitable for the accommodation of vessels of the greatest tonnage, and by means of which such Teasels will be able to reach Manchester. The channel of the Mersey from Garston to Runcorn is to be rendered navi- gable, and will form the means of access to the canal. 41 Runcorn the canal will commence, and it is to be carried a distance of 211 miles to Manchester. The low water chan- r_Vßl is to have a minimum depth of 12 feet, and a maximum 'tenth at spring tides of 40 feet, while the depth of the ,anal is to be 26 feet, or within a few inches of that of the *nes Canal. The estimated cost of the canal works, making the usual allowance of 10 Per cent for contingencies, is £3,920,171; for the works in the estuary of the river Mersey, £1,890,419; for the docks at Manchester and Warrington, £1,121,262; for deviation and railways, £456,172; and for new roads, £16,162; total, £6,904,186. The capital of the company is to be £8,000,000, and newer is taken to borrow on mortgage a further sum of £2,000,000. It is provided under tbe Bill that if at any further time it should be proposed to vest the undertaking in some public body, the company shall not Meet such a scheme with opposition. The scheme was in- troduced into Parliament last year, and after having nar- rowly escaped shipwreck on Standing Orders, it was passed by a Select Committee of the H01.19e of Commons; but after full discussion before a Committee of the Upper House. it was rejected by them in the mouth of August last. The present Bill differs but immate" llv from the project originally presented to lastParliamentac anarn;lbut it contains powers with regard to the low water 1883 scheme was divested bypetthiteSsteaagn,ilin h Standing w the Bill, Committee. There were twenty. six ion but of these, appearances were only entered in respect of eight, including the London and North-Westera Railway Company, the Corporations df Liverpool and Birkenhead, the Mersey and Irwell 'Navigation Commissioners, and the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board. Mr. Pember, Q.C. (with whom were Mr. Michael, Q C., Mr. Balfour Browne, Mr Cripps, Mr. Mash, and Mr. Sington) opened the case for the promoters. He referred to the proceedings in Par- liament last year, and traced out the history of the scheme. Having explained to the committee the proposals of the 411, the learned counsel expatiated on the advantages which would accrue to the trade of Lancashire by the adop- tion and execution of the project. He drew the attention of the Committee to the widespread satisfaction and approval with which the scheme had been received. In conclusion Pember dealt with the allegations of the various peti- tioners against the Bill. On the conclusion of the learned counsel's address the Committee adjourned. On Wednesday counsel for the promoters dealt with the Petitions against the scheme, and then called the first wit- ness, Mr. Daniel Adamson, chairman of the Canal Commit- tee. In the course of his evidence Mr. Adamson said a Manchester merchant had told him, and would tell the Select Committee, that be paid more for the conveyance of Piece goods between Manchester and Liverpool than between Liverpool and Bombay. The witness went into detail on the question of the rates of carriage and the charges at Liverpool, and expressed the opinion that the total direct Saving effected in the cotton trade alone by the construc- tion of the canal would be over half a million sterling per

annum.-- Mr. Adamson was again tinder examination on Thursday. U e said if the bill was not passel "there would possibly be bloodshed in the district concerned." The advantages of the scheme were so thoroughly appreciated in Lancashire that there would be no difficulty in raising the whole of the capital in this county. The amount of this year's subsea-Ip, lions up to a fortnight ago was £25,000 or £26,000. The leading manufacturers, merchants, and capitaligs in the district. wer supporting the, scheme thii year nor"., than ever before. Mr. Reuben Spencer, of Rylands & Son, Limited, was afterwards examined in support of the bill.

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 1 , Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (March 13th) : Though money has been tending towards ease some little time, it was not till the reduction in the bank rate to-day that any effect on prices was noticeable, but on its announcement figures and tone improved, though quotably the beneficial chance is as yet not remarkable. The publication of traffic returns for home lines yesterday had little or no effect on the market as a whole, the reports of earnings preseating nothing of importanae to make a movement general. The London and North-Western return had a depressing effect on their stock, however. Foreign funds have not moved to any extent during the week with the exception of Egyptians, which owing to statements as to the prolongation of the stay of the British forces, have gone distinctly higher in all issues, the 'Unified being li to 2, ditto Preference 2, and ditto Dairsi Sameh better. The following also are higher :—Spanish f. Argentine Hard Dollar I, and Russians whilst Italians and Peruvians are quarter each lower. Mexican Railway Stock has. as usual, jumped about pretty wildly, and the balance of movement on the week is about 2i per cent. The traffic return shows a decrease of £6,200, but this was looked upon as not dbe.ppwint- log, and did not influence prices much. Miscellaneous classes of investments total a moderate number of transactions. The changes of quotations viewed in series are contradictory, but on the whole there appears a slight balance in favour of advances.

Mr. Justice Chitty, on Saturday, ordereid r. Grueber, a solicitor, of Crosby Square, to be struck off the rolls for frauds. STEALING BEEF AT ST. HELENS.—George Hart, an elderly man, was on Thursday charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having stolen a piece of beef, valued at 2s, the property of John Leyland, butcher, Claughton-stree t. The prisoner is an assistant butcher, and was engaged on the previous day at Leyland's slaughter-house in Barrow- street. He cut the piece of beef from the carcase of a cow, and prosecutor afterwards missing it followed the prisoner to a public-house in the town, and found he had the beef in hie possession. Prisoner had been previously convicted, and was sent to gaol for one month. SUMMAR ACCIDENT AT Sr. HELENS.—An accident of a somewhat singular nature occurred at Eccleston, near St. Helens, by which a man named John Liptrot lost a thumb and three fingers. Mr. Liptrot had' been examining a car- tridge, given to him by a miner, in hiswatehmaker's shop at the rear of his dwelling-house, when it exploded and blew off the fingers mentioned. It is stated that he had been told that the cartridge would not go off unless struck with a hammer, but it appeared he had only been scratching it with a pin when it went off. The injured man was removed to the cottage hospital, where he is. we understand, pro- gressing favourably. Admiral Sir Sydney C. Dacres, 0-.C.8., died on Saturday, at Brighton, aged 80 years. The deceased was brother of Sir R. Dacres, Constable of the Tower of London. Wcarzte's QUARREL AT EARLESTOWN.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, Margaret Leveson was sum- moned by Mary Shimmin for using threatening langua.te to her on the 4th Instant.—lt was stated by the complAnant and her witnesses that the parties had,a few words together, In the course of which the defendant threatened to " white- wash " the complainant's house with her blood.—The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six mouths. STAER-BOWRETT BUILDING SOCIETY, Sr. HELENS.—The Inaugural meeting of the Third St. Helens (636th) Starr- Bowkett Building Society was held on Monday evening, in the Assembly-room of the Fleece Hotel, Church-street, St. Helens. The chair was occupied by Dr. McNicoll, and there was a very large attendance. A lecture was given by Mr. J. Barcroft, of Ramsbottom (Mr. R. B. Starr's agent), on the "Rules, working, and advantages of the Starr- Bowkett Societies," in which the lecturer in an able and in- exhaustive manner pointed out the benefits which accrued to a member of one of these societies. div.p: LIBERAL LEGIURE AT RUNCORN. MR. JAMES ..TOMKINSON ON IRELAND. Tee third of a series of lectures in connection with the Iltancern Liberal Association seas delivered in Bethesda schoolroom, on Monde), evening, by Mr. James Tomkinson, the Liberal candidate for West Cheehire. 'roe subject of leeture, Ireland," attracted a large and enthusiastic audience, Mr, Torakinson receiving a gratifying reception. bk. Robert Shaw, the president of the Aesociation, occupied She chair, and on the platform were Messrs. James Handley, LP., S. C. Beckett, T. Handley, B. Kniveton, and Oliver Leak (agent) The ClEtaintran, in introducing the lecturer, delivered a speech in which be dwelt upon the benefit to be derived from such lectures as they bad recently had the advantage of hearing ea Runcorn, and said there could be nothing of Kteater importance then that the working men in a town *lke Runcorn should be able to form correct (mildew of various political,suestions. The subject of teat evening's lecture ougbt to be of considerable interest to every man. Ireland had occupied the attention of this country for a considerable time, and the present Liberal Government had passed an act which he was sure none of those who were acquainted with its provisions were afraid to look into. They believed Ireland had got such a Land Act as no coun- try in the world besides had got.. (Applause.) They were confident that is the long run the people of Ireland would be satisfied and benefited when the provisions of the Act were universally understood and fully accepted. Many of those present could remember when time after time the benevolent of England were appealed to to feed the starving poor of Ireland by charitable means, and this was a proof that something was wrong somewhere. (Ilear, hear.) When the working population of any country could not obtain sufficient to keep them at all times from starvation it was a proof that legislation waseiquired so that those who earned their breed by the sweat of their brow should by their labeler be able to supply the wants of them- selves and faisilieL - (Applause.) It bad been stated that all the mischief to which he had referred was caused by the hie rents and by the landlords taking the money they re- ce ved out of the country, and spending it in England or on the Continent. Consequently, when every few years a bad harvest occurred, the people were reduced to destitution and starvation. The speaker then described the Lend Act in- troduced and passed by Mr. Gladstone, and said every in- telligent !nen who looked at the quesden from a fair stand- point must admit that that Act coerely did justice to Ireland; and that in the end the fruits of that legislation would work lasting good. (Applause.) Referring to the Franchise Bill, Mr. Shaw said he thought they would all come to the conclusion that it was quite time that all Acts of Parliament should cover the whole of Great Britain. (Applause.) It would have been a great injustice to enfranchise the people of this country, and allowed a sore to exist in Ireland that would have been constantly coming to the front, and they would have been told and rightly told that whilst extending I the franchise of the boroughs to the counties of England they had overlooked the Irish people. He thought these facts showed conclusively that they had got a government desirous of doing equal justice to all the subjects under its sway. (Applause.) Mr. Tomnierson, who was warmly :received, then pro- ceeded with his lecture. In order to understand the Irish land question properly, he said, it was necessary to look back upon Ireland's history. In Henry time and Elizabeth's time, and throughout the 17th century, the his- tory of Ireland was practically one of war, confiscation, penal laws, and ruined manufactures. By those cruel, devastating ware in which whoever were the conquerors the peopie suffered, the country was reduced to the most abject state of prostration, famine, disease, and every kind of evil. From time to time the population, headed by some of the original Irish proprietors, rose in arms and acted with all the ferocity cf a population brutalised by the cruel system under which they had lived, in the endeavour to get back their lands. But these risings were invariably put down in a most cruel and relentless manner. Martial law was in- discriminately exercised, and English soldiers throughout the country wreaked their vengeance on innocent and guilty alike. In the 17th century twelve million acres of land out of twenty millions in Ireland were confiscated—the land was taken from the inhabitants, who were driven out to make room for British settlers. in the year 1654 there was a wholesale forcible transplantation of population from the other provinces into the barren province of Connaught under the penalty of death and it was no un- common thing to see a man hanging by the roadside, with a placard on his breast bearing the warning "Hanged for refusing to transplant." But conquest and confiscation were what every country had at some time or other to go through. In time both were forgotten; conquerers and con- quered mixed together; they became allied, and in process of time one people as a whole. This would probably have been the case in Ireland, but the conquerers tried to exter- minate and abolish the Catholic religion—the national religion of the country by cruel penal laws. Under these hive Catholic bishops existed only by connivance; Catholic worship was subj cted to the most humiliating restrictions; the profession of Catholic faith excluded a man from every form of political and municipal power, from any of the learned professiona except medicine, and from almost every means of acquiring wealth, knowledge, dignity, or influ- ence ; subjected a man to unjust taxation, deprived him of the right of bequeathing his property or managing his family as he wished; enabled any Protestant who had a grudge against him to harass hint by a thousand vexations and annoyances, and reduced him to a condition of practical serfdom. What wonder was it that the evictions and the coniscations of the land were not forgotten, and that wounds were not healed when they were so probed by-a set of such cruel and infernal laws ? (Applause.) The com- merce and the manufactures Of Ireland were cruelly and ruthlessly crushed by unjust legislation, and consequently the people were thrown upon the soil as their sole and cnly mode of subsistence. It wauld have been naturally thought that the people so situated would have been in some measure protected in the prosecution of their industry, but instead of that they were left at the mercy of the landlords—good, bad, or indifferent, as the case might be—to rack rent them just as they might choose, and rob them of their property in the soil to their heart's content.: On this subject t. would read to them the testimony of Primate Boulter, given in the 18th century. He was Primate frcm 1724 to 1733, and he reported that there was great distress from want of tillage ; that emigration was going on very largely owing tre desperatim and destitution; that the emigration was chiefle of Protestants; and that it erose from the laying down by landlords of land into pas- ture, and for what purpose did they think? In order to avoid the tithe. The fact was that tithe was levied almost entirely upon tillage, and in order to avoid that landlords were far and wide laying their property down into grass, thereby throwing the whole burden upon the little left in tillage. The Primate also reported starvation consequent upon bad seasons and rack rents, wholesale evictions of men in favour of cattle, " BO that in some of the finest counties, in some cases there is neither house nor cornfield to be seen ix 10 or 15 miles travelling." The tenant right arose chiefly from the system by which farms were re-claimed from the waste by the tenants. The tenants reclaimed the land, per- haps drained it, fenced their fields made their roads, and erected their houses, however humble they might be, and carried out all those other innumerable improvements which constituted the tenant's property in the soil, of which it was altogether unjust to deprive him by being turned out of his holding without compensation, or by having his rent raised upon him. (Applause.) As to the condition of Ireland in 125, he quoted the result of the experience of Sir Walter Scott, who visited Ireland in that year. Sir Walter Scott was certainly no Liberal, much less a Radical, and he so id that his heart was sickened by the widespread manifesta- tions of the wanton and reckless profligacy of human mis- management and the tyrannous selfishness of absenteeism; at the contrast between the naked clamorous beggars, swarming like vermin and appearing to spring out of the ground at every turn, and the boundless luxury and merri- ment surrounding the thinly-scattered magnates wh °condescended to inhabit their ancestral seats. In 1934 rack renting was terribly prevalent in Ireland, and cotter farmers promised to pay rents which they never could pay out of the produce of the Soil. Mr. Inglis, a gentleman who had travelled throughout Europe, and written some valuable works on the different state of the various countries, visited Ireland. and he said that these rents were merely the outbidding of desperate circumstances, and that the chief cause of such a state of things were the necessities of the Irish landlords resulting from their idle- ness, extravagance'' and love of ostentation. This was 50 years ago, and be (the lecturer) would remind the audience that flak was a sufficient answer to the people who said now that the sub-commissioners were reducing rents which had not been touched, much less raised, for 50 years. (Applause.) The population of Ireland was now five millions; 50 years ago it was nearly eight millions. There was greater competition for land then than now, and there ,eaa more cruel rack renting. Therefore to say that the oak-Commissioners were wrong in reducing rents which had not been raised for 50 years was entirely beside the mark. (Applause.) After briefly noticing the Emancipation Act , wrung from an unwilling House of Lords when Ireland was on the verge of revolution, he then alluded to the tithe war. The tithe was collected for the support of the Protestant Church, clergy which did not represent one-fifth of the country. used to send into the fields and take the tenth sheaf and the tenth of the produce, and they could imagine nothing more insultingtfortehlie ioßoman Catholics, who hated o and detested that form n, than to have the cart of the Protestant clergy taking away one-tenth of their produce. (Applause.) Eventually the day came when the people rose up in righteous indignation against such a system,o,and the tithe could not be collected. Troops were ilt the point of the bayonet £14,000 worth of tithes weraendcoalt- lected at a cost of £50,000. (Laughter and applause.) The chief points in- the history of Ireland lead- ing up to the Land Act of Mr Gladstone were briefly touched upon by the lecturer. He shortly sketched that Act, and said they did not claim I that it was absolutely perfect, but on the whole they claimed it was a just and beneficient measure. (Applause.) lie dwelt upon the various clauses of the Bill, particularly drawing attention to the fixing ef a fair rent in case of dis- pute between landlord or tenant by an independent courts, Had the Land Act not been passed he firmly believed that the Irish tenants would have joined together to resist in a bold and united front the payment of rent altogether. (Applause.) Some people had said that if such an Act was given to Ireland the Came protection ought to be given to the tenant farmers in England. But the conditions were totally dissimilar. Estates managed en the English system —those upon which the improvements bed been made and ma.intained by the landlord—were exempted from the pro- violets of the Act. - • must not think that he did not agree to ti+.
