div.p: last session was only a very small instalment of what was due to them, and be contended that the farmer ought to be put in a position of security to prosecute his industry to the best of his ability. (Applause.) The Liberal party and the great mass of the English people had at last determined that full justice should be done to Irelaud. They would say frankly to their Irish brethren, "We confess we have not treated you justly, and that we have shown for you little of that sympathy which ia so necessary to endear one nation with another. It is useless to dwell upon the bitter memories of the past, let us look forward to a brighter future. We show our sympathy by extending frankly and fully the same franchise and privi- leges which we are extending to the householders in Eng- land, gcotland, and Wales." (Loud applause.); There was no concealing the fact that the Tories viewed with shrinking the extension of the suffrage to Ireland. The mental atti- tude of the Tory party to Ireland was one of profound dis- trust, and a desire to rule Ireland as a conquered country, and to keep it down by the point of .the bayonet. The Eng- lish Liberal party said they would have nothing of the sort. (Applause.) They were determined that the sixty miles of water which divided them from Ireland should no more make her a foreign country than the sixty yards of the river Dee which divided Wales from them. They were determined to maintain the union, but they were equally detervained that the union should not be only a name, but that the union between them should be one in deed and in truth. (Applause.) In cocci union Mr. Tomkinson moved the following resolution:— 'The Liberals of Runcorn rejoice in the introduction of a bill for the extension of the Franchise; and hereby express their opinion in publ:c meeting th it such a measure entitles Mr. Gladstone's Government to the increased confidence of the country. They hope that the ministry will employ every legitimate means to ensure the bill being made law daring the present session of Parliament. They also request that a copy of this resolution be signed by the chairman and forwarded to the Prime Minister." _

Mr. B. KNIVETON seconded the resolution, observing that there were two great reforms looming in the near future. One was the land question of England and the other was the drink traffic. (Applause.) They might depend upon it that when these two great questions were settled the pros- perity of England would be largelyaugumented, (Applause.) He for one did not anticipate any great increase in the happiness of the people until these two measures were ac- complished. (Applause.) I The resolution was carried with enthusiasm. ' On the proposition of Mr. JAMES HANDLEY, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer. ' Mr. S. C. I.fEcKETr rn -ved, ant Mr. T. HANDLEY Seconded, a vote of thanks to the Caairman which was heartily carried. In replying, the CHAIRMAN drew attention to the in- creased political power which would be held by the people after the passing of the County Franchise Bill, and said that every Liberal in Runcorn could become a member of the Liberal Association by the payment of is. per annum. He would be entitled to attend the meetings of the association, and could take part in the election of officers and other busi- ness. He hoped as many as could would join the associa- tion, give them the benefit of their advice, and agitate with them for the remedying of abuses, so that England might be happy and free because justice reigned throughout. (Applause.) When Mr. Tomkinsoa had left the building, and just before he entered the conveyance which was waiting to con- vey him to the railway station, he was intercepted by Mr. T. Harty, an official of the customs at Runcorn. As an Irishman Mr. Harty tendered, on behalf of his compatriots in the town, his warmest thanks to Mr. Tomkinson for his able lecture that night, and the eloquent manner in which he had spoken of the wrongs of Ireland. Mr. Tomkinson appeared ranch gratified at this tribute, and shook Mr. Harty cordially by the hand. .

div.head: HANGMAN AT HILTON.
div.p: THE HANGMAN AT HILTON.
BINNS INTERVIEWED.

In fulfilment of a promise to visit Halton, made some time ago, Bartholomew Binns, the public executioner, is at present the guest of Mr. Field, the landlord of the Norton Arms, Halton, who is a personal friend, hailing from the neiehbourhood of Dewsbury, where Binn'eresides. Binns ' arrived at Halton on Wednesday afternoon, and it need hardly be stated that when his presence became known the public-house was beseiged with customers more anxious to see and speak with the hangman than to swallow beer and spirits. The notoriety which belongs to his dread office Binns seems to enjoy very much, and he enters freely into conversation with any person to whom he is introduced, upon his method of hanging, and various other matters con- nected with his craft. This loquaciousness stands the land- lord in good stead, who, whilst his distinguished guest is talking to his visitors, drives a roaring trade. With a Yorkshire eye to the main chance Binns had supplied the , landlord with several pounds of tobacco suede up into ounce packets, each packet bearing his name and address, and these , were quickly purchased as souvenirs of the occasion. I On Thuraday evening our representative and two other I gentlemen of the Press paid a visit to the Norton Arms Hotel intent upon an interview with the now renowned Bar- tholomew . Upon their arrival Binns was in the cellar en- gaged in the interesting occupation of "tapping" two bar- rels of beer, andathey were informed that on the previous I evening he had been the chief executioner of a couple of well fed pigs. They were shown by the landlord into a comfortably-furnished room, but a quarter of an hour elapied and the object of their visit had not made his appearance. It then transpired that Sinus regards members of the re- porting profession as dangerous persons, to be avoided on all I possible occasions, and in whose presence silence is golden. I At length, however, he was prevailed upon to submit to an I interview, and he entered the room in a shuffling gait, and his hands clasped in front of his body. He is a raw-boned, hard-featured, gaunt-looking Yorkshireman, of about fifty years of age, stands about five feet ten inches high, and has a peculiar stoop from the shoulders that gives him a most awkward appearance. Judging from his face he is a mild tempered, cool-headed, calculating fellow, with very little I ferocity in his composition, but during the conversation I that took place he remarked with considerable unction that• Ihe executed his first men in less than half a minute. Con- verse with the reporters with any degree of freedom he would not, but under the soothing influences of several "small lemonade's" and a couple of cigars, he unburdened his mind a little with regard to the execution of Mac Lean at Kirkdale last Monday. In broad Yorkshire dialect he denied emphatically that he was drunk on arriving at Kirk- dale gaol on Saturday afternoon, and with some show of reason asked where he could get drunk when he left Dews- bury at 10-35 a.m. and travelled on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway via Sewerby Bridge, Burnley, Blackburn, and Preston, and arrived at the gaol at two o'clock. A member of the company suggested that perhaps the rapid travelling of , the train had made him nervous—a joke that caused Binns I to laugh heartily. He acknowledged that he had had a I glass of beer, but there was no reason why he should not have one, and had Major L.ggett been there himself, al- though he was a "blue ribboner," he would have drank the same beverage. Was it likely that he would have gone to I the gaol if he had been drunk? he inquired. Marwood never ' went to the gaol until a few hours before the time fixed for the execution; nor was he (Blum) compelled to do so, but he reported himself on Saturday afternoon in order to show that some insinutions made against him on a previous occa- sion could not be repeated, and that the officials might see that he was all right. Of his treatment in the goal he complained very strongly. He alleged that he was placed in a long wide corridor, where the air was so cold that he became benumbed; and worn out with his vigils at his wife's bedside during the previous week, he fell asleep. At seven o'clock he was suddenly awakened by someone shaking him by the shoulders, and jumping to his feet, be exclaimed "Who the are you shaking ?" Discovering that he was in the presence of Major Leggett, the governor of the gaol, he apologised for the expression he bad used. To this Incident pinns azeribcs some of the feeling that Major Leggett exhibited against him. How he came to use such an expression, Binns ingeniously explains in this way. During part of the journey from Dewsbury there occupied the compartment with him a man who persisted in placing his feet on the cushion, and once or twice be rubbed them against Binns's knees. Irritated at this, Binns swore at the man, and when he was awakened by Major Leggett he was under the impression that he was still in the railway train and used the expres- sion he had spoken to the man who had annoyed him. Binns also found fault with the sleeping accommodation provided for him. As he was not out of the gaol from two o'clock on Saturday until ten o'clock on Monday morning it followed that he could not be in otherwise than a fit state to conduct the execution. Speak- ing of the drop be gave APLean, he stated that from the in- formation he had, he calculated that a drop of nine feet six inches would be sufficient, but when he saw the youth a quarter of an hour before the execution, he came to the con- clusion that an increase of eight inches was desirable, and, without informing anyone of his intention, he altered his, apparatus accordingly. Since his appointment he had con- ducted eleven executions, and he had given complete satis- faction at every place except Kirkdale, where he could do nothing right for the officials. No restrictions were placed upon Calcraft or Marwood as to the length or thickness of the ropes they used, but his ropes were either too short or too long, according to Major Leggett. With a grim smile he said he had never had to pull a man by the legs to bang him and never would. He seemed highly amused at the gaol authorities sending for Heath, and asked what use he was without tools. "I'd a watched him Ira tackin my black bag," he added. Speaking of his mode of adjusting the knot, Binns said he had seen every part of the human frame, from childhood up to manhood, dissected, and he was acquainted with the most effective way of securing speedy death. His system he considered by far the best, and he hinted that he should continue to follow it. Just Previous to the departure of his interviewers Binns com- menced to speak of his character and ability. From the sheriff in all the counties where he had officiated except Kirkdale he could obtain a testimonial of his fitness for the ghastly office, and the directors of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, whose servant he had been, would give him a good character. During the 24 years he had worked on the railway he had not missed a day's work. fie added with some pride that he went through the Indian Mutiny as a private soldier in Prince Albert's Own Light In- fantry, and was at the battles of Cawnpore Lucknoiv, and Delhi, while at the conclusion of the rebellion be volun- teered to go to the south-west frontier. For two years be was in New York in the service of the American Govern- ment, and he hinted that he bad not travelled about the world in this way, and was stilt unable to hold his own against the Liverpool gaol officials. We understand that , Blum stays in the neighbourhood for several

PRESENTATION TO MR. B. BROWN OF WIDNES. On Thursday evening Mr. Benjamin Brown was the re- cipent of a present from the members of the Young Men's Bib'e Class of Lacey-street Sunday School, which he has taught for the last 16 years. •Previous to the presentation ceremony a tea, to which about 60 persons sat down, was provided. Subsequently the Rev. H. Harper, circuit su- perintendent, took the chair, and in making the presents- tation, said he entertained for Mr. Brown's feelings a sincere respect, and greatly admired his personal character, fie was what might be termed an all round man— a man who ' could superintend a Sunday School, teach a young men's class,lead a society class, conduct a prayer meeting, till the most important office in the church, and in all these capa- cities render invaluable help. The testimonial that he had the honour to present was a beautiful piece of art; it was an address fit to adorn any drawingroom, and ha laved Mr. Brown might long be spared to look at it and to labour for God and His church. (Applause.) The address, which was beautifully illuminated and en- closed in a gold frame, read as follows:—" Wesleyan Sun- day School, Lacey-street, Widnes. To Benjamin Brown, Esq. We, the members of the Young Men's Bible Class in connection with the above institution, beg to congratulate our late teacher, Benjamin Brown, Esq., on his promotion to the position of superintendent of the Lacey-street Sunday School, and to say that, while we deeply regret his removal from us as our teacher, we cannot but feel that his established piety, superior intelligence, and his kind and genial disposition, eminently fit him for the office, and that the committee in conferring this honour upon bins is I very properly recognising his long and faithful service. We also wish to express unitedly and personally our highest appreciation of his Christian character, our sincere thanks I for all his kindness and for the deep interest he has ever manifested in our welfare, and we most earnestly pray thati 'his efforts as our teacher may be crowned with success, and that God will continue to grant unto him all needful wis- dom, patience, and peace, and abundantly bless and prosper him in the performance of Ms new duties." (Then follow the names of 37 members of the class). The Rev. J. flothersall and Mr. Powlson, who succeeds I Mr. Brown as the teacher of the young men's class, delivered short speeches; and the testimonial was heartily supported by Messrs. E. Martley, J. Duxbury, J. Dean, G. Davies, and F. Rawlinson. Mr. BROWN, in responding, said he scarcely knew how to thank them for the kind things that had beep spoken of him. He mi4ht say that his father was a local preacher for GO years, and his mother was a class leader for many years. It was more than 30 years since he (the speaker) .gava his heart to God, and though there had been many shortcom- ings, to God he ascribed all praise for what he was, and for what little good he had been able to accomplish. (Heir, hear.) He bad been engaged in Sunday school work for 35 years—all his life he might say—and he remembered when he came to Widnes 18 years ago, he spent a portion of his first Sunday in the Sunday school. (Applause.) From that time to the present, with the exception of two years when he was superintendent, he had been the teacher of the Young Men's Class, and he had met with much encourage- ment. lie thanked them heartily for their testimonial, which he could assure them would be highly prized, (Ap- plause.) A miscellaneous entertainment brought tilt proceedings to a close.

A WOMAN FOUND DEAD AT WARRINGTON. Shortly after seven o'clock on Wednesday evening the body of a woman was found lying on the four-foot on the Iron Bridge, at Warrington, on the Cheshire side, under circumstances which point to the conclusion that she was run over and killed by a train, as she had received severe injuries to the bead and back. The name of the deceased was Margaret Skinners, and she was the wife of a private in the Liverpool Regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks, but who is now at Fleetwood. She was thirty years of age. The body was removed to the Norton Arms to await an inquest. An inquiry into the circumstances of the death was held at the Norton Arms Hotel, yesterday afternoon, when evi- dence to the following effect was given.—John Skinners, 2nd Liverpool Regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks hus- band of the deceased, said that he last saw his wife about a fortnight ago, when ha left her to go on duty at Fleetwood. She was then in good health and spirits. The deceased had never shown suicidal symptoms, and they had lived happily together. He had not the least reason to think that she would destroy herself.—Sarah Brereton, living at the Or- ford Barracks, mother of the deceased, said that on Wed- nesday the deceased left the Barracks alone shortly before four o'clock to go to the market to make some purchases. She never appeared in better health and spirits. Witness heard of her death about 9.30. Deceased was near her con- finement, but confinemenl did not with her bring on suicidal tendencies. A comrade of the husband of the deceased was going away by train that evening, and possibly she might have gone to the station to see him off, and thus got on the railway.—Richard Edwards, porter at Arpley Station, said that on Wednesday afternoon he saw the de- ceased on the station platform about seven o'clock. She had a little dog with her, and a basket on her arm.—Job Thompson, guard in the employ of the London and North- Western Railway Company, said that on Wednesday even- ing he was in charge of the 7-15 train from Manchester to Warrington. When leaving off duty witness went across the line, when his attention was arrested by the barking of a dog on the iron bridge on the Cheshire side. The dog sprang eat at him, and he then noticed something lying in the four foot. He went back to the station to stop any trains that might be due, got lights and assistance, and then they found the dead body of the de- ceased. The dog guarded the body and would not let anyone go near it to touch it.—A Juryman remarked that he thought that great credit was due to this witness for having gone back to the station to stop the trains, and the Coroner agreed in that opinion.—In summing up, the Coroner remarked that they had it in evidence that the de- ceased had never exhibited suicidal tendencies, and, there- fore, he thought that the only verdict that they could come to would be an open one, to the effect that the deceased was found dead on the railway, near Arpley, there being no evidence to show how she got there, or how she met with her death.
THE LATE FATAL ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON. THE ADJOURNED INQUEST. .. . _.

The adjourned inquest en the body of Mrs. Hall, who died from injuries received by being knocked down by a horse and cart in Sankey-street, on the 23rd ult., under circum- stances thatdlave already been made public, was held before the Coroner, Mr. Brighouse, at the White Hart Hotel, War- rington, on Monday last.—Mr. Hall, son of the deceased, who again attended to watch the case for the relatives, asked the Coroner if he adhered to his resolve expressed at the first enquiry not to let him question the witnesses ?—The Coroner replied that he adhered to that decision, but would allow Mr. Hall to put questions through him.—Mr. Hall: That I must abide by. I say that this matter cannot rest here.—The Coroner: Do you mean that as a threat P—Mr. Hall: Oh, no.—The Coroner: No threat on your part, nor anything amounting to a threat, or that has the semblance or the smattering of a threat, will deter me from doing that which I think my duty as Coroner for the Hundred of West Derby.—Mr. Hall said that some feeing had been created at Warrington, and the matter would not rest where it was. A decision would be taken as to the legality of the ruling of the Coroner.—The Coroner said that Mr. Hall could take any course he thought fit. The only person who had any power over him was the Lord Chancellor. As a matter of fact that court took precedence over the magistrates' court and county court, and was equal in its power and jurisdiction to the High Court of Justice. Ile had onerous duties to perform, but no threat, either by persons present or by the press, would deter him from doing what he thought was right. If Mr. Hall and others interested in the subject thought fit to ap- proach the Lord Chancellor, he, for one, should be pleased. —A plan of the junction of Sankey and Parker-streets, where the accident occurred, was put in, and Dr. Richmond, house surgeon at the Infirmary, gave evidence touching the injuries received by the deceased. Evidence was also given by several witnesses who saw the accident, who were ques- tioned by Mr. Hall.—Kean, the young man who was driving the pony and cart, was called into the room, and after being cautioned, made a statement to the effect that if Mrs. Hall had net turned back to the footpath there would have been no accident. Instead of going forward or remaining where she was she turned blck, and was knocked down by the off. shoulder of the pony. He was not driving above seven miles an hour.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," adding the opinion that there had been a certain amount of carelessness in the driving.—Kean was then called into the room and censured by the Coroner for his negligence.—At the close of the proceedings Mr. Davies, solicitor, who appeared on behalf of the driver, thanked the Cormier for his remarks in reference to the witnesses being examined by professional men only.

TIE EXANTINVII, SATURDAY, MARGIT 15 1884 • \ (MISS ANNIE HALL WOOD'S CONCERT LATEST NEWS• AT WARRINGTON. I Miss Hallwood closes her series of concerts for the pre. THE SOUP sent season with an unequivocal success. One of the largest and, we should think, best paying audiences ever assembled THE Gr) in the Public Hall was gathered there on Monday evening. And though, as to the main feature of the entertainment, the A telen- attraction must have been chiefly in expectancy, we need —Tb' se have no hesitation in saying that all reasonable anticipa- tions were more than realised. The speciality was, of course, the first appearance in the town of the popular tenor, Mr. Joseph Maas. And in makiag his deind before a War- rington audience we venture to think this gentleman will have no fault to find with the nature of his reception- The utmost enthusiasm was manifested in regard to his singing, and, when we mention that in the programme his name ap- peared four times, and that he responded to three encores it will beat once seen that while the greatest exactions were made by the audience in the exuberance of their method of demonstrating approval, these were no less bounti- fully conceded. We confess to a feeling of agreeable surprise at the unexpected treat which Mr. Maas's singing afforded us. Certainly his interpretation of the test songs—for such they may be considered-40 which we listened removed almost entirely from our mind any predisposition to think his treatment of them inadequate. Undoubtedly Mr. Maas was in splendid voice. The degree of animation as well as of feeling shown throughout his efforts seemed to point to the existence of the happy conditions forcibly expressed in the phrase "good form.' Mr. Maas' strength certainly lies rather in the beauty of his 'voice than the keenness of his artistic perception. Probably now at its best, this voice is both smooth anel sweet in quality, and is manifestly pro- duced with ease and in considerable volume. We scarcely know which of the songs to admire most. "The Message" was, perhaps, richest in variety of feeling, but as showing to advantage his exceptional vocal powers, "When other lips " and " Good night, beloved" were better examples. Suffice it, however, that each'and all were performances of a high order, and that this fact was suitably recognised. There can be no doubt that Mr Maas's early reappearance in the town will be eagerly looked for. The remaining ar- tistes were not less successful in providing a solid back- atoned to the concert. The names comprising Mr Lea's , popular coneert company are already known as favourites with Warrington audiences. It may be noted that both Miss Annie Hallwood and Madame Laura Smart sustained their reputation. To the singing of the first-named lady we have on recent occasions referred pretty fully. Judged, as we suppose we may yet judge it, in the light of amateurity, it doubt- less presents many points of promise. A marked style or, rather, an individuality, is yet the main thing to be acquired. And while the materials are still plastic this process of training is so important in its ultimate bearings that it should be entered upon only under the guidance of an eminent virtuoso. None of the pieces chosen by Miss Hallwood showed to the best advantage such good qualities as she in reality possesses. But despite these criticisms Miss Halltrood gained encores In both "The children's home " and Hee subsequent duet "Home to our mountains" (Il Trovatore), is which Mr. Maas ehr34 with her the bantam, Madame Laura mart Sang 21 With verdure clad with couscießtlous regard for the theme. In this as in "Lo ! here the gentle lark " (Bishop) her vocalisation was both painstaking and effective. Mr. Henry Broadley gave "'he Sullote war song" with all the robustness and spirit which, written as it is in the tempo de Bolero, it peculiarly admits of. Some elever part-songs were tastefully rendered by the company and added mach to the enjoyment ; and Mr. Cantor, the painstaking and accomplished conductor, gave in an in- imitable and supremely droll manner two comic songs. Many of the pianoforte accompaniments were enriched and the effect greatly enhanced by the addition of suitable and well played parts for violin and ante. These were in the hands of Mons. F. Hartung and Mr. Vincent L. Needham respectively, who singly also contributed each a solo on his particular instrument. Mr. Needham, as a flautist, pos- sesses much of the command of technique noticeable in the performances of his collaborateur Mr, De Jong, and the clever fantasia on "Italian Airs:" gave him opportunity for fully displaying that mellowness of tone and delicious power of warbling which so charmingly characterises the playing of both. The violinist is a vivacious foreigner whose chic was early ap- parent in the solo "Ziegeuner Weisen " (Sarasate). But after here displaying his brilliant executive powers Mons. Hartung would have done well to have curtailed the exhi- bition of extending arpeggios playing which in the encore degenerated, in the eyes of the audience, into the merest burlesque by reason of the length to which it was carried, Otherwise the effort was a clever attempt at producing on the violin, simultaneously and unassisted, both the melody and harmony of Haydn's "Hymn to the Emperor."
THE SOUDAN REVOLT. THE GREAT BATTLE. 4,300 ARABS, SLAIN.

A telegram from Souakim, dated Friday, 1-15 p.m., says: —The British loss in yesterday morning's battle has been ascertained up to the present to be 100 killed and 150 wounded. 4,300 of the enemy were killed and several thou- sand wounded. The villages of Hanoi, Tarnav, and Tama- nieh have been destroyed by fire. All the regiments are now rapidly returning to Souakim. Osman Digma has fled to the hills.

div.head: CRUEL WIFE DESERTER AT WARRINGTON. HOW _THE RATEPAYERS' MONEY GOES.
div.p: A CRUEL WIFE DESERTER AT WARRINGTON. HOW _THE RATEPAYERS' MONEY GOES.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, before Alderman Davies and Mr. J. Fairclough, Samuel Brandwood, a file cutter, was brought up in custody on a charge of absconding in December, 1881, and leaving his two children chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union. Mr. Sutton, clerk to the Guardians, prosecuted, and Mr. Brown defended.—Mr. Sutton, in his opening statement, said that it would be impossible to imagine a worse case than the one he had to put before them. The prisoner and his wife were married when young, and, unfortunately, it was one of those cases where the hus- band lived upon the earnings of his wife. He appeared to have lived In comparative ease and comfort until children were born, when the wife could not earn as much money as before. The husband then took himself away, and in con- sequence two of his children became chargeable to the Union, the cost of the chargeability amounting to over .£3O The prisoner was arrested in Sheffield, where it waapreved, be had been earning gccid wages. He had been living with another woman at Sheffield.—Mr. Brown said that the pri- soner did not know that his children had become chargeable until nine months afterwards, and as there were then two warrants out for his apprehension, be was afraid to return. —Mr. Sutton submitted that the prisoner, having been away so long, was liable for the chargeability, whether be knew his children had become chargeable or not.—Wit- nesses having been called to prove the chargeability, prisoner was committed to bard labour for two months.— He was then charged with assaulting and beating his wife, Sophia Brandwood, at Warrington, on the sth September, 1881.—Mr. Davies prosecuted, and described the prisoner's conduct to his wife as a course of constant ill-treatment, his assaults upon her occurring over and over again and being so severe that be actually got a bread knife and held it at her throat. He also took her by the throat when in bed and I pressed her down, said that he would kill her and that "he would swing for her." On the date in question she was nursing her baby in the house when the prisoner came in and asked her for 9d, with which to buy a pigeon. She re- fused to give him the money and he immediately struck her a violent blow on the face, knocked her down on to the floor, blacked her eye, kicked her, and bruised her from top to toe. He then brandished a poker over his head and ran upstairs in pursuit of his little boy, who was al frightened that he actually jumped from the window on to a roof be- low. The wife was compelled to go to her mother's house for proteetion.—Mr. Brown admitted that the prisoner gave his wife" a back hand tap on the nose "—(laughter)—but said that be was aggravated by his wife. The Bench de- cided that the assault had ben a very aggravated one, and committed the prisoner to four months' hard labour, to take place at the expiration of the first sentence. They also made a separate order of maintenance fixing the sum to be paid by the prisoner to his wife at us per weak.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

Tminsnev.—Before W. Wynne Ffoulkes, Esq., Judge. BANKRUPTCY CASK AT WARRINGTON.—James Rowley, a grocer, of Warrington, appeared to undergo his public examination as a bankrupt before Mr. Ffottlkes, Judge.— Mr. Ridgway was the official receiver in the case, Mr. Davies represented the debtor, and Mr. Yearsley appeared for Mr. Mynykyne, one of the principal creditors.—Mr. Ridgway put a question to his Honour as to whether Mr. Davies had his costs paid out of the estate.—His Honour ruled that it was not provided in the statute to allow a debtor's solicitor to be paid, except by the debtor himself.—The defendant was then examined with regard to the financial position of his affairs, and denied that he allowed any furniture to be taken off his premises since he knew that he was insolvent. Several creditors who were in court put questions to the debtor with regard to his property and to his business as a grocer; in reply, he said that he had only been makinit about 30s. a week. He was an uneducated man and had not known exactly how he stood with regard to his creditor and debtor account.—The examination was adjourned. RIVAL BROTHERS AT WARRINGTON. A farmer named James Fisher, sued his brother, John Fisher, also a farmer, for the sum of £lO, alleged to be due under the following circumstances. The action was brought inlrespect to monies expended in repairing a reaping and mowing machine, the property of the defendant, under an agreement made between the two. In September, 1882, there was a sale of farm stock at the Slate House Farm, near Warrington, and the parties to the action attended it, both of them purchasing sundry articles. The plaintiff purchased a reaping and mowing machine which the defendant was desirous of having, as it was more suitable for his work than his own. He therefore agreed to exchange machines. The plaintiff saw that his brother's machine was out of re- pair, and said that he would have it repaired before the ex- change was made, the cost to be charged to the defendant. To this the latter agreed, and left his machine with the plaintiff to repair, taking the one he had exchanged it for with him. The plaintiff had it repaired, and the amount seed for was the price that he paid for tnat being done. A sum of money had been paid into court, which the defence alleged was all that was due—namely, the price of putting in new shafts, and not making general repairs. Before hav- ing the machine repaired, however,The'plaintiff wrote to his brother saying that the cost would be more than he had ex- pected, and would cost at least £lO, to which he received no reply. The defence was a complete denial of the agreement having been that the machine should be "repaired ;" it was to be " re-shafted." Several witnesses having been called on either side, His Honour, in giving judgment, said that it was a rather sad thing to see two brothers come into court and confront each other upon a matter like this transaction. One would have hoped that they would have amicably settled it out of cont. It was not exActly what one liked to see on the part of two brothers, but if they could not decide between themselves it was his duty to do It for them. It was quite clear that One was speaking the truth and that the other was not, and he could not escape putting a very unpleasant construction on the evidence of one or the other. After considering the evidence, and taking due notice of the fact that the defendant, upon re- ceiving the letter apprising him of what was likely to be i the cost, did not reply to t, but burned it instead, he came to the conclusion that the plaintiff had made out his case, and gave judgment for him accordingly with costs.

PRESCOT CHURCH OF ENOLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. —The meeting of this society, which was held on Monday evening last, was unusually attractive, and there was -a very large attendance. The Hey. H. A. Macnaghten pre- sided, and during the evening introduced Mr. Holme, of Liverpool, who gave a very interesting address, from which the young people might learn many useful lessons. A good programme had been provided, the chief feature in it being a dialogue, entitled, " Muddles at home make hus- bands roam," which was very well rendered by the follow- ing —Misses J. Taylor, M. J. Saggerson, M. AlCowherd, M Evans, Sophia Case, and Messrs. W. Woods, W. Baron, J. Seftm, S. Ames, and E. Taylor. Mr. Dickinson, of Prescot, also gave three recitations with good effect. The meeting was closed by the rev, chairman in the usual way, after which several pledges were taken.

div.head: OS MAN DIG MA STILL DANGEROUS.
div.p: OS MAN DIG MA STILL DANGEROUS.

The Central News correspondent telegraphing at 6-30 yesterday morning says " Osman was defeated but not routed." The rebels retired in good order and with great coolness. It is quite possible that Osman may again open fire upon our camp, but it is generally believed in military circles that when the rebels realise their losses they will desist from further attack.

The misleading telegrams from Souakim which were cir- culated only on Thursday morning have caused consider- able annoyance in official and military quarters. It will be remembered that the first of the despatches referred to was timed 10-5 a.m., and stated that Osman Digma had already been completely routed. As a matter of fact at that moment the state of affairs at the front may be described as almost critical, the terrific rush of the enemy having just caused our men to fall back, leaving the Gatlings and Gard- ners behind them. At noon when the second of these misleading telegrams was despatched from Souakim the battle had not yet practically concluded, and had raged without intermission since about half-past eight. Never- theless the telegram referred to gravely set forth that the " battle only lasted half an hour," and that "the British loss was only two killed." The Home authorities take it for granted thit these highly-coloured despatches were simply exaggerated versions of the small skirmish which took place at daybreak. Indeed they could have had no other foundation, for nothing of the battle was known or could have been known at Souakim until the Central News correspondent galloped into camp at 1-40 p.m. Egyptian time,with General Graham's despatches, with which he had been entrusted.

The Central News learns that the War Office yesterday received a telegram from General Graham despatched from Souakim in the afternoon stating that Sheikh Mahomed Ally has expressed opinions that when the news of Osman Digma's defeat becomes generally known amongst the tribes they will disperse and that the road to Berber will be thrown open. The War Office again telegraphed this evening to General Graham asking Tor lists of killed and wounded.

div.head: DYNAMITE OUTRAGES.
div.p: THE DYNAMITE OUTRAGES.

The St. James's Gazette understands that Mr. Jenkin- son, Under Secretary for Crime in Ireland, has been trans- ferred from Dublin to the Home Office, the Government desiring to have his services in forming a spacial detective body in London intended to deal generally with the farces of revelation and political crime, and particularly with the nurces of the various dynamite outrages.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAI, DILL,
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAI, DILL,

The Select House ei Lords Commlttee upon this Bill re.. sumed their inquiry yesterday morning, the members pre- sent being the Duke of Richmond (presiding), the Earl of Dunraven, Viscount Barrington, Lord Lovat, and Lard Norton. It was announced at the outset that the Rochdale Canal Company had withdrawn their petition on the under- standing that clauses for their protection would be inserted in the Bill.

Mr. Walmsley, cotton Spinner and manufacturer, Stock- port, and ex-Mayor of the borough, was examined, and gave strong elide-ma in support of the Bill. He complained warmly of the high transit rates between Stockport and Liverpool, especially with regard to cotton; and he men- tioned that the rate per ton had risen from 53 in 1851 to 108 fid at the present time. By the high charges great in- jury had been done to Manchester and to Lane Wake (espe- cially by 'Elia); and he showed that between 1875 and 1881 the exports of Surat cotton to Italy had increased by as much as 130 per coot., to Germany 517 per cent., and to Belgium 757 per cant., while the exports to the United Kingdom had decreased by 50 per cent. English exports of cotton yarns had also fallen from 28 million tons in 1880 to 19 million tons in 1882. For all these disadvantages the only remedy was reduced rates, and he believed that would be effected by the Ship Canal.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Pope, Mr. Wahnsley said he bought chiefly at Liverpool, as that suited his re- quirements better than ordering direct, for he needed special kinds of cotton, and could there see the samples for himself. He was not prepared to say whether the canal would enable spinners to do away with middlemen or brokers; but it suited his convenience to employ a broker in Liverpool. He had wharves on the canal, but that WAS no advantage, because the canal and railway could combine to keep up the same price.

Replying to an ob-sarvation by the Chairman, Mr Pember, for the promoters, pointed out that even if there was nothing in the bill to prevent the canal combining with other com- panies that would be limited by the bill to a maximum toll of 4s 3d.

IMr. James Timothy Bradbury, managing director for Messrs. John Henry Oarside and Co., cotton spinners and manufacturets, Ashton-under-Lyne, was also examined. He stated that he was chairman of the Association of Master Spinners for the Ashton district, and after giving statistics as to the consumption of cotton by the mills in the district, he expressed the conviction that taking the limits fixed in the bill the construction of the canal would effect a saving of Bs. 61. per ton from Liverpool to Manchester. That would mean a saving to his oe n company of £1,300 a year, and to all the mills in that district of at least £30,000 a year. Other advantages would result from hay- ing the cotton market at Manchester, one of which would be that the selling broker would no longer be required. Three fourths of the whole cotton industry of the United Kingdom woutd benefit by the canal.--In explanation to Mr. Asoinall the witness admitted that in buying cotton at Liverpool, where he generally purchased, he employed a broker; but be maintained that if the cotton were taken direct to Man- chester, merchants would be able to sell for themselves. That practice, he added, was rapidly growing; and he also said he believed there were many buildings in Manchester which could be used as cotton warehouses.

Mr. J. C. FIELDER, manager to Messrs. Ogden and Co., grey cloth agents and merchants, Manchester, who was hon. sec. to the Cotton Famine Relief Fund for Blackburn, on being examined, said the chronic depression in Lanca- shire for the last seven years had had most disastrous results upon the producers, and that the best authorities had estimated the loss of capital in the catton trade in 1877-79 at £20,000,000, and the loss had been added to since. He anticipated great results from the canal, not only in redac- tion of transit charges, but in the development of other in- dustries in Lancashire and a creation of ship building on the banks.—Two other witnesses were examined, and the committee adjourned to Monday.

THE ACTION AGAINST MR. BaAnraucni.—Mr. Bradlaugh acting under the advice of counsel, has pleaded not guilty by statute to each count of the Attorney-ileneral's informa- tion for having sat and voted on February 11. MUNIFICENCE OF THE DUKE OF NORTHUMBERLAND.— The Newcastle Journal announces that the Duke of Northumberland has subscribed £B,OOO towards the Bishop of Newcastle's fund for new churches. ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT BY A WIGAN COUNCILLOR.— Our Wigan correspondent telegraphs that a warrant has been issued for the arrest of Mr. John Yates Mawson, of Wigan, head of the firm of Mawson and Co., sharebrokers and accountants, on a charge of embezzlement. It is rumoured that Mr. Mawson has gone to Spain. Mr. Mawson has been secretary for several local societies and companies, and a member of the Wigan Town Council. His defalcations are said to amount to several thousand pounds. NAVY ESTIMITES.—The navy estimates for 1884-5 are issued. The total sum required is £10,811,770, being a net decrease on the previous year of £87,830. There is an increase of £35,500 for seamen and marines' wages, and of £52,000 for naval stores. The principal decrease is £69,700 for victuals and clothing. Among the other increases are £6,300 for the admiralty office; £12,200- for dockyards, and £19,300 for now works and buildings. There is a decrease under the head of machinery and ships built by contract of .12,600, and of £29,700 for miscellaneous services. A PRESBYTERIAN DISPITTE.—At Bury County Court, yesterday, the judge gave decision respecting the action of Stead and others v. Dixon for recovery of possession of the old Dundee School, Ramsbottom. Thera has been a split in the congregation at the Presbyterian chapel. Large num- bers of the congregation left and took possession of the Dundee school. The Judge decided in favour of the defen- dant, who represents the separatists, on the ground that no trustees were in existence to claim the school.

SHEEP WORRYING IN CHESHIRE : CLE'rEIZ CAPIVRE.— The ravages caused among valuable flocks of sheep in Ches- hire by dogs has been very heavy. Last week a number of sheep were killed near Peckfarton Castle. This week marauding dogs attacked flocks near Malpas. On Wednes- day night Mr. Brassey, Egerton Hall, had three valuable ewes horribly mangled. On Thursday night Mr. Brassey set a trap and yesterday morning the delinquent was found securely fastened by the leg, the animal, strangely enough, being a large sheep dog.

div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARIJAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS:

-- -- The Greek Marriages and City of London Brokers' Bills were read a second time.—The Earl of DALHOUSIE pro,. mised on behalf of the Government to consider the desira- bility of appointing a permanent hangman by the Home Secretary instead of by the Sheriffs. He hoped that the recent scandal would not be repeated.—The House adjourned at 5-25. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

- - GENERAL GRAHAM'S INSTRLICTIONS.—Lord HARLINGTON, replying to Mr. Labouchere, said the instructions given to General Graham had not been altered in any material degree. He could not 'state them in detail until he received fuller information from General Graham. Only one tele- gram, mil that a very short one, had been received from General Graham that afternoon. It stated that certain Sbeihs were becoming peaceful, as the news of Osman's defeat was spreading, and the Berber road would become clear in about ten days. He (14:4 Hartington) had

since asked for further details, and a list of killed and wounded. TEE BANKRUPTCY Ac-r.—lhe ArronbtEr-GENERAL, replying to Viscount Folkestone, said there was nothing in the Bankruptcy Act to prevent receivers from acting as election agents. Doing so would not bring them within the Corrupt Practices Act. PRIVATE BILL LEGISLATION.-011 the motion to go into Committee ef Supply, Mr. SELLAIt called attention to the present system of private Bill legislation in Parliament, and pointed out the necessity of some change as regarded the expense being made. In the last 10 years the total sum spent in private Bill legislation in the two Houses amounted to no less than £6,700,000. He moved a resolution stating that while the House adhered. to the resolution of March, 22, 1872, private Bill legislation called for the attention of earliament, and [required reform. The House, while, maintaining the ultimate control of Parliament over private Bills' was of opinion that a tribunal to take the place of pri- vate Bill committees should be created, which should in- yestigate the facts and deal with the evidence relating to private bills, and, so far as possible, in the locality affected by such Bills, whether •in England, Scotland, or Ireland, report thereon to Parliament —Mr. H. DAVEY seconded the resolution.—Sir J. KENNAWAY deprecated the House losing control of private bill committees.—Mr. BAXTER warmly Supported the resolution, and said that. the expense now at- tending private bill legislation was disgraceful to them as a nation.—Sir J. Mownnes took an objection to the resolu- tion, and Mr. LAING, while admitting that private bill legis- lation was not perfect, strongly objected to bills being treated by a body similar to the Railway Commission. He thought that it was a subject which ought to be left to the Government to deal with.—Sir E. COLEBROOK considered that it would be highly dangerous for the House to part with its power over private bill legislation.— The discussion was continued by Mr. Gregory. Lord Lym- ington, Mr. Dodds, and Mr. Pulestone.—Mr. DLCK PEDDLE supported the motion and said public opinion in Scotland was strongly in favour of a change in the present system.— Mr. Donsox said reform of private bill legislation to be successful must be undertaken by the Government. As that could not be done this session he should vote for going into Committee of Supply.—The resolution was nega- tived.

ABERYSTWITS COLLEGE.-Mr. RENDEL called attention to the present condition of Aberystwith College and pointed out the necessity of State aid being at once given to that institution. He strongly insisted that the college having, notwithstanding the report of the departmental committee, been left out of the scheme for higher education in Wales, great injury would result to the cause of education in the Principality, and discouragement to/a great portion of the people, unless measures were taken to place the colleges In respect of State recognition and support on an equal foot- ing with the colleges at Cardiff and Bangor.—Sir R. Cox- MUM supported the appeal made to the Government. ILEFT SITTING.)

div.head: PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY,
div.p: PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY,
LIMITED.

As usual, the Chai—rm-a-n-o-f-tl-Te- Prudential Assurance Company, Limited, had a very gratifying statement to make in moving the eliv.,ption Of the 03th anwaal report gratoteit tl rl "annual general meeting of the company held last week. Though the operations of the company are already of every widespread character, its business still goes on in- creasing, thus affording additional evidence of the high position the company holds in the public estimation. The funds of the company during the year 1883 had been in- creased by £759,818, the total assets being thus increased to £3,807,217; and it is most satisfactory to note that while this increase in the business hatl taken place there had been a continued reduCtion in the rate of expenditure hi V)th branches of the business. In the ordinary branch the new business for the past year consisted of 9,504 policies, assu- ring the 9am of £1,166,392, and producing a new antlnal income of no less a sum than £46,959. The claims of the year amounted to £86,075, representing 526 deaths and 21 endowment assurances matured. The annual premium in- come at the end of the year was £200,790, being an increase of £35,841 over the year 1582; and the rata of expenditure in this branch slightly exceeded ten per cent on the premium income. In the industrial branch the premiums actually received during the year amounted to £2,504,307 14s 2d, as com- pared with £2,126,022 3s lid in the previous year. The claims of the year were £912,333, the total expenses of the brittle), as compared with those of 1882, showing a reduc- tion in the rate of expenditure of 2-1 per cent on the pre- mium income. The development of the business in the in- dustrial branch the chairman referred to as wonderful, and remarked that there really appeared to be no limit to the amount of bueiness which might be done by this branch. The company have latterly afforded every facility to these who suffered their policies to lapse to come back if they could, and as showing the magnitude of the undertaking we may mention that the postages of these letters alone last year amounted to £6,000. Owing to the extensive opera- tions of the society the board of directors are naturally un- able to keep a strict watch upon the action and conduct of every individual agent and representative but it is satisfac- tory to learn that the Prudential have adopted a system by which any agent who, through undue zeal, runs the risk of compromising the reputation of the company in addition to his own prospects of advancement, will inevitably be brougkt to book. It is also, we may add, the aim of the Board to that nothing but good and safe insurances are effec- ted, and with such an aim before them there is every reason to believe the success of the Company will be not less remarkable in the future than it has been in the past.
CONSECRATION SERVICE AT ST. ALBANS', WARRINGTON.

, -------- - - - - - On Sunday evening last a most interesting ceremony took place at the above church, when some thirty new members were added to the already flourishing Confrater- nity of the Children of Mary. At 6-30 p.m. a procession of some 150 members of the Children of Mary, headed by a cross-bearer, left the sacristy and walked two and two around the church to the Lady-altar, which was specially reserved for them, the aspirants singing as they proceeded, the hymn, "Oh, take me to Thy Sacred Heart." At the close of Vespers, the Rev. Bernard Sanders, 0.5.8., of St. Mary's, Liverpool, addressed the confraternity and the aspirants on the meaning and the origin of the name " Children of Mary," taking his text from Ecclesiasticus, "He that made me rested In my Tabernacle." The reverend preacher founded his discourse on the teaching of St. Thomas, who said that true devotion to Our Lady (devotio a devodendo) must be voluntary, faithful, and lasting, and that the real test of solid devotion was the like- ness and imitation of the prototype. To secure this like- ness and imitation the preacher then exhorted his hearers to give him their attention while he sketched the chief points in Mary's life, which made her so pleasing to Almighty God and which earned for her that highest and most sublime of all titles which a creature of God could possibly covet, namely, the title "fall of grace," by which she became the worthy tabernacle even of theaSon of God. As Mary occupied herself in love of God, and contempla- tion of God, so he exhorted them her children to live in union with God by constant prayer and mediation before God's altar. Again the preacher reminded them that Mary's consent was necessary for the Incarna- tion, so in a sense, their consent was necessary for the rules and obligations of this confraternity, but especially their free consent was necessary for Our Blessed Lord to come and dwell with them month by month in the most Holy Communion df the Altar, in which they received Him into their soul, body, divinity, and all. Lastly, he exhorted them to persevere to the end of their lives, honouring Mary in their homes, in their work, in their choice of companions, and in holy practices by which they acquire the real merits of a Christian Catholic life, which have to be the ground- work of their glory, according to St. Thomas, who says : " The accumulated merits of each individual soul lights up into their Beatific Glory." While the hymn "Immaculate" was sung by the whole congregation, the newly-received aspirants were consecrated by Father Feeney, their chap- lain, assisted by the Rev. Father Furniss, and the whole ceremony concluded with the usual solemn benediction.

TEE POWER OF TWOPERCE.—ZoEDONE has hitherto been a monopoly of the rich; but thanks to the enterprise of CAM- MACK AND Co. It Is now within the reach of everyone who has Twopence In his pocket !—Advt. MR. F. MACCAER AT ST. ERLENS.—On Wednesday evening Mr. F. Maccabe gave his well-known entertain- ment, "Begone Dull Care," in the Assembly Room, Town Hall, St. Helens. There was a large attendance. Mr. John Noble, the secretary of the London and Coun- ties Liberal Union, has issued a circular on behalf of the Executive Committee of that body, urging that it is the duty of every Liberal Association and club "to offer an earnest and hearty support" to the Government in their efforts to pass the Reform Bill during the present session. Wherever public meetings may be held the Union, if desired, will arrange to send deputations. CHIMNEY FIRING AT EARLKSTOWN. At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last, Henry Wheeler, of Fades- town, was charged with having the chimney of his dwelling. house on fire on the 23rd February.—The defendant's wife stated that the chimney was set on fire accidentally.—A fine of 35 ed, including costs, was imposed.—William Wil- liamson of Newton, was summoned for having the chimney of his dwelling-house on fire on the 22nd silt, and was finad a like amount as in the last case. TEMPERANCE SERMON AT TES CO-OPERATIVE MILL— IE connection ui,ll the Earlestown Gospel Temperance Mission, Mr. Morris Jones, of Liverpool. preached a special Temperance Mission in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Suuday evening last. There was a large congregation, who attentively listened to the interesting address. Mr. Jones selected as his text the words "Wash yen, make you clean; put away the evil that is amongst you." After an explanstion of the text, the preacher went on to say that the words were applicable to the condition of England at the present time. He referred to the crime, misery, and degradation that were caused through the drink traffic, adding that it was robbing the Sunday schools and churches of their scholars and members. He pointed out the great and pressing necessity of removing the evil, and appealed to all present to do what they could towards that end.

div.head: Xeittro to the editor.
div.p: Xeittro to the editor.

- ACCIDENT HOSPITAL FOR RUNCORN. Sir,—Seeing in your valuable paper that steps are agato about to be taken with the view of providing an accident hospital must be ray excuse for troubling you with a few remarks. First: If we are to 'have a hospital let it be erected somewhere in the very centre of the town, and not in such a position as our Infectious Hospital. Second: Let the funds be found by the works and other large employers of hands, and by hospital Saturday and Sunday collections—not by the shopkeepers, whose employes rarely, if ever, meet with a serious accident. Third: Let a properly qu aided and thoroughly experienced medical gentleman be appointed to attend to accidents. Fourth: Hospital or no hospital—it is a disgrace that in a town like this there is not a stretcher to be obtained in case of accident. You will soared), credit it, but it is a fact, that men meeting with an accident down at the docks are actually brought to the doctor in a wheel- barrow.—Yours, &c., T. CLWYAFIO WILLIAMS. 34, Rutland-street, Runcorn, 13th March, 1884.

THE WIREDRAWERS' STRIKE. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me space in your valuable paper to draw attention to a matter in connection with the wiredrawers' strike. I see there are bills distributed in the town announcing a football match between Warrington (Ist team) V. Wireworkers of district,on the foothill ground, Wilderspool Cattseway ; admission threepence each." And I am likewise informed that there is a general collection going en in the town, all for the benefit of the wiredrawer!. Now, sir, I wish to ask the promoters of this match and collection if they have taken it into their consideration that ' there are labourers who have been thrown out of work through the strike, and who have nothing to fall back upon I think they have a right to appeal to the generfma sympathy of the public as well as the wiredrawers. They cannot stand by and starve while this strike is going on, not know- , ing when it will end. I hope, therefore,. the tradespeople of the town who contribute to this fund will insist on the society doing something for the poor labourers —I am, eirr A LOVER OF FAIR PLAY. Warrington, March 14th, 1854.

RUNCORN ' IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. At a duly convened meeting of the Runcorn Improve- ment Commissioners, held in the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, Runcorn, on Wednesday, the sth day of March; 1884, at two o'clock in the afternoon, it was unanimously resolved •• That the Commissioners present a PETITION IN PARLIAMENT 'against a Bill intituled 'A Bill to authorize the construction of a Ship Canal to Manchester and for other purpose through ths Law Clerk, and that the costs of and consequent upan such Petition be charged upon the Funds of the Commissioners, and that the Parliamentary and Legal Committee be em- powered to confer with the Law C erk during the pr..,gress of the Petition, and to take any measures they may deem need- ful to protect the interests of the district." W. BROOKES, Secretary. Town Hall, Runcorn, March sth, 18.84. • IFT ALF-HOLIDAY MOVEMENT IN RUNCORN. The Public are hereby informed that the Trades engaged in the following businesses in Runcorn have agreed to CLOSE their Establishments EVERY THURSDAY at One o'clock, commencing March 20th :—Drapers. Bookseller and Stationers, Boot and shoemakers and °loggers Hosiers and Hatters, Clothiers and Tabors, Pawnbrokers, Hair Dressers. N.B.—The Shop l will remain open on the Thursdays im- mediately before Good Friday and Whit-Sunday.

PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED, HOLBORN BARS, LoEaciot.-Thirty-fitth annual report, for the year ending 81st December, 1883. The directors have much pleasure in presenting their report and accounts for the year 1883. The reduction in the rate of expenditure in both branches has been continued uring the year. The funds of the Company have been increased during the year by the sum of £759,818, in the Ordinary Branch £126,255, and in the:lndustrial Branch £633,563, raising the t 'tat assets of the Company to £3,807,217. It will be seen that the Investmen's of the year have been eonfined to the usual first-class securities. ORDINARY BRANCH. The New Business of this Branch for the year consists of 0,504 Policies, assuring the sum of £1,166,392 and producing a New Annual Premium income of £46,959. The claims of the year amount to £86,075, representing 526 Deaths and 21 Endowment Assurances matured. The Annual Premium Income at the end of the year is £200.790, being an increase of £35,841 oveLthe year 1882. The Inerease for 1832 was £22,216, making a total increase in the Premium Income for the first two years of the Quinquennium of £58,057. The rate of expenditurs of the Branch slighly exceeds Ten per cent on the Premium Income. INDUSTRIAL BRANCH. The Premiums actualiv received during the year in this Branch are 22.504,30714 s 28 at compared with the sum of £2,126,022 3s lid rinelved during 1882. being an increase of Premium Receipts of 14378,285 lOs 3d. The I.,crease for 1883 was £276,527 5s 6d, making a total increase in the Premium Receipts for the first two years of the Quinquennium of £854,812 15s 9d. The Claims of the year amount to 1,912,333. The total expenses of this Branch, as compared with those of the previous year, show a reduction in the rate of expendi- ture of Two and a half per cent, on the Premium Income. The Directors have thought it advisable to make a further addition to their number, and they have invited Dr. ROBERT " BAINES, of Harley-street. one of the original Shareholders at the Company, to a seat at the Board. Dr. BAMNEa's election will be submitted to the Meeting for confirmation, The vacancy in the Auditorship has been filled by the ap- pointment of Mr. TAMILAS WEARRIE, of Glasgow. a duly qualified Shareholder.
